questions.short_title: Bauxite Casualties and Safe Carriage in Bulk
questions.text_verbatim: Several casualties have been reported involving ships carrying Bauxite as cargo. Discuss the causes of such casualties and the specific care and action be taken, taking into account the provisions of relevant IMO instruments, when handling and carrying bauxite in bulk.

blocks.h: 1. What bauxite is, and why it was treated as safe

blocks.p: Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium and one of the largest dry bulk trades in the world. For most of the life of the IMSBC Code it was listed as a Group C cargo. The Code defines that group precisely: Group C consists of cargoes which are neither liable to liquefy (Group A) nor to possess chemical hazards (Group B). The practical consequence is the important one, and it is what the answer should open on: a Group C cargo has no transportable moisture limit. No TML means no moisture certificate, no moisture limit, and no lawful basis on which a master could refuse the cargo for being wet.

blocks.h: 2. The casualty that forced the reassessment

blocks.p: The reassessment was forced by casualty, and principally by one. On 2 January 2015 the 10-year-old Bahamas-flag Supramax bulk carrier Bulk Jupiter was lost with 18 of her 19 crew, carrying bauxite. The cargo had been declared as Group C, and IMO recorded that the loss may have been caused by liquefaction of the cargo. The characteristic of the casualty was its speed - the ship was lost so rapidly that there was almost no opportunity to respond.
That single loss exposed a structural gap rather than a single failure. The cargo had been carried in accordance with its schedule, and the schedule was wrong.

blocks.h: 3. The mechanism - dynamic separation

blocks.p: The research that followed established that bauxite's moisture hazard is not classic liquefaction, and that distinction is the heart of this question. The Code now states the two mechanisms side by side in the BAUXITE FINES schedule itself.

ul: Classic liquefaction - the cargo mass loses its internal shear strength under vibration, impaction or ship's motion and behaves as a liquid. The whole body flows; water and solids move together. In the resulting viscous fluid state the cargo may flow to one side with a roll and not completely return, so each roll worsens the list.

Dynamic separation - the schedule's words are that the cargo may suffer instability due to moisture content resulting in dynamic separation and formation of a liquid slurry (water and fine solids) above the solid material, resulting in a free surface effect which may significantly affect the ship's stability. The cargo compacts from underneath, moisture migrates upward, and the ship acquires a free surface where the stability calculation assumed a solid, trimmed cargo.

blocks.p: Two further Code provisions explain why the danger is hard to see. Section 7.2.3 records that some cargoes are susceptible to moisture migration and may develop a dangerous wet base even where the average moisture content is less than the TML, so that although the surface may appear dry, undetected liquefaction may take place. And because a slurry lies on top and moves out of phase with the ship's roll period, the ship develops an atypical motion - a wobble - which is the one warning sign a watchkeeper can actually detect.

The schedule also gives the discharge condition for the hazard: the cargo is not liable to undergo dynamic separation when it is shipped below its TML. Keeping moisture below the limit is therefore not a precaution among others - it is the control.

blocks.h: 4. The regulatory response, in sequence

blocks.p: The sequence matters, because the interim measures have been overtaken and must not be quoted as current requirements.

ul: CCC.1/Circ.2, 20 October 2015 - issued within months of the loss as an interim awareness measure, carrying an indicative moisture limit of 10%.
The Global Bauxite Working Group then researched the material's behaviour and established that bauxite presents a risk caused by moisture and that some bauxite cargoes should be treated as Group A.

CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1, 20 September 2017 - supersedes the 2015 circular. The 10% indicative limit does not survive into Rev.1 and is not a requirement. CCC 4 finalized the TML test procedure for bauxite, the new Group A schedule and the amended Group C schedule.
Amendment 05-19, adopted by resolution MSC.462(101) on 13 June 2019, brought all of it into the Code and entered into force on 1 January 2021.

blocks.h: 5. What governs at this sitting, and which schedule applies

blocks.p: The IMSBC Code is mandatory under SOLAS chapters VI and VII. The edition that governs carriage today is the Code as amended by amendment 05-19 - mandatory since 1 January 2021. State the amendment position precisely, because there is a second amendment in the system and it is not yet law:

ul: Amendment 06-21, resolution MSC.500(105), adopted 28 April 2022. It is deemed accepted on 1 June 2023 and enters into force on 1 December 2023. It is therefore ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE.

The same resolution agrees that Contracting Governments may apply it, in whole or in part, on a voluntary basis from 1 January 2023 - so it may lawfully be applied by a loading State, but it cannot yet be demanded as a requirement.
The distinction to write down is adopted, accepted, in force. They are three different things, and a compliance answer that treats them as one is wrong.

blocks.p: Bauxite carries two individual schedules, and everything else follows from which one the consignment falls into:

rows: Either 30% or less of fine particles under 1 mm (D30 >= 1 mm), or 40% or less of particles under 2.5 mm (D40 >= 2.5 mm), or both
BOTH more than 30% of particles under 1 mm AND more than 40% under 2.5 mm
TML applies. May liquefy and may undergo dynamic separation

blocks.p: There is one further route worth knowing, because an examiner may press on it. A cargo that meets the fines criterion may nevertheless be carried as Group C under the BAUXITE schedule where the shipper provides the master with a certificate, based on a test approved by the competent authority of the port of loading, stating that the moisture freely drains from the cargo so that the degree of saturation is not liable to reach 70%. That is a documented, authority-approved escape - not a commercial assurance.

The governing principle for the ship should be stated explicitly: the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its individual schedule govern - never the commodity name. "Bauxite" on a fixture note is not a classification. The schedule's own physical properties are a bulk density of 1,100 to 2,000 kg/m3 and a stowage factor of 0.50 to 0.91 m3/t, with the angle of repose recorded as not applicable.

blocks.h: 6. Care and action before loading

ul: Obtain the shipper's declaration required by SOLAS regulation VI/2 and section 4 of the Code, giving the BCSN, the group and the cargo's properties, and satisfy yourself that the BCSN matches what is actually being offered.

If the cargo is BAUXITE FINES, or any Group A cargo, require the certificate of TML and the certificate of moisture content. Under section 4.5.1 the TML test must have been conducted within six months of the date of loading - and again where the composition or characteristics of the cargo are variable. Under section 4.5.2 moisture content must be sampled and tested as near as practicable to the commencement of loading and never more than seven days before it.

Under section 4.3.3 the shipper must have established approved procedures for sampling, testing and controlling moisture content so that it remains below the TML while the cargo is on board. Ask for them.
Check where and how the cargo has been stored - open stockpiles in a wet season are the best single predictor of trouble - and the loading port's recent and forecast weather.

Prepare the holds: clean and dry, bilge wells clean, dry and covered as appropriate to prevent ingress of the cargo, and the bilge system of each loaded space tested to prove it works. That last requirement is in the schedule itself. A bilge system that cannot be sounded or pumped is useless precisely when it matters.

Confirm the loading plan and stability, and for a bulk carrier the loading instrument, the SOLAS chapter XII requirements including water level detectors and alarms, and the ESP Code survey status of the ship.

blocks.h: 7. Care and action during loading

ul: For a Group A cargo the rule is absolute: the schedule requires that the moisture content be kept less than its TML during loading operations and the voyage. If it is not, the cargo must not be loaded.

Observe the schedule's weather precautions: the cargo shall not be handled during precipitation, and during handling all non-working hatches of the spaces loaded or to be loaded shall be closed. Handling in precipitation is permitted only under the approved 4.3.3 procedures. Discharge in rain is permitted only where the whole of the cargo in that space is to be discharged in that port.
Inspect what is coming aboard. Visibly wet cargo, free water in the grab or on the conveyor, splattering, or material that flattens and glistens on the stow are all grounds to stop.
The can test is a complementary shipboard screening check, not a substitute for a TML determination. A cargo that fails it should be refused; a cargo that passes it has proved very little.

Where the cargo has been exposed to significant rain or snow between testing and the completion of loading, section 4.5.2 puts the shipper under a duty to establish that the moisture content is still below the TML and to provide the master with evidence of it.

The master is not bound by the shipper's declaration. If there is reason to doubt that the cargo is consistent with it, stop loading and require the shipper to verify the cargo's properties, seeking the advice of the competent authority of the port of loading if necessary.

Trim the cargo reasonably level under sections 4 and 5, both to limit shifting and to reduce the free surface available to any slurry. Where the stowage factor is 0.56 m3/t or less the schedule warns that the tank top may be overstressed unless the cargo is evenly spread to equalize the weight distribution.

blocks.h: 8. Care and action on passage, and if instability develops

ul: The schedule requires that the appearance of the surface of the cargo be checked regularly, including at least daily visual inspections where condition permits. Do it from the hatch opening or access without entering the space, and record what is seen.
The four things to look for are named in the schedule: free water, a liquid slurry above the cargo, a fluid state of the cargo, and flattening of the cargo.
Sound the bilges at regular intervals, pump as necessary and record the quantities. A rising trend is evidence, and the record is what makes it visible.
Treat atypical motion - the wobble - as a warning of cargo instability, not as a curiosity of the loaded condition.

If any of those signs appears, the schedule requires the master to take appropriate actions to prevent cargo shifting, loss of stability due to free surface effect and potential capsize of the ship: reduce speed and alter course to ease the motion, avoid heavy weather and synchronous rolling, avoid ballast changes that would worsen stability, and inform owners, charterers, the flag Administration and the P&I club.

The schedule then says, in terms, that the master shall give consideration to seeking emergency entry into a place of refuge. The Bulk Jupiter lesson is that once a slurry has formed and the ship is wobbling, the time available is very short - so this is an early decision, not a last one.

blocks.p: The examiner's phrase is taken from the IMO circular itself, which asked that extreme care and appropriate action be taken, taking into account the provisions of relevant IMO instruments, when handling and carrying bauxite in bulk. The substance of that care is the sequence above: classify correctly, certify the moisture, refuse what is wet, watch the surface and the bilges, and act on the wobble.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints no mark allocation, and the stem contains two demands - causes and care and action - so give them roughly equal weight. The commonest failure is to spend the whole answer on a general account of liquefaction and never reach the practical care, which forfeits half the question. The second commonest is to give the care as an undifferentiated list of precautions. Answer the care limb in voyage order - before loading, during loading, on passage - because that is how it would be used and it is far easier to mark. Name dynamic separation early: it is the discriminating content, and an answer that never uses the term has not identified what makes bauxite different.

blocks.h: The single idea that carries the answer

blocks.p: Bauxite was reclassified because of a casualty. Everything the question asks for follows from that one sentence: the causes are the reasons the old classification was wrong, and the care and action are the requirements the new classification imposes. Open with that and the answer organises itself.

blocks.h: Dynamic separation is NOT liquefaction - and the distinction earns marks

ul: In liquefaction the cargo mass loses shear strength and the whole body flows; water and solids move together. In the viscous fluid state it may flow to one side with a roll and not completely return.

In dynamic separation the cargo compacts from underneath, moisture migrates upward, and a slurry forms on top of the solid cargo. The danger is a free surface the stability calculation never allowed for.
The behavioural tell follows from the geometry: the slurry sloshes out of phase with the roll, producing the wobble. A liquefying cargo does not do that.
Both mechanisms are switched off by the same control - ship below the TML. The schedule says so expressly for dynamic separation.

blocks.h: Why a Group C classification was so dangerous

blocks.p: Not because Group C is a lax standard, but because of what it switches off. A Group C cargo has no TML, so there is no moisture certificate, no moisture limit and no basis on which a master can lawfully refuse cargo for being wet. The cargo aboard the Bulk Jupiter was carried in accordance with its schedule. The schedule was the defect. One sentence on this shows you understand that compliance and safety are not the same thing.

blocks.h: The amendment position at this sitting - state it precisely

blocks.p: This is the temporal discriminator on the question and it is unusually clean, because the sitting falls inside the window between adoption and entry into force of the current amendment.

ul: Amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), adopted 13 June 2019, in force 1 January 2021. This is the mandatory edition. It carries both bauxite schedules.

Amendment 06-21, resolution MSC.500(105), adopted 28 April 2022, deemed accepted 1 June 2023, in force 1 December 2023 - and expressly open to voluntary application in whole or in part from 1 January 2023.

So at this examination 06-21 is adopted, not yet accepted, not in force, and voluntarily applicable. All four statements are true at once, and being able to say that is what separates a strong answer from a competent one.

blocks.h: Numbers you can state, and numbers you cannot

ul: Can state: the particle-size criteria - more than 30% under 1 mm and more than 40% under 2.5 mm for the Group A schedule, and the mirror-image thresholds for Group C; the six month TML interval and the seven day moisture interval; the 70% degree of saturation in the drainage certificate; bulk density 1,100 to 2,000 kg/m3 and stowage factor 0.50 to 0.91 m3/t; the 0.56 m3/t tank-top overstress threshold.

Cannot state: a TML value for bauxite. TML is a property of the consignment, determined by test for each shipment. Any general figure is wrong by construction, and offering one suggests you think TML belongs to the commodity.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing a generic liquefaction answer. Bauxite's mechanism is dynamic separation, and saying so is the point of the question.
Saying bauxite is a Group A cargo. BAUXITE is Group C; BAUXITE FINES is Group A. Which applies turns on particle size distribution, and the declared BCSN governs.
Quoting the 10% indicative limit as current. It belongs to the 2015 circular and Rev.1 superseded it in 2017.
Offering a TML figure for bauxite.
Treating the can test as a substitute for a TML certificate.
Forgetting that the master may stop loading and require verification. The declaration is a starting point, not a defence.
Omitting the practical shipboard limb - daily surface inspection, bilge sounding and records, and the wobble.
Saying the current amendment is 'in force' when it is only adopted. At this sitting 06-21 is not yet law.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"The shipper hands you a Group C declaration for bauxite. Are you satisfied?" Not necessarily. Ask whether the material meets the Group C schedule's particle size distribution, how and where it has been stockpiled, and what the weather has been. If it is fine material that has been in the open in the wet season, the declaration is questionable and you may stop loading and require verification.

"Your cargo passed the can test. Can you load?" The can test is a complementary screening check. Passing it does not establish that moisture content is below TML - only a certificate based on the proper test procedure does that.

"Fine bauxite, but the shipper offers you a Group C certificate. Is that lawful?" It can be. The BAUXITE FINES schedule permits carriage as Group C where the shipper provides a certificate, based on a test approved by the competent authority of the loading port, that the moisture freely drains so that the degree of saturation is not liable to reach 70%. Check that it is that certificate, from that authority.

"The ship has developed an odd wobble two days out. What do you do?" Treat it as evidence of cargo instability. Reduce speed and ease the motion, inspect the surface where safe, sound and record the bilges, avoid heavy weather, notify owners, charterers, flag and club, and consider a place of refuge early - the schedule requires that consideration in terms.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which SOLAS chapters make the IMSBC Code mandatory? Chapters VI and VII.
Name the two bauxite schedules and their groups. BAUXITE, Group C; BAUXITE FINES, Group A.
What separates them? Particle size distribution - more than 30% below 1 mm AND more than 40% below 2.5 mm marks the fines.
What is dynamic separation? Moisture migrating upward as the cargo compacts, forming a liquid slurry above the solid cargo with a free surface.
When is the cargo not liable to undergo it? When it is shipped below its TML.
Which casualty drove the change? Bulk Jupiter, 2 January 2015, 18 of 19 crew lost.
How recent must the TML and moisture tests be? TML within six months; moisture within seven days.
Which amendment is mandatory today, and which is only adopted? 05-19 is mandatory; 06-21 is adopted and enters into force on 1 December 2023.
What does the schedule tell the master to consider if a slurry appears? Emergency entry into a place of refuge.

blocks.p: Causes then care. Causes: C-M-M - Classification wrong (1), Moisture uncontrolled because Group C has no TML (1), Mechanism is dynamic separation (3). Care in voyage order: D-T-R-W - Declaration and documents before loading (6), Test and refuse what is wet during loading (7), Record bilges and inspect the surface on passage (8), Wobble means act (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Why it matters. Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium and was long listed in the IMSBC Code as Group C - neither liable to liquefy nor chemically hazardous - so no TML applied, no moisture certificate was required and wet cargo could lawfully be loaded. The casualty. On 2 January 2015 the 10-year-old Bahamas-flag Supramax Bulk Jupiter was lost with 18 of her 19 crew; the cargo was declared Group C and IMO recorded that the loss may have been caused by liquefaction. The cargo was carried in accordance with its schedule - the schedule was the defect. The mechanism is DYNAMIC SEPARATION, not classic liquefaction. The cargo compacts from underneath, moisture migrates upward, and a liquid slurry of water and fine solids forms ABOVE the solid material - a free surface effect the stability calculation never allowed for. In classic liquefaction the mass itself loses shear strength and the whole body flows. Because the slurry moves out of phase with the roll, the ship develops an atypical motion, a wobble. The schedule adds the discharge condition: the cargo is not liable to undergo dynamic separation when shipped below its TML. The response, in order. CCC.1/Circ.2, 20 October 2015 - interim, with an indicative 10% moisture limit; then Global Bauxite Working Group research; then CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1, 20 September 2017, which SUPERSEDES it (so the 10% figure is NOT current); then amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), in force 1 January 2021. At this sitting the Code is mandatory under SOLAS chapters VI and VII and the mandatory edition is amendment 05-19. Amendment 06-21, resolution MSC.500(105), is ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE - adopted 28 April 2022, deemed accepted 1 June 2023, in force 1 December 2023, and open to voluntary application in whole or in part from 1 January 2023. Two schedules: BAUXITE - Group C; BAUXITE FINES - Group A. Separated by particle size distribution: the fines schedule applies where there is more than 30% of particles less than 1 mm AND more than 40% less than 2.5 mm; Group C where 30% or less under 1 mm, or 40% or less under 2.5 mm, or both. Fines may still be carried as Group C on a certificate, from a test approved by the competent authority of the loading port, that the moisture freely drains so the degree of saturation is not liable to reach 70%. The declared BCSN and its schedule govern, never the commodity name. Schedule properties: bulk density 1,100 to 2,000 kg/m3, stowage factor 0.50 to 0.91 m3/t. Before loading: shipper's declaration under SOLAS VI/2; for Group A the TML certificate within six months (section 4.5.1) and moisture content within seven days (section 4.5.2); the shipper's approved procedures under 4.3.3; check stockpile exposure and weather; holds clean and dry with bilge wells covered and the bilge system tested; loading instrument and SOLAS XII water level alarms. During loading: moisture below TML during loading and the voyage; no handling in precipitation and non-working hatches closed; reject visibly wet or splattering cargo; the can test is a screening check, never a substitute; after significant rain or snow the shipper must re-establish that moisture is below TML; the master may stop loading and require verification through the competent authority; trim level, and watch tank top loading where the stowage factor is 0.56 m3/t or less. On passage: check the surface at least daily where condition permits, looking for free water, a liquid slurry, a fluid state or flattening; sound and record bilges; treat a wobble as cargo instability; act to prevent shifting, free-surface loss of stability and capsize; and give consideration to emergency entry into a place of refuge. No TML value is quotable - it is determined by test for each shipment.

quick_revision.major_trap: Writing a generic liquefaction answer. Bauxite's hazard is dynamic separation - the cargo compacts from underneath and moisture migrates upward to form a slurry above the solid material, creating a free surface effect - and naming and explaining that mechanism is the point of the question. The second trap is classification: classification and carriage requirements follow the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule, never the commodity name, and on that basis the Code carries two schedules, BAUXITE (Group C) and BAUXITE FINES (Group A), separated by particle size distribution. The third is temporal and cuts both ways at this sitting: the indicative moisture limit of 10% comes from CCC.1/Circ.2 of 2015, which Rev.1 expressly superseded in 2017, so it is not current; while amendment 06-21 is only ADOPTED - it does not enter into force until 1 December 2023 and may only be applied voluntarily - so it must not be described as in force either. The fourth is offering a TML value for bauxite: TML is determined by test for each shipment and no general figure exists.

questions.understand_first: A cargo does not become dangerous because it is reclassified; it was always dangerous, and the classification was wrong. Bauxite sat in the cargo code as a substance that could neither turn fluid nor poison anyone, and the practical effect of that listing was that nobody had to measure how wet it was and no master had a lawful reason to turn it away. A ship carrying it in full compliance with that listing was lost with almost all her crew. What was eventually understood is that the danger is not the whole cargo turning to liquid, but water working its way up through a mass that is settling under the ship's own working, until a soupy layer is lying on top of the solid material - and a ship that was loaded with a firm, trimmed cargo finds herself carrying something that sloshes. Everything the question asks for follows from that: the causes are the reasons the old listing was wrong, and the care and action are what the corrected listing now demands - measure the water, refuse what is too wet, and keep looking at the surface all the way across.
questions.memory_cue: Causes first, care second. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the bauxite question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What bauxite is and why it was treated as safe. 2 The casualty that forced the reassessment. 3 The mechanism - dynamic separation. 4 The regulatory response in sequence. 5 What governs at this sitting and which schedule applies. 6 Care before loading. 7 Care during loading. 8 Care on passage and if instability develops.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for causes and then care, so the route front-loads the mechanism and then follows the voyage in order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish dynamic separation from liquefaction.
retrieval_cards.answer: In liquefaction the cargo mass loses its internal shear strength under vibration, impaction or ship's motion and behaves as a liquid - the whole body flows, water and solids together, and in the viscous fluid state it may flow to one side with a roll and not completely return. In dynamic separation the cargo compacts from underneath, moisture migrates upward, and a liquid slurry of water and fine solids forms above the solid material, producing a free surface effect the stability calculation never allowed for.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating technical point of the whole question, and most candidates blur it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is bauxite a Group A cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not as such. There are two schedules: BAUXITE is Group C, and BAUXITE FINES is Group A, a cargo which may undergo dynamic separation. Which applies turns on particle size distribution, and the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its individual schedule govern - never the commodity name.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying 'bauxite is Group A' is as wrong as the old position that it was always Group C.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What particle size distribution separates the two bauxite schedules?
retrieval_cards.answer: BAUXITE FINES, Group A, applies where the cargo contains BOTH more than 30% of fine particles less than 1 mm and more than 40% of particles less than 2.5 mm. BAUXITE, Group C, applies where the cargo contains either 30% or less of particles under 1 mm, or 40% or less under 2.5 mm, or both.
retrieval_cards.why: Fine, poorly draining material holds moisture; the criteria are the Code's way of identifying it, and they are mirror images of each other.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which IMSBC amendment is mandatory at this sitting, and what is the position of the next one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), adopted 13 June 2019 and in force since 1 January 2021, is the mandatory edition and it carries both bauxite schedules. Amendment 06-21, resolution MSC.500(105), was adopted on 28 April 2022, is deemed accepted on 1 June 2023 and enters into force on 1 December 2023; Contracting Governments may apply it in whole or in part on a voluntary basis from 1 January 2023. It is adopted, not in force, and voluntarily applicable.
retrieval_cards.why: The sitting falls inside the window between adoption and entry into force, so adopted, accepted and in force must be kept apart.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How recent must the TML and moisture content tests be?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under IMSBC section 4.5.1 the shipper must ensure the TML test is conducted within six months to the date of loading, and again where the composition or characteristics of the cargo are variable. Under section 4.5.2 sampling and testing for moisture content must be as near as practicable to the commencement of loading and never more than seven days before it, and where the cargo has been exposed to significant rain or snow the shipper must establish that moisture is still below TML and give the master evidence of it.
retrieval_cards.why: Six months and seven days - two different intervals for two different things, and the rain provision is what catches an open stockpile.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The cargo is fine bauxite but the shipper offers a Group C certificate. Can that be lawful?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, on one specific route. The BAUXITE FINES schedule permits a cargo meeting the fines criterion to be carried as Group C under the BAUXITE schedule where the shipper provides the master with a certificate, in accordance with the result of a test approved by the competent authority of the port of loading, stating that the moisture of the cargo freely drains from it so that the degree of saturation is not liable to reach 70%.
retrieval_cards.why: It is a documented, authority-approved exception with a stated numerical basis - not a commercial assurance, and the master should check that it is that certificate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the can test let you accept the cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The can test is a complementary shipboard screening check only. A cargo that fails it should be refused, but a cargo that passes it has not been shown to have a moisture content below its TML - only a certificate based on the proper test procedure does that.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating a screening check as proof is a classic way of turning a precaution into a false reassurance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the schedule require you to do on passage, and what are you looking for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Check the appearance of the cargo surface regularly, including at least daily visual inspections where condition permits. Look for free water, a liquid slurry above the cargo, a fluid state of the cargo, or flattening of the cargo. If any is observed the master must take appropriate action to prevent cargo shifting, loss of stability due to free surface effect and potential capsize, and give consideration to seeking emergency entry into a place of refuge.
retrieval_cards.why: These are the schedule's own words and its own four indicators - quoting them is worth more than a general instruction to keep a lookout.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The shipper's declaration says Group C. Are you bound by it?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. If there is reason to doubt that the cargo being loaded is consistent with the declaration, the master should stop loading and have the shipper verify the cargo's properties, seeking advice from the competent authority of the loading country if necessary.
retrieval_cards.why: The Bulk Jupiter cargo was declared Group C and carried in accordance with its schedule. The declaration is a starting point, not a defence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Code define Groups A, B and C?
retrieval_cards.answer: Group A consists of cargoes which may liquefy if shipped at a moisture content in excess of their transportable moisture limit. Group B consists of cargoes which possess a chemical hazard which could give rise to a dangerous situation on a ship. Group C consists of cargoes which are neither liable to liquefy (Group A) nor to possess chemical hazards (Group B).
retrieval_cards.why: Group C is defined negatively, which is exactly why it was the dangerous place for bauxite to sit - it switches off the TML machinery rather than imposing a lower standard.

The care half is asking for a practical, ordered sequence a management-level engineer would actually follow.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and its status at this sitting

blocks.p: The instrument is the International Convention on Liability and Compensation for Damage in Connection with the Carriage of Hazardous and Noxious Substances by Sea, 1996, as amended by the Protocol of 2010. The Protocol directs that the two are to be read and interpreted together as one single instrument, and the combined text is what is meant by "the HNS Convention".

The examiner's premise must be handled before anything else. The paper states that the Convention "is expected shortly to come into force". At this sitting it is adopted but NOT in force, and the conditions its entry-into-force article sets have not been met. Those conditions are of three kinds: a minimum number of States must have expressed consent to be bound; among them a minimum number must each hold a substantial registered gross tonnage; and the Secretary-General must have been told that receivers in those States took a stated quantity of contributing cargo in the preceding calendar year. The expectation of imminence was widely held; it is recorded here as the examiner's, and no date is offered, because none existed.

One consequence is worth stating early, because it protects the rest of the answer: the substantive provisions were fixed by the 2010 Protocol and do not change while the instrument waits. So the scope, the heads of damage and the certification scheme can all be answered with confidence even though the Convention is not yet law. The scheme itself is the familiar two-tier shape: strict liability on the owner up to a limit, backed by compulsory insurance and a certificate, with a second-tier Fund financed by the receivers of the cargo.

blocks.h: 2. (a) The substances covered - the seven categories of article 1.5

blocks.p: The first thing to say about limb (a) is the thing most candidates miss. The Convention does not list chemicals. Article 1.5(a) defines hazardous and noxious substances as anything carried on board a ship as cargo which falls within seven categories, each defined by pointing at another IMO instrument. The practical effect is that the scope updates itself whenever those instruments are amended, and no list in the Convention can go stale.

rows: Gas oil, gasoline and other products carried in bulk
MARPOL Annex II, including provisionally assessed X, Y and Z substances
IBC Code chapter 17, and products covered by its paragraph 1.1.6
(iv) Dangerous, hazardous and harmful substances in PACKAGED form
Drummed solvents; class 8 corrosives in IBCs
IGC Code chapter 19, and products covered by its paragraph 1.1.6
(vi) Liquids in bulk with a low flashpoint
A flashpoint not exceeding 60 degrees C, closed cup test
(vii) Solid bulk materials with chemical hazards
The IMSBC Code, so far as also subject to the IMDG Code when carried in packaged form
Ammonium nitrate based fertilizers; seed cake

blocks.p: Article 1.5(b) then extends the definition to residues from the previous carriage in bulk of categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii) - so a tank that has been emptied but not cleaned is still carrying HNS for the purposes of the Convention. Note also the two limits built into the definition: the substance must be carried as cargo, so a ship's own stores and bunkers are not HNS, and category (iv) is the only packaged category.

blocks.h: 3. (a) Bulk HNS and packaged HNS - why the split matters

ul: Article 1.5bis - bulk HNS: categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii), together with the residues in 1.5(b).
Article 1.5ter - packaged HNS: category (iv) alone.

The split is not a classification for its own sake. It fixes the owner's limit of liability under article 9, and the packaged scale is the higher of the two - packaged chemicals are harder to identify, recover and account for after a casualty.

It also matters to the second tier: packaged cargo does not contribute to the Fund in the way bulk cargo does. Where a ship carries both, or where the cargo cannot be determined, the packaged figures apply.

blocks.h: 4. (b) The heads of damage - article 1.6

blocks.p: Limb (b) reads as a technical question and is a legal one. "Damage" is defined in article 1.6 and has four heads:

ol: Loss of life or personal injury, on board or outside the ship, caused by the substances. Note what is not required: no pollution at all. This is the widest departure from the oil regime and it is the single best mark in the limb.
Loss of or damage to property outside the ship.

Loss or damage by contamination of the environment - with the standard restriction that compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit from that impairment, is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken.
The costs of preventive measures, and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

blocks.p: Because the stem says "types of pollution", name the four ways a chemical cargo does harm alongside the legal heads, and the two readings of the question are both satisfied: fire and explosion, toxicity (acute and chronic, to people and to marine life), contamination of water, seabed, shoreline and air, and reactivity - substances that react violently with water, with air or with each other. Article 1.6 also deals with the practical problem that chemical damage often cannot reasonably be separated from damage caused by other things.

blocks.h: 5. (b) What is excluded, and the mechanism that excludes it

blocks.p: The exclusions in article 4 are what make the three conventions fit together, so they lead directly into limb (c).

ul: 4.1 - the Convention applies to claims other than those arising out of a contract for the carriage of goods and passengers. Cargo and passenger claims travel under their own regimes.
4.2 - disapplied to the extent it is incompatible with workers' compensation or social security schemes.

4.3(a) - pollution damage as defined in the Civil Liability Convention is excluded, WHETHER OR NOT compensation is actually payable under that Convention. This is the load-bearing clause. The exclusion bites on the definition, not on the outcome, so a gap in CLC recovery does not push the claim into HNS.
4.3(b) - damage caused by class 7 radioactive material, which has its own nuclear liability regime.
4.4 - warships and State-owned ships on non-commercial service.

blocks.p: The drafting principle to state in one line: these conventions are built to tile, not to overlap. Each defines its territory and then carves out what a neighbouring convention has already claimed.

blocks.h: 6. (c) Why an oil products tanker needs certificates under all three

blocks.p: The examiner's word is "probably", and the hedge is deliberate - the requirement depends on what the ship is carrying and how she is registered. Explaining that dependency is the mark. The three conventions are each defined by a different thing:

rows: The oil being persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil, carried in bulk as cargo (or in the bunkers of such a ship)
Carrying more than 2,000 tons of persistent oil in bulk as cargo
The oil being used, or intended to be used, for the operation or propulsion of the ship - regardless of cargo
Ships over 1,000 gross tonnage registered in a State Party
A ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS

blocks.p: Now apply that to the ship in the question. A products tanker's trade is precisely that she changes cargo:

ul: She always burns bunkers. So the Bunkers Convention reaches her on every voyage, laden or in ballast, whatever the cargo. That certificate is never conditional on the trade.

Some parcels are persistent. A cargo of heavy fuel oil or a persistent product engages CLC. Two facts must both be true - that she is a CLC ship on that voyage, and that the oil is persistent - so CLC applicability is stated conditionally, never as a property of the ship. Note the trap: CLC reaches only persistent hydrocarbon MINERAL oil; a persistent oil of animal or vegetable origin is not a CLC oil at all and is treated as an HNS.

Some parcels are non-persistent, or are chemicals. Gasoline, naphtha and gas oil are low-flashpoint or non-persistent products that fall outside CLC and squarely inside HNS categories (i) and (vi); a parcel of a chemical falls inside (ii) or (iii); and residues of any of these keep the ship within HNS even after discharge.
The parcels change voyage by voyage, and often within one voyage. A products tanker frequently carries several grades at once.

blocks.p: The commercial conclusion follows from the operational one: certificates cannot be obtained at the loading berth. They are issued in advance by or on behalf of the flag State against evidence of insurance, and a missing certificate is a detainable deficiency and a breach of charter. Since which regime applies is decided by the cargo of the day, the only way a products tanker can trade freely is to hold all three certificates all the time. That, and not any single voyage, is why she "probably" requires all three.

blocks.h: 7. (c) The certificate itself, and the two tiers behind it

ul: Under article 12 the owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance or other financial security in the sums fixed by article 9, evidenced by a certificate in the Annex I model form, carried on board and mutually recognised between States Parties. There is a direct right of action against the insurer.

Tier one is the owner's strict liability under article 7, subject to the article 7.2 defences and to the channelling provision in 7.5 which keeps claims off the crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. Liability is limited under article 9, on the higher packaged scale or the lower bulk scale.

Tier two is the HNS Fund under article 14, financed by post-incident contributions from receivers of contributing cargo in States Parties, subject to an overall ceiling on the total payable. The polluter-pays burden is therefore shared between the ship and the cargo interest, which is the same architecture as the oil regime's Fund.
Article 37 - claims are extinguished three years from the date the claimant knew or ought reasonably to have known of the damage, and in no case later than ten years from the incident.

blocks.p: Close by returning to the premise. Because the Convention was not in force at this sitting, an HNS incident then fell to be dealt with under national law, limitation under the LLMC, and P&I cover - which is precisely the gap the Convention exists to close, and precisely why its entry into force was so long awaited.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints no mark allocation and three limbs, so give each limb visible space and let limb (a) run longest - it carries the most content. Deal with the premise first, in three or four lines: state that the Convention is adopted but not in force, and move on. Do not spend a paragraph on it, and do not argue with the examiner. Limb (b) is a legal question wearing technical clothes; answer it from the definition of damage and then add the four chemical risk types so both readings are covered. Limb (c) is the analytical limb and the one that separates candidates - it is not asking you to describe three conventions, it is asking why one ship needs three certificates.

blocks.h: The two ideas that carry the whole answer

ul: HNS defines by reference, not by list. Article 1.5 points at seven other IMO instruments. Say this in your first sentence on limb (a) and the rest of the limb writes itself.

The three conventions tile. Each is defined by a different thing - persistence, use, category - and each carves out what its neighbour has claimed. Limb (c) is that sentence, applied to a ship whose cargo changes.

blocks.h: The premise is a trap, and the trap is agreeing with it too hard

blocks.p: The stem asserts that the Convention is expected shortly to come into force. It was not in force at this sitting and its entry-into-force conditions were not met. The correct handling is neither to repeat the prediction as fact nor to correct the examiner: state the position, name the kinds of condition that had to be satisfied, and give no date. An answer that supplies a confident entry-into-force date is asserting something no candidate in the room could have known - and is more likely to be marked wrong than generous.

blocks.h: Persistence, use, category - the three-word key to limb (c)

ul: CLC - persistence. Persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil in bulk as cargo, or in the bunkers of such a ship. Certificate above 2,000 tons of persistent oil in bulk as cargo.

Bunkers - use. Oil used or intended for the ship's operation or propulsion. Certificate above 1,000 gross tonnage. Applies whatever she is carrying, which is why it is the one certificate that is never conditional.
HNS - category. Whether the cargo falls in one of the seven article 1.5 categories. Certificate where she is actually carrying HNS.
The products tanker needs all three because the cargo of the day decides which regime is live, and certificates are obtained in advance, not at the berth.

blocks.h: The CLC exclusion phrase is worth memorising word for word

blocks.p: Both the Bunkers Convention and HNS exclude pollution damage as defined in the CLC, "whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention". That phrase is doing real work: the exclusion attaches to the definition, not to the outcome. So if a claim falls inside the CLC definition but recovery fails - the limit is exhausted, a defence succeeds, the flag is not a party - it does not fall back into HNS or Bunkers. Candidates routinely assume the regimes act as a safety net for one another. They do not.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Trying to list chemicals for limb (a) instead of giving the seven categories and the instrument each points at.
Forgetting that HNS covers substances carried as cargo only - bunkers and ship's stores are not HNS.
Missing residues under article 1.5(b), which is where a dirty empty tank comes back into scope.
Answering limb (b) as a description of chemical spills without ever giving the heads of damage.
Omitting that the first head - death and personal injury - requires no pollution at all. It is the widest difference from the oil regime.
Treating the three conventions as overlapping safety nets rather than as tiling regimes.
Saying a products tanker "is a CLC ship". She is a CLC ship on a voyage carrying persistent oil in bulk - state it conditionally.
Assuming any persistent oil is a CLC oil. CLC reaches only persistent hydrocarbon MINERAL oil; animal and vegetable oils are HNS however persistent.
Supplying an entry-into-force date.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"Is the ship's fuel oil an HNS?" Not as bunkers - HNS reaches substances carried as cargo. The same fuel oil carried as a cargo parcel is a different matter, and if it is persistent it is more likely a CLC question.

"A cargo of persistent vegetable oil escapes. Which convention?" Not CLC - CLC is confined to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil. It is a noxious liquid substance under MARPOL Annex II and therefore an HNS in category (ii).

"CLC applies but the limit is exhausted. Can the balance be claimed under HNS?" No. Article 4.3(a) excludes CLC pollution damage whether or not compensation is payable. The balance goes to the Fund and Supplementary Fund tiers of the oil regime, not sideways into HNS.

"She is carrying drums of solvent and a bulk parcel of naphtha. Which limit?" Where the cargo is mixed, or cannot be determined, the packaged figures apply - and they are the higher scale.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: How does the Convention define its scope? By reference to seven other IMO instruments, not by a list.

Name the seven categories. Bulk oils; bulk noxious liquid substances; bulk dangerous liquids under the IBC Code; packaged dangerous goods under the IMDG Code; liquefied gases under the IGC Code; low-flashpoint liquids in bulk; and solid bulk materials with chemical hazards.
Which is the packaged category? Category (iv) alone - and it carries the higher limits.
Does HNS damage require pollution? No. The first head is loss of life or personal injury, wherever it occurs.
What limits environmental compensation? Reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken.
What is excluded by article 4.3(a), and on what test? CLC pollution damage, on the definition, whether or not compensation is payable under CLC.
Who pays the second tier? Receivers of contributing cargo in States Parties, through the HNS Fund.
What is the time bar? Three years from knowledge, ten years absolute from the incident.
Why does a products tanker need all three certificates? Because bunkers are always aboard, some parcels are persistent and some are HNS, and the cargo changes voyage by voyage.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three limbs, three keys. Limb (a) - REFERENCE, NOT LIST: seven categories, seven instruments (2). Limb (b) - P-P-E-P: Personal injury, Property, Environment (reinstatement only), Preventive measures (4). Limb (c) - PUC: CLC is Persistence, Bunkers is Use, HNS is Category (6). Then the tiling rule: each carves out what its neighbour defines (5).

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: HNS 1996 as amended by the 2010 Protocol - read together as one single instrument. Adopted, not in force at this sitting
Article 1.5(a) - the seven categories; 1.5(b) - residues; 1.5bis / 1.5ter - bulk and packaged HNS
Article 1.6 - the four heads of damage
Article 4 - scope and exclusions; 4.3(a) the CLC carve-out on the definition
Article 7 - strict liability, defences and channelling; article 9 - limitation, bulk and packaged scales
Article 12 - compulsory insurance, Annex I certificate, direct action; article 14 - the HNS Fund
Article 37 - three years from knowledge, ten years absolute
CLC 1992, in force 30 May 1996 - persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil; certificate above 2,000 tons carried in bulk as cargo
Bunkers 2001, in force 21 November 2008 - oil for operation or propulsion; certificate above 1,000 gross tonnage; limitation preserved under the LLMC
1992 Fund Convention and the 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol - the second and third tiers of the oil regime

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence

blocks.p: The MIW corpus holds no HNS material of any kind. Every article-level statement in this answer is internal verified reuse - carried through a chain of MIW answers back to a session in which the consolidated Convention text was read in full - and it is labelled as such rather than presented as a primary reading made here. Three deliberate omissions follow, and all three are decisions rather than gaps. No count of Contracting States and no contributing-cargo tonnage is stated, because neither could be established for this sitting. No numerical threshold from the entry-into-force article is stated, because the Protocol text is not held; the answer gives the structure of the conditions and no figures. No entry-into-force date is stated, because at this sitting none existed - and a date established afterwards would be worse than an omission, since it would be a fact no candidate in the room could have had. The monetary limits in articles 9 and 14 are described by their shape - a bulk scale, a higher packaged scale, an overall Fund ceiling - and no figure is put on them.

questions.understand_first: Think of this as the chemical version of the oil pollution system, with two twists worth remembering. The first twist is how it decides what it covers. Instead of writing out a list of chemicals, which would be out of date the year after it was signed, it points at the other rulebooks the industry already uses for cargoes and says: anything those books treat as dangerous, carried as cargo, is covered here. So the scope maintains itself. The second twist is what counts as harm. An oil convention is about mess - contamination, cleaning up, lost earnings. A chemical cargo, though, kills people directly, by burning, exploding or poisoning, and it can do that without a drop reaching the water. So the first kind of harm the convention recognises is death and injury, and no spill is required for it. The last part of the question is really about boundaries. Each of the three conventions is switched on by a different thing - one by how sticky the oil is, one by what the oil is being used for, one by which category the cargo falls into - and each is drafted to stand back from whatever its neighbour has already claimed. A tanker that carries a different parcel every voyage moves across all three boundaries in the course of ordinary trading, and since the paperwork has to be in hand before she sails, she carries all of it all the time.
questions.memory_cue: Three limbs, three keys. Limb (a): REFERENCE not list - seven categories, seven instruments (2), then bulk versus packaged (3). Limb (b): P-P-E-P - Personal injury, Property, Environment by reinstatement only, Preventive measures (4), then the article 4 carve-outs (5). Limb (c): PUC - CLC is Persistence, Bunkers is Use, HNS is Category (6), then the certificate and the two tiers (7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the HNS question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Convention and its status at this sitting. 2 (a) The seven categories of article 1.5. 3 (a) Bulk versus packaged HNS. 4 (b) The four heads of damage under article 1.6. 5 (b) The article 4 exclusions and how they work. 6 (c) Persistence, use and category applied to a products tanker. 7 (c) The article 12 certificate and the two tiers behind it.
retrieval_cards.why: Three printed limbs, but limb (a) needs two sections and limb (c) needs two, because the bulk/packaged split and the certificate both carry their own content.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the HNS Convention define the substances it covers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 1.5(a) covers anything carried as cargo within seven categories, each defined by reference to another IMO instrument rather than by a commodity list: bulk oils (MARPOL Annex I); noxious liquid substances (Annex II); dangerous liquids in bulk (IBC Code ch.17); packaged dangerous goods (IMDG Code); liquefied gases (IGC Code ch.19); bulk liquids of flashpoint not over 60 degrees C; and solid bulk materials with chemical hazards (IMSBC Code). Article 1.5(b) adds residues.
retrieval_cards.why: Defining by reference is the whole design - it means the scope updates itself whenever the referenced instruments are amended.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between bulk HNS and packaged HNS, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under article 1.5bis bulk HNS is categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii) together with residues; under article 1.5ter packaged HNS is category (iv) alone. The split fixes the owner's limit of liability under article 9, and the packaged scale is the higher of the two. Packaged cargo also does not contribute to the Fund as bulk cargo does, and where the cargo is mixed or cannot be determined the packaged figures apply.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one place where a classification question has a direct monetary consequence, which is what makes it examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four heads of damage under article 1.6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Loss of life or personal injury on board or outside the ship; loss of or damage to property outside the ship; loss or damage by contamination of the environment, with compensation for impairment other than loss of profit limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and the costs of preventive measures together with further loss or damage caused by them.
retrieval_cards.why: The first head requires no pollution at all, which is the widest single difference between HNS and the oil conventions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A CLC claim fails because the limit is exhausted. Can the balance be recovered under HNS?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article 4.3(a) excludes pollution damage as defined in the Civil Liability Convention whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention. The exclusion attaches to the definition, not to the outcome, so a shortfall in CLC recovery does not move the claim into HNS. It goes to the Fund and Supplementary Fund tiers of the oil regime instead.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely assume the three regimes back each other up. They are drafted to tile, not to overlap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What defines the scope of each of CLC, Bunkers and HNS?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC is defined by persistence - persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried in bulk as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. Bunkers is defined by use - oil used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, whatever she is carrying. HNS is defined by the cargo's category under article 1.5. Persistence, use, category.
retrieval_cards.why: Three words that answer the whole of limb (c); everything else in that limb is application.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why would a products tanker probably need certificates under all three conventions?
retrieval_cards.answer: She always burns bunkers, so the Bunkers certificate is never conditional. Some parcels are persistent oil, engaging CLC. Others are non-persistent products, low-flashpoint liquids or chemicals, engaging HNS - and residues keep her in HNS scope after discharge. Her cargo changes voyage by voyage and often within a voyage, so which regime is live is decided by the cargo of the day; and because certificates are issued in advance by or for the flag State and cannot be obtained at the loading berth, she must hold all three continuously.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner's word is 'probably', so the mark is in explaining the dependency, not in asserting a requirement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A cargo of persistent vegetable oil escapes. Which convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not CLC. CLC 1992 is confined to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil, so an oil of animal or vegetable origin is outside it however persistent it is. It is a noxious liquid substance under MARPOL Annex II and therefore falls within HNS category (ii).
retrieval_cards.why: Persistence alone is not the CLC test - the oil must also be a mineral hydrocarbon, and this is a documented MIW correction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does article 12 require, and what sits behind it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance or other financial security in the sums fixed by article 9, evidenced by a certificate in the Annex I model form carried on board and mutually recognised between States Parties, with a direct right of action against the insurer. Behind it sit two tiers: the owner's strict liability under article 7, limited by article 9, and the HNS Fund under article 14 financed by receivers of contributing cargo up to an overall ceiling.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate is the visible end of a two-tier scheme, and the question asks about certificates.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The paper says the Convention is expected shortly to come into force. What do you write?
retrieval_cards.answer: State that at this sitting it is adopted but not in force and its entry-into-force conditions have not been met - a minimum number of consenting States, a gross-tonnage qualification among them, and a reported quantity of contributing cargo. Record the expectation as the examiner's without repeating it as fact and without correcting him. Give no date, because none existed.
retrieval_cards.why: Both failure modes lose marks: repeating the prediction as fact, and supplying a confident date that could not have been known.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the HNS time bar?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under article 37, rights to compensation are extinguished three years from the date the claimant knew or ought reasonably to have known of the damage and of the identity of the owner, and in no case may an action be brought later than ten years from the date of the incident.
retrieval_cards.why: Three and ten - the same shape as the oil conventions' time bars, and an easy mark if you have the pair.

blocks.h: 1. Particular Average

blocks.p: Particular average is a partial loss. Four elements define it, and they are best given as a list because the examiner is looking for the contrast with general average that follows:

ol: It is a partial loss - not a total loss, actual or constructive.
It is caused accidentally, by a peril insured against.
It is not a general average loss.
It therefore lies where it falls: the loss is borne solely by the interest that suffered it, and is recoverable, if at all, only from that interest's own underwriters.

blocks.p: The examples are ordinary marine damage. Heavy weather stoves in a hatch cover and wets a parcel of cargo; a wave damages the ship's rail; a container is crushed by the working of the ship in a seaway. Nobody chose any of it, nobody else benefited from it, and so nobody else pays for it. The word "average" here means partial loss, not an arithmetical mean - a point worth making in one line, because the everyday meaning of the word misleads candidates every year.

blocks.h: 2. General Average, and how it differs

blocks.p: General average is the opposite case: a loss that somebody chose to suffer, deliberately, to save the whole adventure. The classical definition is Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules:

There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.

Because all three interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - were saved by that act, all three contribute rateably in proportion to their saved values. That is the whole principle, and it is very old: it is a rule of sharing, not a rule of compensation. In Indian law it is given statutory expression in section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, which is drawn from section 66 of the English Act of 1906.

blocks.p: The two classic illustrations make the distinction visible. Cargo damaged by seawater entering a stove-in hatch is particular average. Cargo of the same kind, sound, but deliberately jettisoned to lighten a stranded ship, is general average sacrifice - and so is the water damage done to sound cargo by the ship's own fire main in fighting a fire in the hold, because that damage was the intended price of putting the fire out.

blocks.h: 3. When General Average may be declared

blocks.p: The circumstances are simply the elements of Rule A, all of which must be present together. Take them one at a time, because each is a place where a claim fails:

ol: There must be a common maritime adventure - more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo aboard has no general average, because there is nothing to share with.
There must be a real peril. The danger must be real and substantial, though it need not be immediate. A peril that is merely feared, or that the master has imagined, will not do.
The act must be intentional and voluntary. Something must be chosen. Damage that simply happens to the ship in the casualty is not a sacrifice.
The act must be reasonable. A disproportionate or negligent response is not protected merely because it was deliberate.
The sacrifice or expenditure must be extraordinary. Ordinary running costs, wear and tear, and anything the shipowner was already bound to do under the contract of carriage do not qualify.
It must be for the COMMON safety - for the benefit of the whole adventure, not for the ship alone or for one parcel of cargo alone.
There must be something saved. Contribution is levied on saved values, so if nothing is preserved there is no fund to contribute from and the general average fails for want of a subject.

blocks.p: Two practical points complete the limb. First, fault does not prevent a general average act: the act is still general average even if the peril arose through somebody's negligence, though the party at fault may then face a defence to its own claim for contribution - which is exactly the difficulty the New Jason clause is drafted to meet. Second, it is the shipowner, through the master, who declares general average - not the adjuster, not the underwriters and not the cargo interests. The typical occasions are jettison, damage in extinguishing a fire, voluntary stranding, damage to machinery and boilers in refloating a stranded ship, putting into a port of refuge with the expenses that follow, temporary repairs, and salvage remuneration where the applicable Rules bring it into the adjustment.

blocks.h: 4. How a declaration is made operative - security before release

blocks.p: A declaration on its own achieves nothing. The shipowner has a lien on the cargo for its general average contribution, and the practical machinery exists to convert that lien into security so that cargo can be released:

ul: An average bond - the Lloyd's form is standard - signed by each cargo owner, undertaking to pay the contribution the adjustment finds due and to provide the values needed to calculate it.
An average guarantee from the cargo underwriters, or a general average deposit in cash where the cargo is uninsured or the underwriter is unacceptable.

Cargo is not released until security is in place. This is where general average is felt commercially, and it can be severe - after a major casualty the security demanded may be a very large proportion of cargo value, and cargo may be held for months.
The general average is then "declared" and an adjuster is appointed. In practice the appointment is made by the shipowner, but the adjuster's duty is owed to all the interests.

blocks.h: 5. Average adjusters and their role

blocks.p: An average adjuster is an independent professional specialist - in practice a member of a recognised professional body such as the Association of Average Adjusters - who investigates a marine casualty and prepares the statement of general average, which is the document that says who pays what to whom.
The role, in the order it is performed:

ol: Investigate and collect. Obtain the logs, the protest, the survey reports, the port of refuge accounts, the salvage award and the cargo manifest, and establish what actually happened.
Secure the fund. Arrange the average bonds, guarantees and deposits so the cargo can be released and the contributions can eventually be collected.
Determine what is allowable. Apply the applicable edition of the York-Antwerp Rules and allow or disallow each claimed sacrifice and expenditure. This is the adjudicative heart of the job.
Ascertain the contributory values of ship, cargo and freight at risk, at the place and time the adventure ends.
Apportion. Divide the allowed general average between the interests rateably on those values, and state the result.
Issue the adjustment and deal with the queries, and where necessary handle the parallel particular average and salvage claims so the accounts do not overlap.

blocks.p: Two things the adjuster is not are worth a sentence each, because they are the discriminating points. The adjuster does not declare general average - the shipowner does; the adjuster is engaged after the event. And the adjuster is not the shipowner's advocate: although appointed and paid by the shipowner, the adjuster acts impartially between all the interests, and that independence is what makes the adjustment acceptable to underwriters. An adjustment is nevertheless not binding as a judgment - it may be challenged in court or arbitration - but in practice it is very rarely disturbed.

blocks.h: 6. Which rules actually apply, and on what basis

blocks.p: Finish on the point most answers miss. The York-Antwerp Rules are not law. They are not a convention, no State enacts them, and they bind nobody by their own force. They are a set of contractual rules published by the Comite Maritime International, and they apply only where the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or the charterparty - incorporates them and says which edition.

ul: Three editions are in circulation: 1994, 2004 and 2016, the last adopted by the CMI at New York in May 2016 and referenced by the current BIMCO forms.
The contract decides. A bill of lading naming the 1994 Rules is adjusted on the 1994 Rules however many later editions exist - so a candidate must never say that the newest edition governs.

Within whichever edition applies, the Rule of Interpretation provides that the lettered and numbered Rules govern the adjustment to the exclusion of any inconsistent law or practice, and that the numbered Rules prevail over the lettered Rules where the two conflict.
Where the Rules are not incorporated, the adjustment falls back on the general law of the place where the adventure ends, and in India on the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem prints (16) and asks four things: define particular average, define general average, give the circumstances of a declaration, and explain the adjuster. Four demands, sixteen marks - so budget roughly four marks each and do not let the definitions eat the paper. The commonest failure is a long, comfortable essay on general average that never reaches the adjuster, which throws away a quarter of the question. The second is to answer the third demand with a list of casualties - jettison, fire, stranding - when the examiner has asked for circumstances, which means the conditions under which a declaration is proper. Give the Rule A elements as a numbered test and then name the typical occasions as illustration, in that order.

blocks.h: The single sentence that carries the whole answer

blocks.p: Particular average lies where it falls; general average is shared, because it was chosen. Everything else in the answer is elaboration of that contrast. If you open with it, the definitions organise themselves and the adjuster's role becomes obvious - somebody has to work out the shares.

blocks.h: Rule A, element by element - and where claims actually fail

ul: Common maritime adventure - fails where there is only one interest. A ship in ballast has no general average.
Real peril - fails where the danger was merely apprehended. It need not be immediate, but it must be real and substantial.
Intentional and voluntary - fails where the damage simply happened. This is the line between sacrifice and accident, and it is the line between GA and PA.
Reasonable - fails where the response was disproportionate.
Extraordinary - fails for ordinary running costs, wear and tear, and anything the carrier was already contractually bound to do.
Common safety - fails where the act benefited only the ship, or only one parcel.
Something saved - fails where nothing was preserved, because contribution is levied on saved values and there is then no fund.

blocks.h: Who does what - the three roles candidates confuse

ul: The shipowner declares general average, acting through the master. Nobody else can.
The average adjuster states the adjustment - investigates, allows or disallows, values, apportions. He is engaged after the declaration and he does not make it.
The underwriters pay, each in respect of its own assured's contribution, under the policy.
And the adjuster, though appointed and paid by the shipowner, acts impartially between all interests. Saying he is the owner's representative is a straightforward error.

blocks.h: The York-Antwerp Rules are NOT law - and this is a reliable mark

blocks.p: They are not a convention, no State enacts them, and no ship is bound by them merely by being at sea. They apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says so, and the contract also fixes the edition. Three editions are current in the trade - 1994, 2004 and 2016 - and a contract on the 1994 Rules is adjusted on the 1994 Rules regardless of how many later editions exist. Never write that "the latest edition applies". Where the Rules are not incorporated at all, the adjustment falls back on the general law of the place the adventure ends, and in India on the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.h: Illustrations that are safe to use

ul: Jettison of sound cargo to lighten a stranded ship - the oldest example there is, and the origin of the whole doctrine.
Water damage from firefighting - the water damage to sound cargo is general average; the fire damage itself is not.
Voluntary stranding - beaching a ship deliberately to prevent her foundering.
Machinery and boiler damage in refloating - the classic engineering example, and the one a management-level candidate should reach for.
Port of refuge expenses - putting in, discharging and reloading, and the associated costs.
Maersk Honam, March 2018 - a container-ship fire, general average declared and very high salvage security demanded before cargo was released.
Ever Given, March 2021 - grounding in the Suez Canal, general average declared. Both casualties pre-date this sitting and are safe to cite.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating "average" as an arithmetical mean. It means partial loss.
Answering "circumstances" with a list of casualties instead of the conditions in Rule A.
Forgetting the something saved element - no saved fund, no contribution.
Saying the peril must be immediate. It must be real and substantial; immediacy is not required.
Saying the adjuster declares general average.
Describing the adjuster as the shipowner's representative rather than as an impartial professional.
Saying the York-Antwerp Rules are law, or that the latest edition automatically applies.
Omitting the security stage - bond, guarantee, deposit - which is how general average is actually experienced by cargo.
Quoting a contributory-value percentage. Values are ascertained case by case at the termination of the adventure.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"The ship is in ballast and puts into a port of refuge after an engine breakdown. Is that general average?" No - there is no common maritime adventure, because only one interest is at risk. The expense is the shipowner's alone.

"Cargo is damaged when the master floods a hold to put out a fire. Which average?" Both, in the same hold. The cargo actually burning suffers particular average; the sound cargo damaged by the water suffers general average sacrifice, because that damage was the intended price of the common safety.

"The casualty was caused by the owner's unseaworthiness. Can he still declare general average?" He can declare it - the act is still a general average act - but his own right to recover contribution may be defeated by that fault, which is precisely the mischief the New Jason clause addresses.

"The bill of lading says York-Antwerp Rules 1994. The 2016 Rules exist. Which applies?" The 1994 Rules. The contract fixes the edition and currency is irrelevant.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define particular average. A partial loss, accidental, by a peril insured against, not a general average loss, borne by the interest damaged.
Give Rule A. An extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, to preserve from peril property involved in a common maritime adventure.
Who declares general average? The shipowner, through the master.
What security is taken before cargo is released? An average bond from the cargo owner, an average guarantee from its underwriters, or a cash deposit.
What does the adjuster produce? The statement of general average - the allowances, the contributory values and the apportionment.
Is the adjustment binding? Not as a judgment; it may be challenged, but it is rarely disturbed.
Are the York-Antwerp Rules law? No - contractual only, and the contract names the edition.
Which Indian statute states general average loss? Section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
If nothing is saved, is there a general average? No - there is no fund on which to levy contribution.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Contrast first, then the test, then the people. Contrast: lies where it falls versus shared because chosen (1-2). The Rule A test: C-P-I-R-E-C-S - Common adventure, Peril real, Intentional, Reasonable, Extraordinary, Common safety, Something saved (3). Then the machinery: bond, guarantee, deposit before release (4). Then the adjuster in six moves: investigate, secure, allow, value, apportion, issue (5). Close on: the Rules are contractual and the contract names the edition (6).

blocks.p: The MIW corpus holds no marine-insurance material at all - no York-Antwerp Rules text, no Marine Insurance Act 1963, no adjusting practice material. This answer is authored from established law and practice and carried through MIW internal records, and it is labelled that way rather than dressed as a primary reading. Three deliberate restraints follow. Only Rule A is quoted, because it is short, settled and identical across all three editions in existence at this sitting; the numbered Rules are described by subject rather than quoted, since their wording differs between editions and no edition text is held. No contributory-value formula, percentage or monetary figure appears anywhere, because values are ascertained case by case at the termination of the adventure and any general figure would be false precision - the same restraint applies to the level of salvage security demanded in any particular casualty. And no time limit for a general average claim is stated, because it depends on the applicable law of the contract and on the edition incorporated.
