The second trap is running out of paper before the adjuster: four demands, sixteen marks, roughly four marks each, and a long essay on general average that never reaches the adjuster throws away a quarter of the question. The third is the two role errors - the shipowner declares general average, not the adjuster, and the adjuster acts impartially between all interests rather than as the shipowner's representative. The fourth is saying the York-Antwerp Rules are law, or that the latest edition applies: they are contractual, and the contract fixes the edition, so a bill of lading on the 1994 Rules is adjusted on the 1994 Rules however many later editions exist.
skeleton: Open on the contrast: lies where it falls versus shared because chosen
Particular average - partial, accidental, insured peril, borne alone
General average - Rule A quoted, and the rateable contribution on saved values
The seven Rule A elements as the test for a declaration, then the typical occasions
Security before release - lien, bond, guarantee, deposit
The adjuster in six moves, and the two things he is not
The Rules are contractual; the contract names the edition

questions.understand_first: The word at the centre of this question does not mean what it means in arithmetic. Here it means a partial loss - damage short of losing the thing altogether - and the whole question is about who pays for it. Two answers are possible. If the damage simply happened, by bad luck, then it stays with whoever owned the thing that got damaged, and that is the end of it. But sometimes damage does not simply happen: somebody in charge decides to give something up on purpose, because giving it up is the only way to save the whole venture - throwing cargo over the side to lift a ship off a bank, or flooding a hold to stop a fire spreading. Whoever owned that particular thing has suffered for everybody's benefit, and it would be unfair to leave the loss with them. So the loss is spread across everyone whose property was saved, in proportion to what they got back. That sharing has to be calculated by somebody who has no interest in the outcome - which is why a separate profession exists to do it, and why the last part of the question is about that person rather than about the ships.
questions.memory_cue: Contrast, test, people, rules. Contrast: lies where it falls versus shared because chosen (1-2). The declaration test: C-P-I-R-E-C-S - Common adventure, Peril real, Intentional, Reasonable, Extraordinary, Common safety, Something saved (3). Machinery: bond, guarantee, deposit before release (4). The adjuster in six moves - investigate, secure, allow, value, apportion, issue (5). Close: contractual, and the contract names the edition (6).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Particular average. 2 General average and how it differs. 3 When general average may be declared - the Rule A elements. 4 How the declaration is made operative, through security. 5 The average adjuster and his role. 6 Which rules apply and on what basis.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem sets four demands against sixteen marks, so the route keeps the definitions short and guarantees the adjuster is reached.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define particular average.
retrieval_cards.answer: A partial loss caused accidentally by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss, and which is borne solely by the interest that suffered it. 'Average' here means partial loss, not an arithmetical mean.
retrieval_cards.why: The four elements are the mirror of general average, and the last of them - borne alone - is the contrast the whole answer turns on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: It is short, settled and identical across every edition in circulation, so it is the one thing in this question safe to quote word for word.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conditions must be satisfied before general average can be declared?
retrieval_cards.answer: A common maritime adventure with more than one interest at risk; a real and substantial peril, though not necessarily immediate; an intentional and voluntary act; a reasonable act; an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure rather than ordinary running cost; an act for the common safety and not for one interest alone; and something actually saved, since contribution is levied on saved values.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asked for circumstances, meaning conditions - answering with a list of casualties instead is the commonest way to lose this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Cargo is damaged when the master floods a hold to fight a fire. Which average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both, in the same hold. The cargo actually burning suffers particular average, because that damage was the accidental consequence of the peril. The sound cargo damaged by the firefighting water suffers general average sacrifice, because that damage was deliberately incurred for the common safety.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the cleanest illustration that the difference lies in whether the damage was chosen, not in what was damaged.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What security is taken before cargo is released, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: The shipowner has a lien on the cargo for its general average contribution. It is converted into security by an average bond on the Lloyd's form signed by each cargo owner, an average guarantee from the cargo underwriters, or a cash general average deposit where the cargo is uninsured. Cargo is not released until security is in place.
retrieval_cards.why: This is how general average is actually experienced by cargo interests, and it is the stage most answers omit entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does an average adjuster do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Investigates and collects the casualty documents; arranges the bonds, guarantees and deposits that secure the fund; allows or disallows each claimed sacrifice and expenditure under the applicable Rules; ascertains the contributory values of ship, cargo and freight at the termination of the adventure; apportions the allowed general average rateably; and issues the statement of general average.
retrieval_cards.why: Six moves in order - investigate, secure, allow, value, apportion, issue - which is far easier to write under pressure than a description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the average adjuster declare general average, and whom does he act for?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The shipowner declares general average, acting through the master; the adjuster is engaged afterwards. And although he is appointed and paid by the shipowner, the adjuster acts impartially between all the interests - that independence is what makes the adjustment acceptable to underwriters.
retrieval_cards.why: Two role errors that appear constantly, and both are single-sentence marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The bill of lading names the York-Antwerp Rules 1994 but the 2016 Rules exist. Which applies?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 1994 Rules. The York-Antwerp Rules are not law - they are contractual, and they apply only because the contract of carriage incorporates them and names the edition. Currency is irrelevant, and the newest edition never applies automatically.
retrieval_cards.why: A 2023 examiner set a question expressly on the 1994 Rules seven years after the 2016 edition appeared, which shows exactly how live this point is.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship in ballast puts into a port of refuge after a breakdown. Is that general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. There is no common maritime adventure, because only one interest is at risk. Without a second interest there is nobody to share with and nothing to contribute from, so the expense falls on the shipowner alone.
retrieval_cards.why: It isolates the first Rule A element, which candidates assume rather than check.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The casualty was caused by the owner's own fault. Can general average still be declared?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes - the act is still a general average act, because Rule A looks at the nature of the act and not at the origin of the peril. But the party at fault may face a defence to its own claim for contribution, which is the difficulty the New Jason clause is drafted to meet.
retrieval_cards.why: It separates two questions candidates merge - whether there IS a general average, and who can recover on it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Every proposition of the York-Antwerp Rules, of average-adjusting practice and of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 used in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: The True Source corpus at 319524c holds NO marine-insurance material of any kind - no Rules text, no Indian Act, no adjusting practice material. These propositions are authored from established law and practice and carried through MIW internal records of QP2509-Q3 and QP2312-Q3. They are labelled INTERNAL_REUSE_VERIFIED and authoritative secondary rather than primary throughout, and only Rule A is quoted verbatim.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The absence of any contributory-value formula, percentage, monetary figure or claim time limit
reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate. Contributory values are ascertained by the adjuster at the termination of the adventure and are case-specific; the time limit depends on the applicable law of the contract and the edition incorporated. Any general figure would be false precision. Treat the appearance of one as a regression.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That three editions of the York-Antwerp Rules - 1994, 2004 and 2016 - were in circulation at this sitting and that the contract fixes which applies
reverify_before_publication.why: The 2016 edition was adopted by the CMI in May 2016, nearly seven years before this sitting, and no edition falls between this sitting and the donor's 29 months later. The same-year QP2312-Q3 prints a stem expressly on the 1994 Rules, which independently confirms that currency does not determine the applicable edition. Re-check that no further edition has been published before publication, without altering the answer.

The fourth is the one most often never reached.

questions.short_title: Collision off the Indian Coast - Action under the Merchant Shipping Act
questions.text_verbatim: An Indian flag vessel collided with another vessel off the coast of India, as a result few lives were also lost and vessel damaged. In accordance with the provisions under the Merchant Shipping Act, what steps should be initiated and who should initiate such steps for the safety of the ships and the marine environment.
decomposition: What has actually happened - the three events this casualty contains, and the one it does NOT
Immediate steps on board, in the order the master must take them
The reporting chain - who tells whom, and under what obligation
Steps for the safety of the ships - survey, detention, salvage, refuge and directions
Steps for the marine environment - preventive, because no pollution has yet occurred
Investigation and inquiry - the national and international systems, and why they must be kept apart
Liability and the certificates behind it, and a direct answer to the 'who' in the stem

Both donors read "resulting in the loss of lives, vessel damage, AND AN OIL SPILL". THIS PAPER PRINTS NO OIL SPILL: "as a result few lives were also lost and vessel damaged." The casualty therefore contains THREE events, not four. blocks.h: 1. What has actually happened - three events in one casualty

blocks.p: Before any list of steps, break the casualty into its elements, because each element triggers a different part of the Act and the marks follow the elements:

ol: A collision - engaging both masters' duties after a collision, the COLREGs question of fault, and the apportionment of loss.
Loss of life - which makes this a very serious marine casualty and the marine safety investigation mandatory.
Damage to the vessels - engaging seaworthiness, survey, class, the power of detention, and possibly salvage.

blocks.p: Note carefully what the stem does not say: no pollution has occurred. The question nevertheless asks about steps "for the safety of the ships and the marine environment", so the environmental duty is squarely in issue - but it is in issue as a duty to prevent a discharge from a damaged ship, not as a response to a spill. That distinction is the discriminating point of this question and it should be stated explicitly, because the Indian statutory power is drafted to reach a threatened discharge as well as an actual one.

The governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and it is worth saying at the outset that the Act is enabling as much as prohibitory: much of what follows is a matter of powers conferred on the Director-General of Shipping and the Central Government, not merely of duties imposed on the master.

blocks.h: 2. Immediate steps on board - the Master, and the order matters

ul: Muster, account for all persons, and search for the missing. Lives have been lost; this is the overriding first duty and everything else waits on it.

Render assistance to the other vessel and to every person in danger, so far as he can without serious danger to his own ship and those on board; stand by; and exchange identifying particulars - name, port of registry, and the ports from and to which she is bound. This is the master's duty after a collision under the Act, reinforced by SOLAS regulation V/33.

Assess the damage before moving. Sound all tanks and bilges, establish the extent of flooding, contain it, and assess stability and residual longitudinal strength. A damaged ship that proceeds without that assessment is the second casualty.

Prevent a discharge. Even with no release so far, the ship is a damaged ship with oil aboard: isolate any breached or threatened tank, transfer internally to sound tanks where stability permits, and implement the SOPEP - which addresses the probability of a discharge, not only an actual one.
Broadcast and report - a distress or urgency message as the situation requires, and a danger message under SOLAS regulation V/31 where the casualty endangers navigation.

PRESERVE THE EVIDENCE. Secure the VDR before it overwrites, and preserve charts, deck and engine logs, bell book, movement and alarm printouts, ECDIS and radar records, and the position and time. Lives have been lost and there will be both an investigation and litigation.

blocks.h: 3. The reporting chain - who tells whom

rows: Activates the company's ISM emergency response
DG Shipping, through the nearest Mercantile Marine Department
The statutory casualty report under the Act
Search and rescue for the missing; pollution readiness at sea
The nearest coastal State authority and port authority
The master of the other vessel
Exchange of particulars, and coordination of assistance
P&I club, hull underwriters, classification society
The other vessel's flag State, if foreign
It is a substantially interested State in the investigation

blocks.p: Alongside these sits a MARPOL Protocol I report, which is required where there is a discharge or a probability of a discharge - and a damaged tanker or a damaged ship with bunkers in a breached space is exactly that.

blocks.h: 4. Steps for the safety of the ships

ul: Damage survey. Survey by the classification society and by the Administration; repairs, or approved temporary repairs, before she proceeds; conditions of class imposed as necessary.

DETENTION. Under sections 334 to 336 the Director-General of Shipping, or a surveyor authorised by him, may detain a ship that is unseaworthy or unsafe by reason of the condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading. This is the power that stops a damaged ship sailing, and it is the clearest "who" in the whole answer.

Salvage and towage where she cannot proceed under her own power - typically on Lloyd's Open Form, no cure no pay - within the Act's Part XIII, sections 390 to 404, and the Merchant Shipping (Wrecks and Salvage) Rules, 1974.

A place of refuge. Where the ship must be brought into sheltered water, the coastal State decides, on the basis of a case-by-case assessment. The operative IMO guidance is resolution A.949(23), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, read with A.950(23) on Maritime Assistance Services. There is no right to a place of refuge; there is a duty on the coastal State to weigh the request objectively.

DIRECTIONS. The powers in Part XA allow the Central Government and the Director-General to direct the owner, master or salvor to take, or to refrain from taking, specified action. This is what converts advice into a compellable order, and it is available on a threat of pollution.
Navigational safety - marking the casualty, navigational warnings, and an exclusion zone where necessary.

blocks.h: 5. Steps for the marine environment - preventive, because nothing has yet escaped

blocks.p: This limb must be answered in the preventive voice. Nothing has been discharged; the object is to keep it that way, and to be ready if that fails.

ul: The ship acts first. Implement the SOPEP, stop or prevent the source - isolate the damaged space, transfer oil internally where stability allows, plug and patch - and rig the ship's own containment and absorbent means.

Assess and declare the risk honestly to the Coast Guard and DG Shipping, including the quantity and grade of oil in the threatened spaces, so that a response can be staged before it is needed rather than after.

The national machinery is placed on standby. The Indian Coast Guard is the authority responsible for marine pollution response at sea in India's maritime zones, under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan, which is organised on tiered response levels. On these facts the plan is engaged in its readiness rather than its response posture.

THE LEGAL ENGINE - Part XA, sections 356J, 356K and 356L. The Central Government and the Director-General may give directions to the owner, master or salvor for the prevention or containment of pollution; may themselves take whatever measures they consider necessary; and may recover the cost of doing so. It is the preventive reach of that power which makes it apply here, and saying so is the mark.

Coordination with the State pollution control board, the fisheries and environment departments and the port authority, so that a response, if it becomes necessary, is not being organised from a standing start.

Funding is already in place through the P&I entry and the compulsory insurance behind the ship's CLC or Bunkers certificate, with a direct right of action against the insurer. That is why those certificates matter operationally and not just at survey.

blocks.h: 6. Investigation and inquiry - two systems, and both are engaged

blocks.p: Keep these apart. Merging them is the commonest way to lose marks on this question.

ul: NATIONAL - under the Act. A casualty must be reported. A preliminary inquiry is then conducted by a person appointed for the purpose, and where the circumstances warrant it there is a formal investigation before a court with assessors. That court may find fault and may cancel or suspend the certificate of a master, mate or engineer. Its orientation is therefore partly disciplinary.

INTERNATIONAL - the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/6. Its purpose is expressly the prevention of recurrence, and expressly not the apportionment of blame or liability.

It is MANDATORY here. A very serious marine casualty includes one involving a death, and a marine safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty must be conducted. Note that on these facts it is the loss of life that triggers it - environmental damage would have to be severe to do so, and here there has been none.

India, as flag State of the vessel, is the marine safety investigating State. If the other vessel is foreign, her flag State is a substantially interested State and is entitled to participate. The coastal State is likewise substantially interested. The final report goes to the IMO.

Hold the two apart. One can take a certificate away; the other must never be used to apportion blame. A candidate who says the Casualty Investigation Code determines liability has misunderstood the instrument.

blocks.h: 7. Liability, and a direct answer to the examiner's 'who'

ul: Collision liability is apportioned according to the degree of fault of each vessel, on the COLREGs breaches established. Claims are pursued in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts under the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, by action in rem against the vessel with arrest, or in personam.

The loss of life claims rank high. Under section 9(1) of that Act, claims for loss of life or personal injury occurring in direct connection with the operation of the vessel carry a maritime lien, ranking second - immediately after crew wages.
Limitation of liability for maritime claims is available under the LLMC as amended, the 2012 increases having entered into force in 2015.

Pollution liability, if a discharge follows, under CLC 1992 where she is a CLC ship carrying persistent oil, and otherwise under the Bunkers Convention 2001. State CLC applicability conditionally - it turns on the ship and the cargo, never on the casualty.
Wreck removal under Part XIII if a wreck results.

blocks.p: The examiner asks who should initiate. Answer it in one line and do not leave it implied: the Master initiates everything on board and the first reports; the owner and the Designated Person Ashore mount the company response and notify the insurers and class; the Director-General of Shipping receives the report, detains, directs, and orders the inquiry; the Indian Coast Guard executes search and rescue and any pollution response at sea; the Central Government holds the Part XA powers to act and recover cost; the classification society and the Administration survey and approve repairs; and the coastal State decides on a place of refuge.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem prints no marks and asks two things: what steps, and who initiates them. Most candidates answer the first and forget the second entirely, which is half the question. The safest structure is to break the casualty into its elements first - collision, loss of life, damage - because each element opens a different part of the Act and the answer then writes itself in the examiner's own order. Then take the steps in time order: on board, reported, ships made safe, environment protected, investigated, paid for. Finally, give the "who" explicitly in a closing paragraph, naming each actor against what he does. That closing line is cheap to write and it is a whole limb of the question.

blocks.h: The fact this paper does NOT give you - and why it changes the answer

blocks.p: Read the stem again: there is no oil spill. Later sittings of this same question add "and an oil spill" - this one does not. Yet it still asks about the marine environment. So the environmental limb is about preventing a discharge from a damaged ship, not about cleaning one up. Write it in the preventive voice: isolate and transfer, implement the SOPEP against the probability of a discharge, declare the risk honestly, place the response machinery on standby. The Indian power in Part XA still applies, because it is a power to prevent as well as to contain - and saying that in terms is the discriminating mark. An answer that describes booms, skimmers and shoreline clean-up is answering a different paper.

blocks.h: The three section-number groups you can safely quote

ul: Sections 334 to 336 - unseaworthy and unsafe ships, and the power of detention.
Part XA, sections 356J, 356K and 356L - directions to owner, master or salvor to prevent or contain pollution; the power of the Government to act itself; and cost recovery.
Part XIII, sections 390 to 404 - wreck and salvage, with the Merchant Shipping (Wrecks and Salvage) Rules, 1974.

For the collision Part and the investigations and inquiries Part, name the Part and describe the machinery but do not invent a section number. An examiner is far more forgiving of "the Part of the Act dealing with investigations" than of a confidently wrong number.

blocks.h: Two investigations, and they are not the same thing

rows: Expressly not for apportioning blame or liability
May cancel or suspend a certificate
Appointed person, then a court with assessors
The marine safety investigating State - here India as flag State

blocks.p: Both run on the same casualty and neither displaces the other. What triggers the Code here is the loss of life, which makes this a very serious marine casualty and the investigation mandatory.

blocks.h: Which places-of-refuge guidance applies - check the date

blocks.p: The operative IMO guidance at this sitting is resolution A.949(23), adopted in December 2003, read with A.950(23) on Maritime Assistance Services. The 33rd Assembly adopted a replacement in December 2023 - after this examination - so the newer number should not appear in an answer to this paper. The substance a candidate needs is unchanged either way: there is no right to a place of refuge, the coastal State decides, and the decision is a case-by-case objective assessment weighing the risk of keeping the casualty at sea against the risk of bringing her in.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering the "what" and forgetting the "who". The stem asks both, in terms.
Writing a spill-response answer when no spill has occurred. Read the stem.
Putting the reports before the search. Muster and search for the missing come first.
Omitting evidence preservation, and the VDR in particular - it overwrites.
Treating the Casualty Investigation Code as a way of establishing liability.
Forgetting that a death makes this a very serious marine casualty and the investigation mandatory.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 or the DGMA. Neither exists at this sitting.
Inventing section numbers for the collision or inquiry Parts.
Saying the ship has a right to a place of refuge. She has a right to have her request considered.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"No oil has escaped. Why are you talking about pollution at all?" Because the stem asks about the marine environment, and because the Part XA directions power and the MARPOL Protocol I reporting obligation are both engaged by the probability of a discharge from a damaged ship, not only by an actual one.

"Who can stop the ship sailing?" The Director-General of Shipping, or a surveyor authorised by him, by detaining her as unseaworthy or unsafe under sections 334 to 336.

"The other vessel is foreign-flagged. Does that change the investigation?" India remains the marine safety investigating State for her own vessel, and the other flag State becomes a substantially interested State entitled to participate. The report goes to IMO.

"The families of the deceased want to claim. Where do they stand?" Claims for loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel carry a maritime lien under section 9(1) of the Admiralty Act, 2017, ranking second - immediately after crew wages - and are pursued in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which Act governs? The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
What is the master's first duty? Muster, account for everybody and search for the missing; then render assistance to the other vessel so far as he can without serious danger to his own.
Whom does he report the casualty to? DG Shipping, through the nearest Mercantile Marine Department.
Under what power can the ship be detained? Sections 334 to 336, unseaworthy and unsafe ships.
Which Part carries the pollution directions power? Part XA - sections 356J, 356K and 356L.
Does that power need an actual discharge? No. It reaches prevention as well as containment.
What makes this a very serious marine casualty? The loss of life.
What is the purpose of the Casualty Investigation Code? To prevent recurrence - expressly not to apportion blame.
Who decides on a place of refuge? The coastal State, case by case. There is no right to one.
Who is responsible for pollution response at sea in India? The Indian Coast Guard, under the national contingency plan.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Split the casualty, then follow the clock. Split: C-L-D - Collision, Loss of life, Damage (1). Then the clock: S-R-S-E-I-L - Search and stand by (2), Report up the chain (3), Ships made safe by survey, detention, salvage and refuge (4), Environment protected preventively (5), Investigation twice over (6), Liability and who does what (7).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held by the MIW corpus and was not read for this paper. The corpus holds the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 instead - an Act that is 35 months in this sitting's future - which is the register inversion these 2023 sittings were warned about, and nothing from it is consumed. The statutory propositions here are authoritative secondary, carried through an MIW answer authored under the same statute, and the section-number discipline is inherited without relaxation: only 334 to 336, 356J to 356L and 390 to 404 are asserted, and the collision and inquiry Parts are named at Part level with the machinery described but no number given. This paper introduces no new section number. Three further restraints are deliberate. The National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan is not held, so it is named without any provision, revision or tier threshold being asserted. The number of lives lost is not supplied - the stem says only "few", and all that matters legally is that at least one was lost. And the location within India's maritime zones is not asserted, because territorial sea, contiguous zone and exclusive economic zone carry different coastal-State powers and the stem says only "off the coast of India".

The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative statute; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, 35 months after this sitting. Entry 6 expressly adjudicated the pastpapers case and left point-in-time examination content as DG Shipping. See the paper anchor section 7.

THE DONOR IS 23 MONTHS LATER AND WAS SWEPT BEFORE USE. THE MISSING OIL SPILL IS A DONOR DELTA, NOT A TEMPORAL ONE, BUT IT IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE IT INTERACTS WITH ONE. The donors' spill-response prose is not carried. What IS carried is the Part XA power, and it is carried in its PREVENTIVE form - a power exercisable on a threatened discharge. That reading is what allows the environmental limb to be answered at full depth on facts where nothing has escaped.

questions.understand_first: Two ships have hit each other, people have died and both ships are hurt. The question looks like a memory test about an Act, and it is really about sequence and authority. Sequence, because the things that must happen have a natural order that has nothing to do with the order of the statute: you find out whether everyone is alive, you help the other ship, you find out whether your own ship is still safe to move, you stop anything harmful escaping, and only then do you start telling people. Authority, because the second half of the question asks who acts, and the answer is that nobody does all of it. The master can do everything on board and nothing ashore. The owner can spend money and call in the insurers but cannot compel anything. The national administration can stop the ship from sailing, can order the owner to do something and can do it themselves and send the bill. The coast guard is the one that actually goes out. And the decision that matters most in a bad casualty - whether a damaged ship may come into shelter - belongs to none of them, but to the coastal state, weighing the harm of letting her in against the harm of keeping her out. Notice also what the question does not say: nothing has leaked. So the environmental part is about stopping a leak that has not happened, which is a different job from cleaning one up, and the legal powers are worded widely enough to reach it.

retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Split the casualty into its three events. 2 Immediate steps on board. 3 The reporting chain. 4 Steps for the safety of the ships. 5 Steps for the marine environment, preventively. 6 Investigation and inquiry, national and international. 7 Liability, and a direct answer to who initiates.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Has there been an oil spill in this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The stem gives a collision, loss of life and damage to the vessel, and no discharge. It still asks about the marine environment, so the environmental limb is about preventing a discharge from a damaged ship - isolate and transfer, implement the SOPEP against the probability of a release, and place the national response on readiness rather than mounting it.
retrieval_cards.why: Later sittings of the same question add an oil spill, so a candidate working from a remembered answer will describe a clean-up that never happened.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the master's first duty, and what comes immediately after?
retrieval_cards.answer: Muster, account for all persons on board and search for the missing - lives have been lost, so this overrides everything. Then render assistance to the other vessel and to persons in danger so far as he can without serious danger to his own ship and those on board, stand by, and exchange identifying particulars.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely start with the reports; the reports come after the people.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under what power can a damaged ship be stopped from sailing, and by whom?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under sections 334 to 336 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, dealing with unseaworthy and unsafe ships, the Director-General of Shipping or a surveyor authorised by him may detain a ship that is unsafe by reason of the condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sharpest 'who' in the answer and one of only three section-number groups that can safely be quoted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Part of the Act carries the pollution powers, and does it need an actual discharge?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part XA, sections 356J, 356K and 356L. The Central Government and the Director-General may give directions to the owner, master or salvor, may take measures themselves, and may recover the cost. The power reaches the prevention of pollution as well as its containment, so a threatened discharge from a damaged ship engages it.
retrieval_cards.why: The preventive reach is what allows the environmental limb to be answered at full depth on facts where nothing has escaped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which IMO guidance on places of refuge applies to a April 2023 casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.949(23), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, adopted in December 2003, read with A.950(23) on Maritime Assistance Services. The 33rd Assembly replacement was adopted in December 2023, eight months after this sitting, and should not be cited. The substance is the same either way: there is no right to a place of refuge, and the coastal State decides case by case.
retrieval_cards.why: The current-instrument register is inverted for this sitting, so the resolution a present-day reference would give is the wrong one here.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the national inquiry from the Casualty Investigation Code investigation.
retrieval_cards.answer: The national inquiry under the Act establishes the facts, may find fault and may cancel or suspend a certificate - it is partly disciplinary. The investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/6, exists to prevent recurrence and expressly not to apportion blame or liability. Both run on the same casualty and neither displaces the other.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying the Code determines liability inverts its stated purpose, and the two systems reaching different conclusions is normal rather than contradictory.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes this a very serious marine casualty, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The loss of life. A very serious marine casualty is one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment, and a marine safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty is mandatory. On these facts it is the death that triggers it - there has been no environmental damage at all, let alone severe damage.
retrieval_cards.why: It fixes which limb of the definition is doing the work, which matters because this paper's casualty has no spill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who initiates what?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Master initiates everything on board and the first reports. The owner and the Designated Person Ashore mount the company response and notify insurers and class. The Director-General of Shipping receives the report, detains, directs and orders the inquiry. The Indian Coast Guard executes search and rescue and any pollution response at sea. The Central Government holds the Part XA powers to act and recover cost. Class and the Administration survey and approve repairs. The coastal State decides on a place of refuge.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks who in terms, and it is the half of the question most answers leave implied.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do the families of the deceased stand in the order of claims?
retrieval_cards.answer: Claims for loss of life or personal injury occurring in direct connection with the operation of the vessel carry a maritime lien under section 9(1) of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, ranking second - immediately after claims for crew wages - and are pursued in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts.
retrieval_cards.why: The order was published inverted in MIW material once, with salvage first and wages second; the correct order has wages first and loss of life second.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which statute and which administration do you name?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the Directorate General of Shipping, with the Mercantile Marine Departments as its field offices. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced roughly three years after this sitting and the administration was not renamed until later still, so neither belongs in an answer to this paper.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the standing statutory trap for every 2023 paper, and the corpus holds the wrong Act, which makes it easy to reach for.

cross_links.label: QP2304 Q4 - the collision in which a loss-of-life maritime lien would arise

blocks.h: 1. What a maritime lien is

blocks.p: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself - against the res, the thing - and not against any person. Four features define it, and they should be given as a list because the rest of the answer follows from them:

ol: It attaches to the vessel by operation of law, not by agreement. Nobody grants it and nobody signs anything.
It arises at the moment the claim arises. There is no registration and no notice - which is why it is sometimes called a secret lien. Nothing on the ship's papers reveals it.
It is inchoate until enforced. It sleeps with the ship, and is crystallised by arrest and, ultimately, by forced sale.
It ranks ahead of registered mortgages - which is its whole commercial significance, because the mortgagee has done everything the law asks of him and still comes second.

blocks.p: The justification is practical rather than technical. A seafarer left unpaid in a foreign port, a salvor who has saved a ship, a port whose dues are unpaid, the dependants of somebody killed by the ship's operation - none of them can realistically pursue an owner through a chain of single-ship companies in another jurisdiction. The lien gives them the ship instead.

blocks.h: 2. How the lien travels with the property

blocks.p: This is the second printed demand and it has a precise answer. The lien follows the vessel - the phrase in both the Convention and the Indian Act is that it continues to exist on the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership, or of registration, or of flag.

ul: Sale does not defeat it. A buyer who pays full value in good faith, with no notice of the claim, still takes the ship subject to the lien.
Re-registration does not defeat it, and neither does a change of flag. The lien is attached to the hull, not to the register.
A change of name or of manager does not defeat it.

So it is defeated by only two things. Time - the lien is extinguished after one year unless, before that period expires, the vessel has been arrested or seized and that arrest has led to a forced sale; and for the crew wages lien the period is two years. Time runs continuously, without suspension or interruption, from the claimant's discharge from the vessel in a wages claim and from when the claim arises in the others - though any period during which the vessel was under arrest is excluded.

And forced sale by the court. On a judicial sale the vessel vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges. That is precisely what makes a court sale worth more than a private one: the buyer gets a clean ship, and the liens transfer to the proceeds of sale instead.

blocks.h: 3. In rem and in personam

rows: A person - the owner, charterer or operator
That person's assets, wherever they are
The vessel, and the fund her sale produces
Worthless if the defendant is a one-ship company with no assets
Only reaches what the ship is worth

blocks.p: The connection between the two limbs of the question is the point worth making explicitly: the maritime lien is what gives the claimant a right in rem against the ship. Without it he has only a personal claim against whoever happens to own her.

In practice, arrest is the whole mechanism. The vessel is arrested by order of the court; she cannot trade; and the owner or his P&I club must put up security - a club letter of undertaking, a bank guarantee or a payment into court - to obtain her release. Most claims are settled at that point, because the daily cost of an arrested ship exceeds the claim. If security is not provided, the court orders a forced sale and the proceeds become the fund out of which the claims are settled. The two proceedings are not alternatives: a claimant may pursue in rem and in personam together, and in India the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts covers both.

blocks.h: 4. Which convention deals with maritime liens

blocks.p: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force since 5 September 2004. It is the successor to the earlier Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967, neither of which attracted wide support.

State the Indian position honestly, because it is a fair oral question: India is not a party to the 1993 Convention. Its scheme nevertheless governs in India, because the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 reproduces it - the same five liens, in the same order, with the same travelling rule and the same time limits. So the Convention answer and the Indian answer coincide, and it is worth saying why they coincide.

blocks.h: 5. What the convention secures - the five claims

blocks.p: Article 4 secures five claims by a maritime lien, and the order in which they are listed is the order in which they rank. Learn them in order, because the last demand of the question depends on it:

ol: Wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the complement in respect of their employment on the vessel, including costs of repatriation and social insurance contributions payable on their behalf.
Loss of life or personal injury occurring, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel.
Reward for salvage services, including special compensation relating thereto.
Port, canal and other waterway dues, and pilotage dues, and any other statutory dues related to the vessel.
Claims based on tort arising out of loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss or damage to cargo and containers carried on her.

blocks.p: Two exclusions complete the picture. No maritime lien attaches to secure a claim arising from damage in connection with the carriage of oil or other hazardous or noxious substances for which compensation is payable under another regime, or from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel, products or waste. The reasoning is clean: those claims already have their own strict-liability conventions with compulsory insurance behind them, so they do not need a lien as well.

blocks.h: 6. How the liens rank among themselves

ul: All maritime liens rank ahead of registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges.
Among themselves they rank in the order listed above - wages, then loss of life, then salvage, then dues, then tort.

But salvage jumps. A salvage lien takes priority over all liens which attached to the vessel BEFORE the salvage operations. The logic is that without the salvor there would have been no ship for anybody else to claim against, so the last rescuer is paid before the earlier creditors.
Salvage liens rank among themselves in INVERSE order of time - the most recent salvage first, for the same reason.
Liens (a), (b), (d) and (e) rank pari passu among themselves where the fund is insufficient, and are abated rateably.

Other liens granted by national law rank after the five Convention liens and after registered mortgages, and are extinguished after six months, or sixty days after a sale to a bona fide purchaser, whichever expires first.

blocks.h: 7. The order of settlement after forced sale

blocks.p: This is the last printed demand and it should be given as a clean numbered list. Under article 12, the proceeds of the forced sale are distributed in this order:

ol: The costs and expenses of the arrest, seizure and subsequent sale - including the costs of upkeep of the vessel and crew from the time of arrest, and the wages and associated sums incurred during that period. These come off the top, before any claimant, because without them there would be no fund at all.
Optionally, the costs of wreck removal, where the national law of the State of forced sale gives them that priority.
The five maritime liens of article 4, in their article 5 order - wages, loss of life, salvage, dues, tort - with salvage jumping ahead of any lien that attached before the salvage.
The right of retention of a shipbuilder or shiprepairer, satisfied after the article 4 liens.
Registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges.
Other maritime liens granted under national law.
Any residue to the owner, and the vessel is delivered to the purchaser free of every one of these claims.

blocks.h: 8. The Indian statutory position, kept separate

blocks.p: Keep this as its own short section rather than mixing it into the Convention answer, and the examiner can see that you know they are two instruments.

ul: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - in force 1 April 2018 - consolidated Indian admiralty law and conferred admiralty jurisdiction on the High Courts.
Section 9(1) lists the same five maritime liens in the same order: wages first, loss of life second, salvage third, dues fourth, tort fifth.

Section 9(2) carries the travelling rule and the time limits - the lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and is extinguished after one year, or two years for the wages claim, unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale.

Section 10 gives the overall order of priority in an admiralty proceeding: first, claims where there is a maritime lien; second, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; third, all other claims - with claims in a single category ranking equally, and various salvages ranking in inverse order of time.
Section 8 is the vesting provision: on a court sale the vessel passes to the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges.

Sections 5 and 6 provide respectively for arrest of a vessel in rem and for admiralty jurisdiction in personam - the two terms the question asks about, expressly separated by the Indian statute itself.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem sets five demands against sixteen marks with no printed allocation: define the lien, explain how it travels, explain in rem and in personam, name the convention, and give the order of settlement. That is roughly three marks each, so nothing may be allowed to run long. The commonest failure is a leisurely definition followed by a rushed or missing order of settlement - and the order is the single most concrete, most markable item in the question. Write the definitions tightly and give both ordered lists as numbered lists: the five liens, then the seven-step distribution. A numbered list is faster to write than prose and far easier to mark.

blocks.h: The single idea that carries the answer

blocks.p: The lien attaches to the ship, not to the owner. Everything follows from that one sentence. It is why the lien survives a sale - the ship has not changed even though her owner has. It is why the claimant sues the ship in rem rather than a person in personam. It is why arrest is the remedy. And it is why the whole question ends in a distribution of a fund: once the ship is sold, the ship is gone, and all that is left is the money she made.

blocks.h: The five liens, in order - and the one that jumps

ol: Wages - master, officers and complement, including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions.
Loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel.
Salvage reward, including special compensation.
Port, canal, waterway and pilotage dues.
Tort claims for loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel - excluding cargo and containers.

blocks.p: Wages first. This has been published the wrong way round before, with salvage first and wages second, and it is worth being certain: the seafarer comes ahead of the salvor in the list. But salvage jumps ahead of any lien that attached before the salvage operations - which is not the same thing as salvage ranking first in the list. Hold those two statements together and you have the whole of the ranking limb.

blocks.h: Why salvage jumps, and why the newest salvage is paid first

blocks.p: Both rules have the same justification and it is worth one sentence, because it makes them impossible to forget. Without the salvor there would be no ship to claim against at all. Every earlier creditor's security exists only because the salvor preserved it, so the salvor is paid before them. And where there have been several salvages, the most recent one preserved the fund for all the earlier ones - hence inverse order of time.

blocks.h: The three ways a lien ends

ul: Time. One year - two years for wages - running continuously without suspension or interruption, unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale before it expires. The period under arrest is excluded.
Forced sale. The ship vests in the purchaser free of everything, and the liens transfer to the proceeds.
Payment or settlement of the underlying claim.
Note what does not end it: sale, change of registration, change of flag, change of name, or a purchaser's good faith and lack of notice.

blocks.h: India is not a party - say so, and say why it does not matter

blocks.p: India has not acceded to the 1993 Convention. A candidate who says "India is a party" is wrong, and a candidate who therefore concludes that the Convention scheme does not apply in India is also wrong. The correct position is that the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 reproduces the Convention's scheme in domestic law - the same five liens, the same order, the same travelling rule, the same one-year and two-year limits. So the answer is the same, but for a different reason, and being able to say that is a distinguishing mark.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Putting salvage first in the list of liens. Wages are first; salvage is third but jumps ahead of earlier-attached liens.
Saying a lien must be registered. It arises by operation of law, with no registration and no notice - hence "secret lien".
Saying a bona fide purchaser without notice takes free of it. He does not; only a forced sale gives a clean ship.
Confusing in rem with arrest. Arrest is the procedural remedy by which an in rem claim is enforced.
Treating in rem and in personam as alternatives. They may be pursued together.
Forgetting the two-year period for wages - it is the one exception to the one-year rule.
Omitting that the costs of arrest, sale and upkeep come off the top, before any claimant.
Saying India is a party to the 1993 Convention.
Including cargo damage among the tort liens. Cargo and containers are expressly excluded.
Running out of time before the order of settlement, which is the most concrete thing in the question.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"The ship was sold to a new owner and reflagged before your claim was brought. Is your lien gone?" No. It continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and it binds the new owner even if he bought in good faith without notice.

"So how does anyone ever buy a ship safely?" Through a forced sale by the court. The vessel then vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, mortgages and charges, and the claims attach to the proceeds instead. That is why a judicial sale commands a better price than a distressed private one.

"Salvors saved her in January and again in June. Who is paid first?" The June salvors. Salvage liens rank in inverse order of time, because the later service preserved the fund for the earlier claimant.

"A cargo owner's containers were crushed. Does he have a maritime lien?" No. The tort lien expressly excludes loss of or damage to cargo and containers carried on the vessel. He has a maritime claim and may arrest, but not a lien, so he ranks after the mortgagee.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What is a maritime lien? A privileged claim against the vessel herself, arising by operation of law, without registration or notice, ranking ahead of registered mortgages.
Name the five liens in order. Wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; dues; tort excluding cargo.
Which convention? The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 - Geneva, 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004.
Is India a party? No - but the Admiralty Act, 2017 reproduces its scheme.
How long does a lien last? One year, and two years for crew wages, running continuously.
What defeats it? Only forced sale, or the lapse of that period without an arrest leading to a forced sale.
What is paid first out of the sale proceeds? The costs and expenses of arrest, seizure, sale and the upkeep of vessel and crew.
Where do registered mortgages come? After all the maritime liens, and after a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention.
Difference between in rem and in personam? In rem is against the ship as defendant, enforced by arrest; in personam is against a person.
Which Indian sections? Section 9 for the liens and their priority, section 10 for the overall order, section 8 for vesting on sale, sections 5 and 6 for in rem and in personam.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Five liens: W-L-S-D-T - Wages, Loss of life, Salvage, Dues, Tort (5). Remember that salvage sits third but jumps earlier-attached liens, and that multiple salvages run backwards in time (6). The distribution: Costs off the top, then the five liens, then the yard, then the mortgage, then national liens, then the owner (7). And the one-line spine for the first half: the lien attaches to the ship, so it survives the owner and is enforced against the ship (1-3).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence

blocks.p: This question rests on two independent evidence streams which agree, and that is unusually strong for a legal question in this paper. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 was read verbatim in the MIW corpus - sections 8, 9 and 10 in full - so the Indian limb is primary verified. The 1993 Convention is NOT held by the corpus, and its articles are carried through an MIW record of an answer whose verification states that the certified United Nations text was read directly; that limb is therefore internal verified reuse rather than a reading made here. The two were compared provision by provision and correspond exactly, which is what one would expect given that the Indian Act gives domestic effect to the Convention's scheme - and it means an error in one stream would have shown up as a disagreement with the other. Three restraints are deliberate. No monetary figure or SDR value appears, because maritime liens are not capped and the question does not reach limitation of liability. The optional wreck-removal priority is described as optional and is not asserted to be part of Indian law, because whether India has exercised that option is not established from held sources. And the printed stem's phrase "debtor's claims" is loose - the claims distributed are the creditors' claims against the debtor's vessel - but the printed wording is preserved and answered as plainly meant rather than corrected.

quick_revision.recall_15s: The one idea: the lien attaches to the ship, not the owner. WHAT IT IS. A privileged claim against the vessel herself - the res - not against a person. It attaches by operation of law, not by agreement; it arises the moment the claim arises, with no registration and no notice (hence a secret lien); it is inchoate until enforced, then crystallised by arrest and forced sale; and it ranks ahead of registered mortgages. Its justification is practical: an unpaid seafarer or a salvor cannot realistically chase a one-ship company through a foreign jurisdiction, so the law gives him the ship. HOW IT TRAVELS. It continues to exist on the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership, or of registration, or of flag, and it binds a bona fide purchaser without notice. It ends in only three ways: time - ONE YEAR, and TWO YEARS for crew wages, running continuously without suspension or interruption (from discharge for wages, from accrual for the rest, excluding any period under arrest) unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale before it expires; forced sale by the court, on which the vessel vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, mortgages and charges and the liens move to the proceeds; or payment. IN REM v IN PERSONAM. In personam is against a person and is worthless against an assetless single-ship company. In rem is against the ship herself as defendant, and the maritime lien is what gives the right in rem. The remedy is arrest: the ship cannot trade, so the owner or his P&I club puts up security - club letter of undertaking, bank guarantee, or payment into court - and most claims settle there. No security means forced sale. The two are not alternatives and may be pursued together. THE CONVENTION. India is NOT a party, but the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 reproduces its scheme. THE FIVE LIENS (article 4), in ranking order - W-L-S-D-T: 1 Wages of master, officers and complement, including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions; 2 Loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel; 3 Salvage reward including special compensation; 4 Port, canal, waterway and pilotage dues; 5 Tort for loss or damage by the operation of the vessel, EXCLUDING cargo and containers. Excluded from lien altogether: oil and HNS damage compensable under another regime, and nuclear. RANKING (article 5). All liens beat registered mortgages. They rank in the listed order - but SALVAGE JUMPS ahead of every lien that attached BEFORE the salvage, because without the salvor there would be no ship to claim against; and several salvages rank in INVERSE ORDER OF TIME. Liens (a), (b), (d) and (e) rank pari passu and abate rateably. National liens rank after the five and after mortgages. questions.understand_first: Most debts follow a person. This one follows a thing. If a ship runs up an obligation she cannot pay - unpaid crew, a salvor who saved her, a port whose dues are outstanding, someone killed by the way she was operated - the law gives the claimant a hold over the vessel herself rather than over whoever happens to own her. That matters because the owner is often a company formed to own one ship and nothing else, sitting in a country the claimant will never reach. The hold is invisible: nothing is registered and nothing appears on her papers, so a buyer can pay a fair price for a ship in good faith and still inherit the claim. There is only one way to buy her genuinely clean, and that is to buy her from a court, because the court's sale wipes the slate and moves everyone's claim onto the money instead of the hull. Once that happens the argument stops being about the ship and becomes an argument about a pot of cash, and the last part of the question is simply the queue: who gets paid, in what order, out of what is left.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the maritime lien question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a maritime lien is. 2 How it travels with the property. 3 In rem and in personam. 4 Which convention deals with it. 5 The five claims it secures. 6 How the liens rank among themselves. 7 The order of settlement after forced sale. 8 The Indian statutory position, kept separate.
retrieval_cards.why: Five printed demands against sixteen marks, so the route keeps every section short and guarantees the order of settlement is reached.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a maritime lien?
retrieval_cards.answer: A privileged claim against the vessel herself rather than against any person. It attaches to the res by operation of law and not by agreement, arises the moment the claim arises without registration or notice, remains inchoate until enforced by arrest and forced sale, and ranks ahead of registered mortgages.
retrieval_cards.why: Four features, and every later part of the answer is a consequence of one of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five maritime liens in their ranking order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Wages and other sums due to the master, officers and complement, including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions; loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel; reward for salvage including special compensation; port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues; and tort claims for loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, excluding cargo and containers.
retrieval_cards.why: Wages first - this list has been published inverted with salvage first, and the order is the whole basis of the settlement limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Salvage is third in the list. So when does salvage get paid first?
retrieval_cards.answer: A salvage lien takes priority over every lien that attached to the vessel before the salvage operations, because without the salvor there would have been no ship for the earlier claimants to claim against. Where there have been several salvages they rank among themselves in inverse order of time, the most recent first, for the same reason.
retrieval_cards.why: Two statements that look contradictory and are not - salvage ranks third in the list but jumps everything that pre-dates it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the lien travel with the property, and what ends it?
retrieval_cards.answer: It continues to exist on the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and binds even a bona fide purchaser without notice. It ends only on payment, on a forced sale by the court, or by lapse of time - one year, and two years for crew wages - running continuously without suspension or interruption unless an arrest or seizure leading to a forced sale intervenes first.
retrieval_cards.why: The travelling rule is the second printed demand, and the two-year wages exception is the detail most often dropped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can anyone buy a ship free of maritime liens?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only by buying at a forced sale ordered by the court. The vessel then vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges, and the claims attach to the proceeds of sale instead. A private sale, however honest and however full the price, does not clear the liens.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a judicial sale commands a better price than a distressed private one, which is the commercial point of the whole doctrine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish in rem from in personam.
retrieval_cards.answer: An action in personam is brought against a person - the owner, charterer or operator - and is recovered from that person's assets, so it is worthless against an assetless single-ship company. An action in rem is brought against the ship herself as defendant and is enforced by arrest, producing security or, failing that, a fund by forced sale. The maritime lien is what gives the claimant the right in rem, and the two may be pursued together.
retrieval_cards.why: The link between the lien and the in rem right is the connection between two limbs of the question, and stating it explicitly earns the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which convention deals with maritime liens, and is India a party?
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force since 5 September 2004, succeeding the Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967. India is not a party, but the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 reproduces its scheme in domestic law.
retrieval_cards.why: Both halves matter - naming the convention, and not claiming India has acceded to it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the order of settlement of claims after a forced sale.
retrieval_cards.answer: First the costs and expenses of arrest, seizure and sale, including the upkeep of the vessel and crew from the time of arrest. Then, optionally, wreck-removal costs where national law so provides. Then the five maritime liens in their ranking order. Then a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention. Then registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges. Then other maritime liens under national law. Any residue goes to the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most concrete item in the question and the one candidates most often never reach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A cargo owner's containers were crushed by the ship's operation. Does he have a maritime lien?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The tort lien covers loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel but expressly excludes loss of or damage to cargo and containers carried on that vessel. He has a maritime claim and may be able to arrest, but without a lien he ranks after the registered mortgagee.
retrieval_cards.why: The exclusion is easy to miss and it changes where a large and common class of claimant stands in the queue.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian provisions give effect to this scheme?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, in force 1 April 2018. Section 9(1) lists the same five liens in the same order; section 9(2) carries the travelling rule with the one-year and two-year limits; section 10 gives the overall order - liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims - with salvages in inverse order of time; section 8 vests the vessel free of everything on a court sale; sections 5 and 6 provide for arrest in rem and jurisdiction in personam.
retrieval_cards.why: It lets you answer the question twice over - once on the convention and once on Indian law - and show that you know they are two instruments.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Every provision of the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 used in this answer - sections 4, 5, 6, 8, 9(1) to 9(4) and 10

This is the primary-verified limb of the question and it independently confirms the correction recorded at known_traps.md Entry 21 - the section 9(1) order is wages first, loss of life second, salvage third.

reverify_before_publication.why: The Convention is NOT held by the True Source corpus. Its articles are carried through the MIW internal record of QP2404-Q3, whose verification record states that the certified United Nations text was read directly. Corroborated provision by provision against the Indian Act, which IS held and was read here, but that corroboration is not a substitute for the Convention text.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That India is not a party to the 1993 Convention
reverify_before_publication.why: Carried from the donor rather than established from a treaty-status source held here. It is a status fact and status facts date, so it must be re-checked before publication - though the answer does not depend on it, since the Indian position is given from the Admiralty Act 2017 directly.

reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate on both counts. Maritime liens are not capped and this question does not reach limitation of liability, so any figure would belong to a different instrument. Whether India has exercised the article 12(3) option is not established from held sources, so the Indian order is given from section 10 instead.
