blocks.h: 1. Why these devices exist, and where the losses actually are

blocks.p: The examiner's opening words - "recent stress on the control of emission" - are, at this examination, very recent indeed, and the answer should say so precisely rather than generally.

ul: EEDI has for some years required a new ship's attained Energy Efficiency Design Index not to exceed a required index that tightens by phase. That put a number on design efficiency and is what first drove these devices onto newbuildings.

The decisive change is only months old. Under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76), the EEXI - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index - and the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator became applicable from 1 January 2023, with the SEEMP Part III required on board from the same date. EEXI extended a design-efficiency requirement to the existing fleet for the first time, and it is the single reason retrofit energy-saving devices moved from optional to commercially necessary.

CII is the new pressure and it has not yet bitten. 2023 is the first data-collection year for operational carbon intensity, so no ship has yet been assigned a rating - the first ratings follow in the next reporting cycle. Owners are therefore acting in anticipation of a rating, which is exactly why efficiency devices are being fitted now rather than later.

Policy context. The operative IMO policy instrument is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018, with its ambitions on carbon intensity and on total annual emissions. Commercially, charterers are already pricing efficiency, and fuel remains the largest controllable operating cost.

The engineering consequence is direct. CO2 emitted is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so a percentage saved in propulsive efficiency is the same percentage saved in emissions. There is no separate abatement step - which is why hydrodynamics became a compliance subject.

blocks.p: To discuss the devices sensibly, first name where the energy actually goes, because every device attacks one of these losses:

ul: Axial loss - energy left behind in the accelerated slipstream. Reduced by a larger, more slowly turning propeller.
Rotational loss - the propeller leaves the water spinning, and that rotation does no useful work. Attacked before the disc by pre-swirl and after it by post-swirl.
Frictional and sectional loss - blade drag. Attacked by section shape and blade area.
Tip and hub vortex loss - concentrated vortices shed at the blade tips and at the boss. Attacked by tip-loaded blade designs and by boss cap fins.
Non-uniform inflow - the hull delivers the propeller a badly distorted wake field, which costs efficiency and causes cavitation and vibration. Attacked by wake equalizing devices.

blocks.h: 2. The efficiency framework that classifies all four limbs

blocks.p: The four limbs are not an arbitrary list. They map exactly onto the components of quasi-propulsive efficiency, which is the product of three terms:

rows: How well the propeller converts delivered power into thrust in uniform flow
The interaction between hull and propeller - thrust deduction and wake fraction
The correction for a non-uniform, rotating inflow
(b) puts rotation in; (c) takes it back out

blocks.p: So the shape of the answer is: (a) works on the flow INTO the disc, (b) puts rotation IN ahead of it, (c) takes rotation OUT behind it, and (d) improves the disc itself. Say that in one sentence and the four limbs become a system rather than a list.

blocks.h: 3. a) Wake Equalizing Devices

ul: The problem. Behind a full-form single-screw hull the inflow to the propeller is strongly non-uniform: there is a wake peak at the top of the disc, where the water is moving slowly with the hull, and there is afterbody separation. Each blade therefore passes cyclically from fast to slow water, giving cyclic blade loading, cavitation, hull pressure pulses, vibration and erosion as well as lost efficiency.

The principle. An appendage fitted ahead of the propeller which accelerates and straightens the slow water in the upper part of the disc and suppresses separation. It raises hull efficiency and, just as importantly, improves the environment the propeller works in.

The forms. The classic wake equalising duct - a pair of half-ring nozzles on the afterbody either side of the sternframe; flow-guiding fins and stern spoilers; and, at design stage, stern tunnels and changes to the afterbody form itself.
Note that the categories are not watertight. A combined duct with internal pre-swirl fins belongs to both this limb and limb (b), and saying so shows understanding rather than confusion.

Gain and limits. Indicatively a few per cent, up to high single figures on a suitable hull - and the vibration and cavitation benefit is often worth as much as the fuel. Best on full-form, high block coefficient, single-screw ships at moderate speed. On fine, fast hulls the added appendage drag can exceed the gain, so the device must be matched to the hull and not simply bought.

blocks.h: 4. b) Pre-swirl Devices

ul: The problem. A propeller does not only push water aft; it also spins it. The rotational kinetic energy left in the slipstream is pure loss - it produces no thrust at all.

The principle. Impart rotation opposite to the propeller's own direction in the flow upstream of the disc. The propeller must first undo that counter-rotation before imparting its own, so less net swirl leaves the disc and more of the delivered power goes into axial thrust.

The forms. Fixed radial pre-swirl stators mounted on the hull or the stern boss ahead of the propeller - characteristically asymmetric, with different fin numbers, angles and lengths port and starboard, because the wake behind a single-screw hull is itself asymmetric. Pre-swirl ducts combining a nozzle with internal stator fins, which are the most widely retrofitted device on full-form ships. And at design stage, asymmetric or twisted afterbodies that build the pre-swirl into the hull.

Gain and limits. Indicatively a few per cent. The device is tuned to a design draught, speed and loading, so the benefit falls away in ballast or at part load, and a badly matched stator can cost efficiency rather than gain it.

Engineering cautions. The fins add wetted surface and drag; they must be designed not to excite blade-rate vibration; and they are a fatigue-critical welded appendage in unsteady flow, so weld detail, inspection and cathodic protection matter.

blocks.h: 5. c) Post-swirl Devices

blocks.p: The principle is the mirror image of limb (b): whatever swirl the propeller does impart, recover it downstream - turn slipstream rotation into axial thrust, or remove the concentrated hub vortex.

ul: Propeller boss cap fins. Small fins on the boss cap, rotating with the propeller, which break up the hub vortex. Indicatively low single figures, among the cheapest retrofits available, and they also reduce hub-vortex cavitation and the rudder erosion it causes.

Rudder bulb. A bulb on the rudder aligned with the propeller boss, filling the low-pressure hub region, reducing the hub vortex and the associated drag. Commonly supplied with boss cap fins and a twisted rudder as a matched package.

Rudder thrust fins. Fins set in the slipstream which convert residual swirl into forward force. They are angled oppositely above and below the shaft line, because the swirl reverses sense across the disc - a detail worth stating, because it shows you understand what they are doing.
Twisted and asymmetric rudders. The leading edge is twisted to match the local swirl angle, which reduces rudder drag and cavitation erosion and improves manoeuvring.
Free-rotating vane wheels. A larger-diameter freewheeling wheel abaft the propeller, theoretically attractive but structurally troublesome in service, and not widely adopted.

Gain and limits. Low single figures individually, and more when designed as a system - a boss cap fin, a rudder bulb and a twisted rudder developed together deliver more than the sum of three catalogue items. They sit in unsteady, cavitating, erosive flow, so material selection, cathodic protection and inspection matter, and a lost fin is a hazard to the rudder and propeller.

blocks.h: 6. d) High-efficiency Propellers

ul: Larger diameter at lower revolutions. This is the single most effective measure of all and should be stated first. Accelerating a larger mass of water to a smaller velocity increase cuts axial loss directly. It is enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and a suitable aperture, and it aligns naturally with slow steaming.
Tip-loaded and contracted-tip designs. End plates or winglets at the blade tip weaken the tip vortex, so the tip can carry more load without the vortex loss that would normally follow.
Curved-tip designs achieve the same effect more smoothly, with a better pressure distribution and less cavitation risk.

Contra-rotating propellers. Two coaxial propellers turning in opposite directions, the after one recovering the rotational energy of the forward one. This offers the largest single gain available, but requires concentric shafting and a complex sterntube and bearing arrangement - which is why it remains rare in large merchant ships.

Ducted propellers. An accelerating (Kort) nozzle for heavily loaded propellers at low speed - hence tugs and trawlers, where thrust at bollard pull matters more than free-running efficiency. A decelerating nozzle where cavitation and radiated noise dominate.

Blade geometry. Skew spreads each blade's passage through the wake peak over a range of angles, cutting pressure pulses and vibration; and section shape, pitch distribution and blade area ratio are matched to the ship's actual operating profile - which, with slow steaming, is often no longer the profile she was designed for.

blocks.h: 7. Selection, verification and the cautions common to all four

ul: Nothing here is generic. Every device is matched to a particular hull, draught, speed and loading condition, and the design tools are CFD followed by model testing. A manufacturer's published gain was obtained on somebody else's hull.

The operating profile has moved. Slow steaming means many ships now run well away from their design point, so a device tuned to the original condition may deliver much less - and a propeller re-matched to the actual profile may deliver more than any appendage.
Devices interact. Fitting a pre-swirl stator changes the flow a post-swirl device sees. They are designed as a package, and gains are not additive.

Housekeeping first. A fouled hull or a rough, damaged propeller will lose more than any of these devices gains. Hull and propeller cleaning and coating come before an energy-saving device, and it is worth one sentence to say so.

Verification. A claimed gain must be demonstrated in service against a measured baseline - the ISO 19030 approach to measuring changes in hull and propeller performance - and not assumed from the brochure.

Structural and class consequences. These are welded appendages in unsteady, cavitating flow. They need classification society approval, fatigue-conscious detailing, cathodic protection, and inclusion in the docking and survey regime. A detached fin damages the rudder or the propeller.

Compliance credit. Because these devices reduce the power needed for a given speed, they feed directly into the EEXI calculation for an existing ship - alongside the alternative of engine or shaft power limitation - and into the operational carbon intensity that will be rated. That is the link back to the examiner's opening sentence.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints four limbs at (4) each, so this is one of the few questions on the paper where the examiner has told you exactly how to divide your time. Give each limb equal space and do not let limb (d) run away - it is the one candidates know most about and it is worth exactly the same four marks as boss cap fins. Spend a short opening on the driver and the loss mechanisms, because it frames all four limbs and it answers the first clause of the stem, which is about why the devices exist. Within each limb use the same four-part shape - problem, principle, forms, gain and limits - because a consistent shape is faster to write and much easier to mark.

blocks.h: The one sentence that turns four limbs into a system

blocks.p: (a) fixes the flow going IN, (b) puts rotation IN, (c) takes rotation OUT, and (d) improves the disc itself. Write that early. It maps onto quasi-propulsive efficiency as the product of hull efficiency (a), relative rotative efficiency (b and c) and open-water efficiency (d) - and an answer that shows the four limbs are the three efficiency terms is doing something no list of devices can do.

blocks.h: The regulatory driver AT THIS SITTING - get the date right

ul: EEXI and operational CII became applicable on 1 January 2023 - about three months before this paper. That is what "recent" means here, and saying so precisely is worth more than a general remark about decarbonisation.

EEXI is the reason retrofits matter. It extended a design-efficiency requirement to existing ships for the first time, and an owner who cannot meet it must either fit efficiency measures or accept engine or shaft power limitation.

No ship has a CII rating yet. 2023 is the first data year, so ratings follow later. Owners are fitting devices in anticipation - which is a better explanation of "recent stress" than saying ratings are being enforced.
The SEEMP Part III is required on board from the same date.
The governing policy instrument is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018. Do not reach for anything later.

blocks.h: Where the losses are - the list every device attaches to

ul: Axial - energy in the accelerated slipstream. Beaten by bigger and slower.
Rotational - the slipstream is spinning. Beaten by pre-swirl and post-swirl.
Frictional and sectional - blade drag. Beaten by section and area.
Tip and hub vortex - beaten by tip loading and boss cap fins.
Non-uniform inflow - beaten by wake equalizing devices.
If you can name the loss each device attacks, you can answer any version of this question, including the ones that name devices you have never met.

blocks.h: Numbers: what you can say and how to say it

blocks.p: Never give a single precise percentage for a device. Published gains are obtained on a particular hull at a particular draught and speed, and they do not transfer. Say "indicatively a few per cent", "low single figures", "up to high single figures on a suitable hull" - and then always attach the condition: full-form or fine, laden or ballast, design speed or slow steaming. An examiner marks the qualification, not the number. The one comparative statement worth making firmly is that larger diameter at lower revolutions is the most effective single measure, and that contra-rotating propellers offer the largest gain of the propeller designs at the highest mechanical complexity.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Letting limb (d) eat the answer. Four marks each - the examiner has said so.
Confusing pre-swirl and post-swirl. Pre-swirl is ahead of the disc and imparts rotation against the propeller's direction; post-swirl is behind it and recovers what the propeller imparted.
Treating a wake equalising duct as a pre-swirl device. It equalises the inflow; only a duct with internal stator fins does both - and it is worth saying so rather than blurring them.
Giving one precise percentage for a device, with no hull or condition attached.
Forgetting that a device is tuned to a condition and loses its benefit in ballast or at part load.
Omitting the vibration and cavitation benefit of wake equalisation, which is often worth as much as the fuel.
Ignoring the structural, class and inspection consequences of a welded appendage in cavitating flow.
Claiming gains are additive when devices are fitted together.
Missing that hull and propeller cleaning comes first - a fouled hull loses more than any device gains.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"Your owner wants a pre-swirl stator fitted. What do you ask first?" What hull form, what draught and what speed she actually operates at - because the device is tuned to a condition, and a ship trading in ballast or slow steaming well below her design point may see very little. And whether the hull and propeller are clean, because that comes first.

"Are the gains additive?" No. A pre-swirl stator changes the flow the post-swirl device sees. They must be designed as a package, and the combined gain is less than the sum of the individual claims.

"Why is a Kort nozzle used on a tug and not on a container ship?" An accelerating nozzle helps a heavily loaded propeller at low speed, which is a tug's condition. On a fast, lightly loaded propeller the nozzle's own drag exceeds the benefit.

"Boss cap fins are cheap. Any downside?" They rotate with the propeller in unsteady, cavitating, erosive flow. Material, attachment and cathodic protection matter, and a detached fin is a hazard to the rudder.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What are the components of quasi-propulsive efficiency? Open-water, hull and relative rotative efficiency.
Which term does a wake equalising device improve? Hull efficiency - it changes the flow the hull delivers.
Why is a pre-swirl stator asymmetric? Because the wake behind a single-screw hull is itself asymmetric.
What is the hub vortex, and what removes it? A concentrated vortex shed at the boss; boss cap fins and a rudder bulb.
Why are rudder thrust fins angled oppositely above and below the shaft line? Because the swirl reverses sense across the disc.
What is the most effective single propeller measure? Larger diameter at lower revolutions.
Which propeller design gives the largest gain, and why is it rare? Contra-rotating - concentric shafting and a complex sterntube arrangement.
When would you fit a decelerating nozzle? Where cavitation and radiated noise dominate.
How would you prove the gain in service? Against a measured baseline, on the ISO 19030 approach.
Which instrument made retrofits commercially necessary, and when? EEXI, applicable from 1 January 2023.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Driver, then losses, then the four limbs in flow order. Driver: EEDI-EEXI-CII, and the key date 1 January 2023 (1). Losses: A-R-F-T - Axial, Rotational, Frictional, Tip and hub (1). Then the framework: three efficiency terms, four limbs (2). Then flow order: IN - IN - OUT - DISC - the flow going IN (3), rotation put IN (4), rotation taken OUT (5), and the DISC itself (6). Close on matching, interaction and verification (7).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence

blocks.p: The two halves of this answer stand on different evidence and are labelled accordingly. The regulatory driver in section 1 rests on corpus readings - the MARPOL Annex VI GHG instrument chain fixes the EEXI and CII application date of 1 January 2023 and the operative SEEMP guidelines, and it is what allows the answer to say precisely how recent the "recent stress" was. The technical content of all four limbs is declared engineering practice: the MIW corpus holds no naval-architecture or energy-saving-device material at all, and this material is carried through internal records of the character-identical donor and of the high-efficiency-propeller family. Three restraints follow. No precise efficiency figure is given for any device - every gain is an indicative range with its hull, draught and speed condition attached, because a published percentage obtained on one hull does not transfer and a bare number is the commonest way this subject is answered badly. No proprietary device or manufacturer is named, since generic type and principle are what earn marks and product names date. And no CII rating band, reduction factor or EEXI reference-line figure is stated - the question does not need them, and at this sitting no ship had yet been assigned a rating at all, so a rating discussion would be premature as well as unnecessary.

notes: THE REVERSAL FALLS ALMOST ENTIRELY ON ONE SECTION, AND THAT IS WHY THE RISK IS MEDIUM RATHER THAN HIGH. The four technical limbs are hydrodynamics and carry no amendment boundary at all - a pre-swirl stator worked the same way in 2023 as in 2025. The opening section, which supplies the 'recent stress on the control of emission' the examiner asks about, is entirely sitting-relative and was re-derived from scratch.

EEXI AND CII WERE THREE MONTHS OLD AT THIS SITTING. MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76) made EEXI and the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator applicable from 1 January 2023, with the SEEMP Part III required on board from the same date. The donor, 22 months later, describes a regime with three full years of operation behind it. The answer states the position as it was: very recent, and driving anticipatory retrofits.

NO SHIP HAD A CII RATING AT THIS SITTING, AND THE ANSWER SAYS SO. 2023 is the first data-collection year for operational carbon intensity, so the first ratings follow in the next reporting cycle. A statement that ships are being rated, or any discussion of rating bands and consequences, would be a forward-contamination defect. The answer explains the commercial pressure as ANTICIPATION of a rating, which is both correct and a better explanation of the stem's 'recent stress'.

THE 2023 IMO GHG STRATEGY IS THREE MONTHS FUTURE AND IS ABSENT. It was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023. The operative policy instrument at this sitting is the INITIAL IMO GHG STRATEGY OF 2018. April 2023 falls before the 7 July boundary on every possible sitting day, so this resolves in one direction without any day-level reasoning - the first clean call on that boundary in the batch.

THE EU ETS IS ABSENT AND MUST STAY ABSENT. Its extension to maritime transport begins 1 January 2024, nine months after this sitting. It is a natural thing to reach for in a commercial-driver paragraph and it does not exist here.

MEPC.346(78) IS THE OPERATIVE SEEMP GUIDELINE, NOT MEPC.395(82). The latter is 2024 and is 18 months future. The register records the 2024 instrument as current, which is an inversion for this sitting.

steps.title: Why these devices exist, and where the losses actually are
points: EEDI put a number on design efficiency for new ships and tightens by phase
EEXI and the operational CII became applicable on 1 January 2023 - three months before this sitting
EEXI extended a design-efficiency requirement to EXISTING ships, which is why retrofits became necessary
2023 is the first CII data year, so no ship has yet been rated - owners are acting in anticipation
the operative policy instrument is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018
CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so propulsive efficiency IS emission reduction
the losses: axial, rotational, frictional and sectional, tip and hub vortex, and non-uniform inflow

steps.title: The efficiency framework that classifies all four limbs
points: quasi-propulsive efficiency is the product of open-water, hull and relative-rotative efficiency
open-water efficiency is improved by the propeller itself - limb (d)
hull efficiency, (1 - t) / (1 - w), is improved by changing the flow the hull delivers - limb (a)
relative rotative efficiency is where pre-swirl and post-swirl act - limbs (b) and (c)
so (a) works on the flow in, (b) puts rotation in, (c) takes rotation out, (d) improves the disc

steps.title: a) Wake Equalizing Devices
points: problem - strongly non-uniform inflow with a wake peak at the top of the disc and afterbody separation
consequences - cyclic blade loading, cavitation, hull pressure pulses, vibration and erosion
principle - an appendage ahead of the propeller accelerating and straightening the slow upper-disc water
forms - wake equalising duct as paired half-ring nozzles, flow-guiding fins, stern spoilers, stern tunnels
combined duct-and-fin devices belong to both this limb and limb (b)
gain a few per cent up to high single figures; the vibration benefit is often worth as much as the fuel
best on full-form high-block single-screw ships; on fine fast hulls the appendage drag can exceed the gain

steps.title: b) Pre-swirl Devices
points: problem - rotational kinetic energy left in the slipstream is pure loss
principle - impart rotation opposite to the propeller's direction upstream, so less net swirl leaves the disc
forms - fixed radial pre-swirl stators, characteristically asymmetric because the wake is asymmetric
pre-swirl ducts with internal stator fins - the most widely retrofitted device on full-form ships
asymmetric or twisted afterbodies at design stage
gain a few per cent, tuned to a design draught, speed and loading, so it falls away in ballast
cautions - added wetted surface and drag, blade-rate vibration, and a fatigue-critical welded appendage

steps.title: c) Post-swirl Devices
points: principle - recover downstream the swirl the propeller does impart, or remove the hub vortex
propeller boss cap fins - rotate with the propeller, break up the hub vortex, among the cheapest retrofits
rudder bulb aligned with the boss - fills the low-pressure hub region and reduces the hub vortex
rudder thrust fins - convert residual swirl into forward force, angled oppositely above and below the shaft line
twisted and asymmetric rudders - leading edge matched to the swirl angle, less drag and cavitation erosion
free-rotating vane wheels - theoretically attractive, structurally troublesome, not widely adopted
low single figures individually, more as a designed package; erosive flow makes material and inspection matter

steps.title: d) High-efficiency Propellers
points: larger diameter at lower revolutions - the single most effective measure, cutting axial loss
enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and aligned with slow steaming
tip-loaded and contracted-tip designs - end plates or winglets weakening the tip vortex
curved-tip designs achieving the same more smoothly with less cavitation risk
contra-rotating propellers - the largest gain, but concentric shafting and a complex sterntube arrangement
ducted propellers - accelerating nozzle for heavily loaded low-speed propellers, decelerating where noise dominates
blade geometry - skew, section shape, pitch distribution and blade area ratio matched to the actual profile

steps.title: Selection, verification and the cautions common to all four
points: every device is matched to a particular hull, draught, speed and loading, by CFD and model testing
slow steaming has moved the operating profile away from the design point
devices interact and gains are NOT additive - they are designed as a package
hull and propeller cleaning come first; fouling loses more than any device gains
verify a claimed gain in service against a measured baseline, on the ISO 19030 approach
welded appendages in cavitating flow need class approval, fatigue detailing, cathodic protection and survey
the gain feeds into EEXI, alongside engine or shaft power limitation, and into operational carbon intensity

quick_revision.recall_15s: THE DRIVER, dated precisely. EEDI put a number on new-ship design efficiency (attained must not exceed required, tightening by phase). The decisive change is months old: under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76), EEXI and the operational CII became applicable on 1 JANUARY 2023, with SEEMP Part III required on board from the same date. EEXI extended a design-efficiency requirement to EXISTING ships for the first time - that is why retrofits became commercially necessary, the alternative being engine or shaft power limitation. No ship has a CII rating yet: 2023 is the first data year, so owners are fitting devices in anticipation. Policy: the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018. Engineering link: CO2 is a fixed multiple of fuel burnt, so a percentage of propulsive efficiency is a percentage of emissions. WHERE THE LOSSES ARE - A-R-F-T plus inflow: Axial (energy in the slipstream, beaten by bigger and slower); Rotational (the slipstream spins - beaten before the disc by pre-swirl and after by post-swirl); Frictional and sectional (blade drag); Tip and hub vortex; and non-uniform inflow from the hull. THE FRAMEWORK. Quasi-propulsive efficiency = open-water x hull x relative rotative. Open-water is improved by (d); hull efficiency, (1-t)/(1-w), by (a); relative rotative by (b) and (c). One sentence: (a) fixes the flow IN, (b) puts rotation IN, (c) takes rotation OUT, (d) improves the DISC. a) WAKE EQUALIZING DEVICES. Problem: strongly non-uniform inflow behind a full-form single screw - a wake peak at the top of the disc and afterbody separation, giving cyclic blade loading, cavitation, hull pressure pulses, vibration and erosion. Principle: an appendage ahead of the propeller that accelerates and straightens the slow upper-disc water and suppresses separation, raising hull efficiency. Forms: the classic wake equalising duct (paired half-ring nozzles either side of the sternframe), flow-guiding fins, stern spoilers, stern tunnels and afterbody form change. A duct with internal pre-swirl fins belongs to both (a) and (b). Gain: a few per cent up to high single figures on a suitable hull - and the vibration and cavitation benefit is often worth as much as the fuel. Best on full-form, high-block, single-screw, moderate speed; on fine fast hulls the appendage drag can exceed the gain. b) PRE-SWIRL DEVICES. Impart rotation opposite to the propeller's direction upstream, so the propeller undoes it first and less net swirl leaves the disc. Forms: fixed radial pre-swirl stators, characteristically ASYMMETRIC because the single-screw wake is asymmetric; pre-swirl ducts with internal stator fins - the most widely retrofitted device on full-form ships; asymmetric or twisted afterbodies at design stage. Gain a few per cent, tuned to a design draught, speed and loading, so it falls away in ballast or at part load and a badly matched stator can cost efficiency. Cautions: added wetted surface and drag, blade-rate vibration, and a fatigue-critical welded appendage. c) POST-SWIRL DEVICES. Recover downstream whatever swirl the propeller imparts, or remove the hub vortex. Propeller boss cap fins - rotate with the propeller, break up the hub vortex, low single figures, among the cheapest retrofits, and they cut hub-vortex cavitation and rudder erosion. Rudder bulb aligned with the boss, filling the low-pressure hub region. Rudder thrust fins converting residual swirl to forward force, angled oppositely above and below the shaft line because the swirl reverses sense. Twisted / asymmetric rudders - leading edge matched to the swirl angle. Free-rotating vane wheels - attractive in theory, troublesome in service. Low single figures individually, more as a designed package; erosive cavitating flow makes material, cathodic protection and inspection matter, and a lost fin threatens rudder and propeller. d) HIGH-EFFICIENCY PROPELLERS. Larger diameter at lower revolutions is the single most effective measure - a larger mass of water accelerated to a smaller velocity increase - enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and aligned with slow steaming. Tip-loaded / contracted-tip designs with end plates or winglets weakening the tip vortex; curved-tip designs doing it more smoothly. Contra-rotating - two coaxial propellers turning oppositely, the after recovering the forward's rotation: largest gain, but concentric shafting and a complex sterntube arrangement. Ducted - accelerating (Kort) nozzle for heavily loaded propellers at low speed (tugs, trawlers); decelerating where cavitation and radiated noise dominate. Blade geometry - skew to spread passage through the wake peak, plus section shape, pitch distribution and blade area ratio matched to the ACTUAL profile. COMMON CAUTIONS. Matched by CFD and model testing to one hull and condition; slow steaming has moved the operating point; gains are NOT additive; clean the hull and propeller first; verify against a measured baseline on the ISO 19030 approach; and they need class approval, fatigue detailing, cathodic protection and survey. Give NO single precise percentage - always an indicative range with the hull and condition attached.

quick_revision.major_trap: Letting limb (d) swallow the answer. The paper prints (4) against each of the four limbs, so high-efficiency propellers are worth exactly as much as boss cap fins, and an answer that spends half its length on contra-rotating propellers has thrown marks away. The second trap is confusing pre-swirl with post-swirl: pre-swirl acts ahead of the disc and imparts rotation against the propeller's direction so that less net swirl leaves it; post-swirl acts behind the disc and recovers what the propeller has already imparted. The third is quoting a single precise percentage for a device - published gains are obtained on one hull at one draught and speed and do not transfer, so give an indicative range and always attach the condition. The fourth is temporal: at this sitting EEXI and CII are barely three months old and NO ship has a CII rating, so the driver is anticipation of a rating rather than enforcement of one, and neither the 2023 GHG Strategy nor the EU ETS exists yet.

questions.understand_first: A propeller wastes energy in a small number of identifiable ways, and once you know what they are, every device in this question explains itself. Some of the energy goes into water thrown backwards faster than it needed to be - fixed by pushing a bigger column of water more gently, which means a larger, slower propeller. Some goes into spinning the water rather than moving it aft, and spinning water pushes nothing; that waste can be attacked twice, once by twisting the flow the opposite way before it reaches the blades so the propeller has less spin left to give it, and once by catching the spin afterwards and turning it back into forward push. Some is wasted because the hull does not hand the propeller a clean, even stream of water - the flow arriving at the top of the circle is sluggish and disturbed - so each blade is loaded and unloaded as it goes round, which costs efficiency and also shakes the ship and eats the blades. And some leaks away in tight whirlpools shed at the blade tips and at the hub. The reason all this suddenly became urgent is that fuel burnt and carbon emitted are the same quantity measured two ways, so anything that improves the hydrodynamics is now a compliance measure and not merely an economy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the propulsion-efficiency devices question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why the devices exist and where the losses are. 2 The efficiency framework that classifies the limbs. 3 Wake equalizing devices. 4 Pre-swirl devices. 5 Post-swirl devices. 6 High-efficiency propellers. 7 Selection, verification and the common cautions.
retrieval_cards.why: Four printed limbs at four marks each, wrapped in an opening that answers the stem's 'why' and a closing that stops the answer reading as a catalogue.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the components of quasi-propulsive efficiency, and which device type improves each?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is the product of open-water efficiency, hull efficiency and relative rotative efficiency. Open-water efficiency is improved by the propeller design itself; hull efficiency, expressed as one minus thrust deduction over one minus wake fraction, is improved by wake equalizing devices; and relative rotative efficiency is where pre-swirl and post-swirl devices act.
retrieval_cards.why: It turns four apparently unrelated limbs into three efficiency terms, which is what separates a system answer from a list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish pre-swirl from post-swirl devices.
retrieval_cards.answer: Pre-swirl devices sit ahead of the propeller and impart rotation opposite to the propeller's own direction, so the propeller must undo that counter-rotation first and less net swirl leaves the disc. Post-swirl devices sit behind the propeller and recover the swirl it has already imparted, converting slipstream rotation into axial thrust or removing the hub vortex.
retrieval_cards.why: Before or behind, and rotation put in or taken out - the two are constantly confused and the distinction is the heart of limbs (b) and (c).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What problem does a wake equalizing device solve, and what does it deliver besides fuel?
retrieval_cards.answer: Behind a full-form single-screw hull the inflow is strongly non-uniform, with a wake peak at the top of the disc and afterbody separation, so each blade passes cyclically between fast and slow water. The device accelerates and straightens the slow upper-disc water and suppresses separation. Besides fuel it delivers reduced cyclic blade loading, cavitation, hull pressure pulses, vibration and erosion - often worth as much as the fuel saving.
retrieval_cards.why: The vibration and cavitation benefit is the part most candidates omit, and on many ships it is the reason the device was fitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a pre-swirl stator usually asymmetric?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the wake field behind a single-screw hull is itself asymmetric - the propeller's rotation and the hull's flow interact differently on the two sides. The stator is therefore built with different fin numbers, angles and lengths port and starboard to match the flow it actually sees.
retrieval_cards.why: A single detail that demonstrates the device is matched to a real flow field rather than bolted on symmetrically for neatness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the main post-swirl devices and what each does.
retrieval_cards.answer: Propeller boss cap fins, rotating with the propeller to break up the hub vortex. A rudder bulb aligned with the boss, filling the low-pressure hub region. Rudder thrust fins, converting residual swirl into forward force and angled oppositely above and below the shaft line because the swirl reverses sense. Twisted or asymmetric rudders, with the leading edge matched to the local swirl angle. And free-rotating vane wheels, attractive in theory but troublesome in service.
retrieval_cards.why: Five named devices with a mechanism each is exactly what a four-mark limb needs, and the thrust-fin angling detail shows real understanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the single most effective high-efficiency propeller measure?
retrieval_cards.answer: A larger diameter turning at lower revolutions. Accelerating a larger mass of water to a smaller velocity increase cuts axial loss directly. It is enabled by long-stroke low-speed engines and a suitable aperture, and it aligns naturally with slow steaming.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates reach for exotic blade designs when the biggest gain is the simplest change, and saying so first frames the whole limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why would you fit a Kort nozzle to a tug but not to a container ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: An accelerating nozzle benefits a heavily loaded propeller working at low speed, which is a tug's or trawler's condition at bollard pull. On a fast ship with a lightly loaded propeller the nozzle's own drag exceeds any benefit. A decelerating nozzle is a different case, used where cavitation and radiated noise dominate.
retrieval_cards.why: It tests whether the candidate understands that a device is matched to a loading condition rather than being generally good.

retrieval_cards.prompt: An owner fits a pre-swirl stator and boss cap fins together. Do the claimed gains add up?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The pre-swirl stator changes the flow that the post-swirl device sees, so the two interact and the combined gain is less than the sum of the individual claims. They should be designed as a matched package by CFD and model testing on the actual hull, and the result verified in service against a measured baseline.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating catalogue percentages as additive is the commonest commercial error in this field and a reliable examiner question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the 'recent stress on the control of emission' at this sitting, precisely?
retrieval_cards.answer: EEXI and the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator became applicable on 1 January 2023 under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76), with the SEEMP Part III required on board from the same date - about three months before this examination. EEXI extended a design-efficiency requirement to existing ships for the first time, the alternative to efficiency measures being engine or shaft power limitation. 2023 is the first CII data-collection year, so no ship has yet been rated and owners are acting in anticipation.
retrieval_cards.why: Dating the driver precisely is worth more than a general remark about decarbonisation, and it keeps later instruments out of the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What should you do before fitting any energy-saving device?
retrieval_cards.answer: Clean and inspect the hull and propeller. A fouled hull or a rough, damaged or unpolished propeller will lose more efficiency than any of these devices can gain, so hull and propeller husbandry comes first. Then establish what draught, speed and loading the ship actually operates at, because every device is tuned to a condition.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows the candidate can rank measures by value rather than reciting the most technically interesting one.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The absence of any precise efficiency percentage, any proprietary device or manufacturer name, and any CII band, reduction factor or EEXI reference-line figure
reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate on all three counts. Published gains are hull-, draught- and speed-specific and do not transfer, so every figure here is an indicative range with its condition attached. Product names date and earn no marks. And the numerical CII and EEXI parameters are not required by the question and would be premature at a sitting where no ship had been rated.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A four-limb technical question with a regulatory preamble that is doing real work. The stem asserts that emission control has DRIVEN the development of these devices, so the answer must establish the causal link - fuel burnt equals carbon emitted, so hydrodynamics became a compliance subject - and must date that driver correctly for the sitting. The four limbs then map onto the three components of quasi-propulsive efficiency, and the best answers show that rather than listing devices.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as four limbs at (4) each - the only limb-by-limb split printed anywhere on this paper. Equal space to each limb, with a short framing section before and a short synthesis section after, neither of which may be allowed to displace limb content.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For the preamble: a dated, specific account of the regulatory driver rather than a general remark about decarbonisation. For (a): the non-uniform wake and its consequences, the principle of accelerating and straightening the upper-disc flow, named forms, and the hull-form dependence. For (b): rotational loss, counter-rotation imparted upstream, the asymmetric stator and the pre-swirl duct, and the tuning to a condition. For (c): recovery downstream, with boss cap fins, rudder bulb, thrust fins and twisted rudder named and each given a mechanism. For (d): larger diameter at lower revolutions first, then tip loading, contra-rotating, ducted propellers and blade geometry. Throughout: indicative ranges rather than precise figures, and the conditions attached.

Establish specifically that EEXI and CII applied from 1 January 2023 and that 2023 is the first data year, so no rating existed at the sitting
Confirm that the 2023 GHG Strategy, the EU ETS maritime extension and MEPC.395(82) are all after the sitting, and exclude them

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - and unusually asymmetric. The four technical limbs are hydrodynamics and carry no amendment boundary at all, so a 22-month donor gap is harmless on them. The opening section is entirely sitting-relative and sits only three months after a major entry into force and three months before a major policy adoption, so it had to be re-derived from scratch and cannot inherit a single sentence from the donor.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the instruments are international and no Indian statutory limb is engaged. The Merchant Shipping Act boundary does not arise.
technical_ambiguities: The categories in the printed limbs are not watertight - a duct with internal stator fins is both a wake equalizing device and a pre-swirl device, and saying so is better than forcing it into one limb
'Wake equalizing' is often used loosely for any pre-propeller appendage, including pure pre-swirl stators
Published efficiency gains are hull-, draught- and speed-specific and do not transfer between ships
Gains from multiple devices are not additive, because each changes the flow the next one sees
Slow steaming has moved many ships away from the design condition to which a device would be tuned
A high-efficiency propeller and an energy-saving appendage are alternatives as much as complements, since re-matching the propeller to the actual operating profile may deliver more than any appendage
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Open by dating the regulatory driver precisely - EEDI, then EEXI and CII from 1 January 2023 with no ratings yet - and close that section with the loss decomposition, so every device can later be attached to a named loss. Then each limb in the same four-part shape - problem, principle, forms, gain and limits - at equal length. blocks.h: 1. The background - the gap the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: The International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage was adopted on 23 March 2001 and entered into force on 21 November 2008. It exists to close a specific and well-recognised hole.

ul: CLC 1992 reaches only tankers. Its definitions confine it to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried in bulk as cargo - and to the bunkers of such a ship.

Every other ship in the world fleet fell outside it. A large bulk carrier, container ship or cruise ship may carry several thousand tonnes of heavy fuel oil in her own bunker tanks - more than the entire cargo of a small tanker - and a grounding could release it.

Before 2001 there was no dedicated regime for that oil. No strict liability, no compulsory insurance, no certificate and no direct action against an insurer. A claimant had to prove fault under national law and then hope the owner was solvent and reachable.

The Convention closes the gap by taking the CLC architecture and applying it to bunkers - which was deliberate, because it meant the existing P&I machinery could simply be extended rather than rebuilt.

blocks.h: 2. Its relevance - where it sits in the liability architecture

blocks.p: Its relevance is best shown by putting it in its place among the three regimes, because that is also the frame for the comparison the question asks for:

rows: Persistent oil carried as cargo by a tanker
Yes - the 1992 Fund and the Supplementary Fund
The fuel of every ship, whatever she carries

blocks.p: So the Bunker Convention completes the map, and it does so without a cargo-financed second tier. That single omission is the source of most of the differences the rest of this answer sets out - most importantly the fact that the Convention sets no limit of its own.

blocks.h: 3. (a) Pollution damage and exclusions

blocks.p: Definition first, as the question directs. Under article 1.9, pollution damage means:

ul: loss or damage caused OUTSIDE the ship BY CONTAMINATION resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, wherever it occurs - provided that compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit from that impairment, is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and
the costs of preventive measures, and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

blocks.p: How it differs from CLC. The structure of the definition is identical - contamination outside the ship, the reinstatement proviso, preventive measures. What differs is the oil. CLC reaches only persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried as cargo; the Bunker Convention reaches bunker oil, defined at article 1.5 as any hydrocarbon mineral oil, INCLUDING LUBRICATING OIL, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of it. Note three things in that definition: it is not confined to persistent oil, it expressly includes lubricating oil, and it turns on the oil's use rather than on its carriage.
The exclusions:

ol: Article 4.1 - the CLC carve-out. The Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention. This is the load-bearing exclusion and the wording matters: the carve-out attaches to the definition, not to the outcome. So if a CLC claim fails - the fund is exhausted, a defence succeeds, the flag State is not a party - the claim does not fall back into the Bunker Convention.
Article 4.2 - warships and State-owned ships used on government non-commercial service.

Geographic scope, article 2 - the Convention applies exclusively to pollution damage in the territory, including the territorial sea, and in the exclusive economic zone of a State Party; but to preventive measures wherever taken, which is a deliberately wider reach so that a response mounted on the high seas is still covered.
Note that the shipowner's defences are a different thing and should not be listed here - they go under limb (c).

blocks.h: 4. (b) Time limits for claims

blocks.p: This limb is short, and its point is that there is no difference at all - which is itself the answer and should be stated plainly. Under Bunkers article 8, and identically under CLC article VIII:

ul: Rights to compensation are extinguished unless an action is brought within THREE YEARS from the date the damage occurred;
and in no case later than SIX YEARS from the date of the incident;
where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six years run from the date of the first occurrence.

blocks.p: Two refinements are worth a line each. The provision extinguishes the right rather than merely barring the remedy, which is stronger than an ordinary limitation period. And the contrast that shows breadth is with HNS, where the period runs three years from KNOWLEDGE of the damage rather than from its occurrence, with a ten-year long stop - a deliberately more generous scheme, because chemical harm may not be apparent for years.

blocks.h: 5. (c) Liability of the shipowner

blocks.p: Definition first. Under article 3.1 the shipowner at the time of an incident is strictly liable for pollution damage caused by any bunker oil on board or originating from the ship. Strict liability means no proof of fault is required. There are only three defences, under article 3.3, and they are the same three CLC provides:

ol: an act of war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection, or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon;
an act or omission done by a third party with intent to cause damage;
the negligence of an authority responsible for the maintenance of navigational aids.

blocks.p: Here is the sharpest difference in the whole question, and it runs in opposite directions:

rows: The 'shipowner', defined at article 1.3 to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager AND operator
Channels INWARD - article III bars claims against crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor
Spreads OUTWARD - article 3.2 makes them jointly and severally liable
One defendant, easy to identify, backed by a certificate
Several possible defendants, any of whom may be sued for the whole

blocks.p: This is the difference candidates most often get backwards, so state it in one memorable line: CLC funnels liability in; Bunkers spreads it out.

blocks.h: 6. (c) Limitation of liability - the structural difference

blocks.p: The second half of limb (c), and structurally the most important difference of all.

ul: CLC has its own, self-contained limits. Article V sets a tonnage-based scale - 4,510,000 units of account for a ship not exceeding 5,000 gross tonnage, 631 units of account for each additional ton, subject to an overall ceiling of 89,770,000 units of account. The owner constitutes a limitation fund with the court, and the fund is available exclusively to pollution claimants. Behind it stand the 1992 Fund and the Supplementary Fund. The right to limit is lost where the damage resulted from the owner's personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.

The Bunker Convention sets NO figure at all. Article 6 expressly preserves the shipowner's right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, such as the LLMC as amended - and stops there.

Three consequences follow, and they are the marks in this half of the limb. First, the limit is tonnage-based under a general convention, not a pollution-specific one. Second, the bunker claim shares one general limitation fund with every other claim arising from the same incident - cargo, wreck removal where applicable, personal injury - instead of having a fund to itself. And third, there is no second tier: no bunker equivalent of the IOPC Fund exists, so once the LLMC fund is exhausted the claimant has nowhere else to go.
The practical result is that a large bunker spill from a very large ship can exhaust the available fund in a way a comparable CLC incident would not.

blocks.h: 7. (d) Compulsory insurance and financial security

blocks.p: Definition first. Under article 7, the registered owner of a ship of more than 1,000 gross tonnage registered in a State Party must maintain insurance or other financial security - a bank guarantee or a certificate from a compensation fund - to cover liability for pollution damage, in an amount equal to the applicable limits of liability and not exceeding an amount calculated under the LLMC as amended. A certificate in the annexed model form is issued to each ship and carried on board.

rows: The CARGO - more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo
The registered owner alone, although liability is wider
The applicable limitation regime, capped at the LLMC calculation

ul: Note the asymmetry inside the Bunker Convention itself, which is a good discriminating point: liability under article 3 is wide - owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator - but the duty to insure under article 7 falls on the registered owner alone. A claimant therefore has several possible defendants but only one certificate to look at.

Direct action against the insurer is provided in both. The insurer may invoke the defences the shipowner himself could have invoked, and - importantly - may limit liability even where the shipowner has lost the right to limit. The insurer may also plead the shipowner's own wilful misconduct.
In practice the security is a P&I club undertaking - the club issues a "blue card" to the flag State, which issues the certificate. Issue may be delegated to a recognised organisation.

Article 7.12 is the enforcement teeth: a State Party must ensure that ships of ANY flag entering or leaving its ports carry the certificate. So the Convention reaches ships registered in non-party States the moment they call at a party State's port, and a missing certificate is a detainable deficiency.

blocks.p: Taken together, the four limbs give the summary the question is really asking for: the Bunker Convention borrows CLC's definitions and its time limits, widens who is liable, narrows nothing, and gives up CLC's dedicated limitation fund and its second tier in exchange.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints four limbs at (4) each plus an unmarked opening on background and relevance, so budget the opening at about two or three minutes and give the four limbs equal space. Note the exact command: "Define the following under Bunker Convention and explain how they differ from other similar Convention such as CLC 92". That is a two-step instruction and the marks follow it: define the Bunker position FIRST, then compare. An answer that opens each limb with a comparison has inverted the examiner's own order and will read as a general essay on two conventions. Use the same shape in every limb - Bunker definition, then the CLC difference - and it is fast to write and impossible to mark down.

blocks.h: The one sentence that carries the comparison

blocks.p: The Bunker Convention borrows CLC's definitions and its time limits, widens who is liable, and gives up CLC's dedicated fund and its second tier. Every difference in the question is an instance of that sentence: limb (a) is a borrowed definition with a different oil, limb (b) is identical, limb (c) is the widening, and limb (d) is the different threshold that follows from having no cargo to measure.

blocks.h: CLC funnels IN, Bunkers spreads OUT - the difference most often reversed

ul: CLC channels liability INWARD to the registered owner alone. Article III expressly bars claims against servants, agents, crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. One defendant, and everyone else is protected.
Bunkers spreads liability OUTWARD. Article 1.3 defines 'shipowner' to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, and article 3.2 makes them jointly and severally liable.
But note the twist inside the Bunker Convention: the duty to insure under article 7 falls on the REGISTERED OWNER alone, even though liability is wide. Liability is broad; the certificate is narrow.

blocks.h: The limitation point is structural, and it is where the best marks are

blocks.p: CLC contains its own limits and its own fund. The tonnage scale runs from 4,510,000 units of account for a ship of not more than 5,000 gross tonnage, rising by 631 units of account per additional ton, to a ceiling of 89,770,000 units of account; the fund is constituted with the court and is available exclusively to pollution claimants; and the 1992 Fund and Supplementary Fund stand behind it. The Bunker Convention contains no figure whatever. Article 6 simply preserves limitation under whatever regime applies, in practice the LLMC as amended. Three consequences: the limit is tonnage-based under a general convention; the bunker claim competes with every other claim from the same incident in a single fund; and there is no second tier at all. A candidate who says "the Bunker Convention limit is X" has missed the entire point - the Convention has no limit of its own.

blocks.h: The two thresholds - cargo against ship

ul: CLC certificate: more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo. A cargo threshold - so the same ship may need the certificate on one voyage and not on another.
Bunkers certificate: gross tonnage over 1,000. A ship threshold - so it does not change with the trade, which is exactly why the Bunker certificate is carried permanently.
That difference is not arbitrary. CLC measures the risk by the cargo, because the cargo is the hazard; Bunkers measures it by the ship, because the ship's own fuel is roughly a function of her size.

blocks.h: The carve-out phrase - memorise it word for word

blocks.p: "Whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention." Article 4.1 excludes CLC pollution damage on that basis, and the HNS Convention uses the identical formula. It means the exclusion attaches to the definition and not to the result. A claim that falls within the CLC definition is outside the Bunker Convention even if CLC recovery fails entirely - because the limit is exhausted, because a defence succeeds, or because the flag State is not a party. The regimes tile; they are not safety nets for one another.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying the Bunker Convention has a limit. It has none - article 6 refers out to the LLMC.
Reversing the channelling: CLC is the exclusive one; Bunkers is the wide one.
Forgetting that the insurance duty falls on the registered owner alone although liability is wider.
Giving the CLC threshold as a tonnage or the Bunkers threshold as a cargo quantity. Cargo for CLC, ship size for Bunkers.
Saying bunker oil must be persistent. It need not be - the definition turns on use, and expressly includes lubricating oil.
Listing the shipowner's defences under the exclusions limb. Exclusions are what the Convention does not apply to; defences are answers to a claim it does apply to.
Saying a failed CLC claim can be brought under Bunkers. It cannot - whether or not compensation is payable.
Missing that preventive measures are covered wherever taken, while damage is confined to the territory, territorial sea and EEZ.
Forgetting that the time limits are identical - which is a complete answer to limb (b) and a mark in itself.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"A tanker in ballast spills her own bunkers. Which convention?" CLC still reaches her - it covers oil in the bunkers of a ship constructed or adapted to carry oil in bulk as cargo, and the Bunker Convention's article 4.1 excludes CLC pollution damage. So the answer is CLC, and the reasoning matters more than the answer.

"The owner's LLMC fund is exhausted by cargo and injury claims. What does the bunker claimant get?" A rateable share and nothing more. There is no second tier behind the Bunker Convention, which is precisely the structural weakness the comparison should draw out.

"The ship is registered in a State that is not a party. Does she need a certificate in an Indian port?" Yes. Article 7.12 requires a State Party to ensure that ships of any flag entering or leaving its ports carry the certificate.

"The owner lost his right to limit. Can the insurer still limit?" Yes. On direct action the insurer may limit even where the shipowner is not entitled to, and may raise the defences the shipowner could have raised, plus the shipowner's own wilful misconduct.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: When was the Bunker Convention adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted 23 March 2001; in force 21 November 2008.
What gap does it fill? Pollution from the bunkers of non-tankers, which CLC never reached.
Define bunker oil. Any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of it.

Define pollution damage. Loss or damage outside the ship by contamination, with environmental impairment limited to reasonable reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken, plus the costs of preventive measures.
Who is the 'shipowner'? The registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator - jointly and severally liable.
What are the three defences? War or an exceptional natural phenomenon; a third party's intentional act; and negligence of a navigational-aid authority.
What is the limit of liability? The Convention sets none - article 6 refers out to the LLMC as amended.
What is the insurance threshold? Gross tonnage over 1,000, against CLC's 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo.
What is the time bar? Three years from when the damage occurred, six years absolute from the incident.
Is there a bunker fund? No. That is the main structural difference from CLC.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence

blocks.p: Neither treaty text is held by the MIW corpus. The corpus classifies the whole liability-and-compensation family as citation and index only, with verified status facts and no text - so every article-level statement in this answer is internal verified reuse of an MIW record in which both the 2001 Bunkers Convention and the 1992 Civil Liability Convention were read in full from the official published texts. It is labelled that way throughout and is not presented as a reading made here. The position is nevertheless reasonably strong, because two independent MIW answers ten months and twenty-nine months from this sitting trace to that same full-text reading and state the same article content. Three restraints are deliberate. No LLMC limitation figure is reproduced: the Bunker Convention has no limit of its own, the comparison the question asks for is structural, and the LLMC table would add length without adding a mark. No currency conversion is given for any unit of account, since SDR rates move daily and no held source fixes one at this sitting. And India's party status is not asserted, nor is the number of States party to either convention - both are status facts that date, neither could be established for this sitting, and no printed limb requires either. The two monetary limits that are given were checked for their in-force dates against the sitting: the CLC amounts took effect in 2003 and the LLMC increases on 8 June 2015, twenty years and eight years before this examination.

quick_revision.recall_15s: BACKGROUND. The Bunker Oil Pollution Damage Convention was adopted 23 March 2001 and entered into force 21 November 2008. The gap: CLC 1992 reaches only persistent hydrocarbon MINERAL oil carried in bulk as cargo (and the bunkers of such a ship), so every non-tanker - bulk carriers, container ships, cruise ships carrying thousands of tonnes of heavy fuel in their own tanks - had no strict liability, no compulsory insurance, no certificate and no direct action. It borrows CLC's architecture deliberately, so existing P&I machinery could be extended rather than rebuilt. RELEVANCE: it completes the map - CLC (tanker cargo oil) - BUNKERS (every ship's fuel) - HNS (other cargoes) - and it is the only one of the three with NO second tier. That single omission drives most of the differences. (a) POLLUTION DAMAGE AND EXCLUSIONS. Article 1.9: loss or damage caused OUTSIDE the ship BY CONTAMINATION from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, with compensation for impairment of the environment (other than loss of profit) limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; plus the costs of preventive measures and further loss caused by them. The structure is IDENTICAL to CLC's - what differs is the OIL. Article 1.5 bunker oil = any hydrocarbon mineral oil, INCLUDING LUBRICATING OIL, used or intended for the OPERATION OR PROPULSION of the ship, and residues - not confined to persistent oil, and turning on use not carriage. Exclusions: article 4.1 - CLC pollution damage, WHETHER OR NOT compensation is payable under that Convention (the carve-out bites on the definition, so a failed CLC claim does NOT fall back here); article 4.2 - warships and State non-commercial ships; and article 2 scope - damage in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ, but preventive measures WHEREVER taken. Do not list the shipowner's defences here - they belong to limb (c). (b) TIME LIMITS - IDENTICAL IN BOTH, and saying so is the answer. Article 8 (and CLC article VIII): THREE YEARS from the date the damage occurred, and in no case later than SIX YEARS from the date of the incident; a series of occurrences runs the six years from the first. The right is EXTINGUISHED, not merely barred. Contrast HNS: three years from KNOWLEDGE, ten years absolute. (c) LIABILITY - the direction is the mark. Article 3.1: the shipowner at the time of the incident is strictly liable for pollution damage from bunker oil on board or originating from the ship. Three defences (same as CLC): act of war or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; a third party's act done with intent to cause damage; and the negligence of a navigational-aid authority. CLC channels INWARD - article III fixes the registered owner ALONE and bars claims against servants, agents, crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. BUNKERS SPREADS OUTWARD - article 1.3 defines 'shipowner' to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager AND operator, and article 3.2 makes them JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY liable. CLC funnels in; Bunkers spreads out. (c) LIMITATION - the structural difference and the best marks. CLC has its OWN limits (article V): 4,510,000 units of account up to 5,000 GT, +631 per additional ton, ceiling 89,770,000 units of account; the fund is constituted with the court and reserved to pollution claimants; behind it stand the 1992 Fund and the Supplementary Fund; the right to limit is lost on personal intent or recklessness with knowledge. THE BUNKER CONVENTION SETS NO FIGURE AT ALL - article 6 merely preserves limitation under the applicable regime, in practice the LLMC as amended. Three consequences: the limit is tonnage-based under a GENERAL convention; the bunker claim shares ONE fund with every other claim from the incident; and there is NO second tier. (d) COMPULSORY INSURANCE. Article 7: the registered owner of a ship of more than 1,000 gross tonnage registered in a State Party must maintain insurance or other financial security up to the applicable limit, capped by the LLMC calculation, evidenced by a certificate in the annexed model form carried on board. THRESHOLDS: Bunkers = SHIP SIZE (over 1,000 GT); CLC = CARGO (more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo). Note the asymmetry: liability is wide, but the duty to insure falls on the REGISTERED OWNER alone. Direct action against the insurer in both, and the insurer may limit even where the shipowner cannot. In practice a P&I 'blue card' supports the flag State's certificate. Article 7.12 - port States enforce it on ships of ANY flag, so a missing certificate is a detainable deficiency. SUMMARY LINE: the Bunker Convention borrows CLC's definitions and time limits, widens who is liable, and gives up CLC's dedicated fund and its second tier.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Bunker Oil Pollution Damage Convention 2001 - article 1.5 defining bunker oil as any hydrocarbon mineral oil including lubricating oil used for the operation or propulsion of the ship; article 1.9 defining pollution damage as loss or damage outside the ship by contamination with environmental impairment limited to reasonable reinstatement; article 3 imposing strict, joint and several liability on a widely defined shipowner subject to three defences; article 4.1 excluding CLC pollution damage whether or not compensation is payable under that Convention; article 6 preserving limitation under the applicable regime and setting no figure of its own; article 7 requiring compulsory insurance for ships over 1,000 gross tonnage with a certificate and direct action; and article 8 barring claims after three years from the damage and six years from the incident. Compared throughout with CLC 1992 articles I, III, V, VII and VIII.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the Bunker Convention has a limit of liability. It has none of its own - article 6 simply preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, in practice the LLMC as amended, which means the bunker claim shares one general fund with every other claim from the incident and has no second tier behind it. That is the structural heart of the comparison. The second trap is reversing the channelling: CLC channels inward to the registered owner alone and bars claims against everyone else, while the Bunker Convention spreads outward to the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally - and yet the duty to insure still falls on the registered owner alone. The third is the thresholds: CLC is triggered by the CARGO (more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk), Bunkers by the SHIP (over 1,000 gross tonnage). The fourth is thinking a failed CLC claim can be brought under the Bunker Convention - article 4.1 excludes CLC pollution damage whether or not compensation is payable, so the exclusion bites on the definition and the regimes tile rather than backing each other up.

questions.understand_first: Two ships can spill the same oil and, until fairly recently, only one of them would have been covered by a proper compensation system. The older system was written after tanker disasters, so it was built around the idea of a ship whose cargo is oil. That left an odd gap: a large container ship or bulk carrier is not carrying oil as cargo at all, but she is carrying several thousand tonnes of heavy fuel to burn, which is more than the whole cargo of a small tanker, and if she goes on the rocks that fuel comes out. Anybody harmed by it had to fall back on ordinary law - prove somebody was at fault, find out who actually owns the ship, and hope there is money behind the name. The newer convention copies the older one almost point for point to fix that: no need to prove fault, insurance made compulsory, a certificate carried aboard, and the right to sue the insurer directly. Two things are different, and they pull in opposite directions. It casts the net of who can be sued much wider, catching the manager and operator as well as the owner on paper. But it never wrote down a ceiling of its own, and it never set up a fund financed by anyone else - so when the money runs out, it runs out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Bunker Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The background and the gap it closes. 2 Its relevance and place between CLC and HNS. 3 (a) Pollution damage and exclusions. 4 (b) Time limits. 5 (c) Liability of the shipowner. 6 (c) Limitation of liability. 7 (d) Compulsory insurance and financial security.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) prints two demands - liability and limitation - so it needs two sections, and limitation is where the structural difference lies.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define bunker oil and pollution damage under the Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Bunker oil means any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of it. Pollution damage means loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, with compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken, together with the costs of preventive measures.
retrieval_cards.why: The question says 'define', so the definitions must come first and be given accurately before any comparison.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the oil covered differ between CLC and the Bunker Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC reaches only persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried in bulk as cargo, and the bunkers of such a ship. The Bunker Convention reaches bunker oil defined by its use - any hydrocarbon mineral oil used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship - so it is not confined to persistent oil and it expressly includes lubricating oil.
retrieval_cards.why: Carriage versus use is the single distinction that decides which convention applies to any given spill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A CLC claim fails because the fund is exhausted. Can the balance be claimed under the Bunker Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article 4.1 excludes pollution damage as defined in the CLC whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention. The exclusion attaches to the definition, not to the outcome, so a shortfall in CLC recovery does not move the claim into the Bunker Convention.
retrieval_cards.why: The regimes are drafted to tile, not to act as safety nets for one another, and the phrase is identical to the HNS carve-out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the time limits, and how do they compare?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three years from the date the damage occurred, and in no case later than six years from the date of the incident; where the incident consists of a series of occurrences the six years run from the first. They are identical in the Bunker Convention and in CLC. The right is extinguished rather than merely barred. HNS differs - three years from knowledge of the damage, with a ten-year long stop.
retrieval_cards.why: That the two are identical is itself the answer to the limb, and the HNS contrast shows you know why the periods are set differently.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is liable under each convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under CLC, the registered owner alone - article III channels liability inward and bars claims against servants, agents, crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. Under the Bunker Convention, the 'shipowner' is defined to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, and article 3.2 makes them jointly and severally liable. CLC funnels liability in; Bunkers spreads it out.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the difference most often stated backwards, and the one-line summary makes it hard to reverse.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Bunker Convention's limit of liability?
retrieval_cards.answer: It has none of its own. Article 6 preserves the shipowner's right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, in practice the LLMC as amended. So the limit is tonnage-based under a general convention, the bunker claim shares a single limitation fund with every other claim arising from the same incident, and there is no second tier - no bunker equivalent of the IOPC Fund.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting a Bunker Convention figure is the single commonest error on this question, and the absence of a limit is the structural point.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are CLC's own limits?
retrieval_cards.answer: 4,510,000 units of account for a ship not exceeding 5,000 gross tonnage, rising by 631 units of account for each additional ton, subject to an overall ceiling of 89,770,000 units of account. The owner constitutes a limitation fund with the court, available exclusively to pollution claimants, with the 1992 Fund and the Supplementary Fund behind it.
retrieval_cards.why: The contrast only works if you can show what CLC has that the Bunker Convention does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What triggers the compulsory insurance requirement under each convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under the Bunker Convention it is the ship - a gross tonnage over 1,000, registered in a State Party. Under CLC it is the cargo - carrying more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo. CLC measures the risk by the hazard being carried; the Bunker Convention measures it by the size of the ship, because her own fuel is roughly a function of that.
retrieval_cards.why: Cargo threshold against ship threshold, and the reason for the difference is worth a sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Liability is wide under the Bunker Convention. Who has to insure?
retrieval_cards.answer: The registered owner alone. Article 3 makes the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally liable, but the article 7 duty to maintain insurance and hold the certificate falls on the registered owner only. A claimant therefore has several possible defendants but a single certificate to look at.
retrieval_cards.why: The asymmetry inside the Convention is a discriminating point that shows the candidate has read past the headline.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the certificate requirement reach a ship registered in a non-party State?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Article 7.12 requires each State Party to ensure that ships of any flag entering or leaving its ports carry the certificate, so the requirement reaches a non-party-flagged ship the moment she calls at a party State's port. A missing certificate is a detainable deficiency.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the Convention is effectively universal in practice despite binding only its parties.
