The real subject is the architecture of the pollution-liability system - why three conventions exist, what each is triggered by, and what the Bunker Convention gave up in exchange for its wider reach.

Then, limb by limb: the article 1.9 definition of pollution damage with the reinstatement proviso and preventive measures, and the article 4 exclusions with the 'whether or not compensation is payable' formula; the identical three-year and six-year time bar; strict liability with the three defences and the contrast between CLC's inward channelling and the Bunker Convention's outward spread; the fact that the Bunker Convention sets no limit of its own and refers out to the LLMC, with no second tier; and the article 7 insurance requirement with its ship-size threshold against CLC's cargo threshold, the certificate, direct action and port-State enforcement on any flag.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - and established rather than assumed. CLC 1992 has been in force since 30 May 1996 and the Bunker Convention since 21 November 2008, twenty-seven and fourteen years before this sitting. Neither was amended across the donor gap. The only date-sensitive elements are the two monetary limits, and both were checked: the CLC amounts took effect in 2003 and the LLMC increases in 2015.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the question is international and sets no Indian limb, so the Merchant Shipping Act boundary that governs this batch does not reach it. India's party status is not asserted.
technical_ambiguities: 'Exclusions' in limb (a) means what the Convention does not apply to, and is a different thing from the shipowner's defences under article 3.3 - the two are routinely merged
The Bunker Convention has no limitation figure of its own, which reads like an omission and is in fact its defining structural feature
Persistence and mineral origin are two separate CLC tests, and the Bunker Convention requires neither persistence
Liability under article 3 is wide but the insurance duty under article 7 is narrow, which looks like an inconsistency and is deliberate
The geographic scope for damage and for preventive measures is deliberately different - EEZ for the one, wherever taken for the other
A tanker's own bunkers fall under CLC, not under the Bunker Convention, which surprises candidates who read the Bunker Convention as covering all fuel

blocks.h: 1. a) The human element, and how IMO and ILO divide the work

blocks.p: The starting point is the finding that drives the whole subject: the great majority of marine casualties originate in human performance rather than in equipment failure. Steel and machinery have become steadily more reliable; the people operating them have not changed. IMO's own framing of this is resolution A.947(23), Human element vision, principles and goals for the Organization, adopted on 27 November 2003, which commits the Organization to address the human element in all its work.
The two organisations divide the subject cleanly, and stating the division early is what turns limb a) from a list of conventions into an overview:

ul: IMO regulates the seafarer as the OPERATOR of a ship - is he competent, is he fit for duty, is the ship safely manned and safely managed?
The ILO regulates the seafarer as a WORKER - is he paid, housed, fed, rested, cared for when sick, and able to go home?

They interlock wherever working conditions become safety conditions, and hours of rest is the clearest example: it appears in STCW because a tired watchkeeper is dangerous, and in the MLC because excessive hours are an abuse of labour. The examiner's own words - "such as maritime labour and welfare" - point the answer squarely at that overlap.

blocks.h: 2. The IMO regime - competence, safe operation and fitness for duty

ul: STCW 1978 as amended is the competence instrument. The Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012, are the operative revision. Part A of the Code is mandatory and Part B is guidance, and the Part A tables set out, for each function, the competence, the knowledge understanding and proficiency, the methods of demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so certification rests on demonstrated competence, not on time served.

The Manila amendments added the human-element competences directly: leadership and teamworking, and engine-room and bridge resource management, together with alcohol limits for masters, officers and seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.

Fitness for duty - regulation I/9 medical fitness standards; regulation VIII/1 rest periods, expressly for the purpose of preventing fatigue; regulation VIII/2 watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

Quality and responsibility - regulation I/6 training and assessment, I/8 quality standards systems operated by Administrations and independently evaluated, I/11 revalidation, and I/14 the responsibilities of companies for valid certificates, familiarisation and documentation.

Safe manning - SOLAS regulation V/14, with the principles in resolution A.1047(27) of 30 November 2011. Manning is where competence meets workload, and an under-manned ship generates fatigue no rest table can cure.

The ISM Code, as amended through MSC.353(92), is the management layer: element 6 resources and personnel, element 7 shipboard operations, element 8 emergency preparedness and drills, and element 9 reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences - which is the feedback loop through which human error is supposed to be learned from rather than punished.

blocks.h: 3. The ILO regime - MLC 2006, the fourth pillar

ul: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 was adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference and consolidated a large body of earlier ILO maritime instruments into one. It is universally described as the fourth pillar of the international regime, standing beside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW.
Three parts. The Articles set out general obligations; the Regulations state the principle; and the Code gives effect to it in Part A Standards and Part B Guidelines.

Article VI is the provision to quote. The Regulations and Part A Standards are MANDATORY; Part B Guidelines must be given DUE CONSIDERATION. And Article VI.3 permits substantial equivalence - a Member may implement a Part A Standard differently provided the provision is substantially equivalent, which is what allows a single Convention to work across very different national systems.
Article IV states the seafarers' employment and social rights the Convention exists to secure, and the Convention is organised into five Titles.

blocks.h: 4. What the maritime labour and welfare regime actually requires

rows: Minimum requirements to work on a ship
Minimum age; medical certificate; training and qualification; regulated recruitment and placement, with no fee charged to the seafarer
The seafarers' employment agreement; wages; hours of work and hours of rest; leave; repatriation; manning levels; and the abandonment financial security
Accommodation and recreational facilities; food and catering provided free of charge and of appropriate quality and quantity
Health protection, medical care, welfare and social security
Medical care comparable to that available ashore; shipowners' liability; health and safety protection and accident prevention; access to shore-based welfare facilities; social security
Certification, inspection, port State control and complaint procedures - see the next section

ul: The provision to know precisely under Title 2 is Standard A2.3.5, which gives Members an election: either a maximum of 14 hours of work in any 24-hour period and 72 hours in any 7 days, or a minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7 days. In practice almost every flag adopts the rest-hours formulation, because it aligns with STCW.

Abandonment is worth a line, because it is the provision most often tested: a financial security certificate must be carried on board, and the support it must fund is defined - adequate food, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board and necessary medical care, together with outstanding wages and repatriation.

blocks.h: 5. Title 5 - what makes the labour regime enforceable

blocks.p: Title 5 is what distinguishes the MLC from earlier ILO conventions, which were rights without machinery. It borrows the enforcement architecture of the IMO conventions wholesale.

ul: A Maritime Labour Certificate, valid for not more than five years, with an intermediate inspection.

A Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance in two parts - Part I drawn up by the competent authority, listing the national requirements, and Part II by the shipowner, stating the measures adopted to meet them. Appendix A5-I lists the matters to be inspected and certified.

Port State control under Regulation 5.2.1, in which the certificate and the DMLC are accepted as prima facie evidence of compliance - so an inspection normally begins and ends with the documents, unless there are grounds to look further.
Onshore seafarer complaint-handling under Regulation 5.2.2, and on-board complaint procedures under Title 5 - a seafarer may complain without going through the master alone.

Article V.7 - no more favourable treatment. Ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified the Convention are not to be treated more favourably in the ports of a State that has. This is what gives the Convention practical universality.
Regulation 5.3 places responsibilities on labour-supplying States - which matters directly to India, as one of the world's largest suppliers of seafarers.

blocks.h: 6. Where the two organisations act jointly, and the state of the regime at this sitting

ul: Joint ILO/IMO Guidelines on the fair treatment of seafarers in the event of a maritime accident - a direct response to the criminalisation of seafarers after casualties.
Abandonment is handled jointly: the MLC financial security requirement on one side, and the joint ILO/IMO database on abandonment of seafarers on the other.
ILO Convention No. 185 on seafarers' identity documents, which underpins shore leave and transit.

The state of the MLC at this sitting must be stated carefully, and it is the discriminating temporal point of the whole question. The Convention is in force as amended through the 2018 amendments. A further set of amendments was adopted in 2022 - covering, among other things, the inclusion of social connectivity in the recreational facilities required on board, appropriately-sized personal protective equipment, and the facilitation of repatriation of the body or ashes of a seafarer who dies during a voyage. Those amendments are ADOPTED but NOT YET IN FORCE. They should be described as coming, not as required - and a candidate who states them as current obligations has made exactly the error the tacit-amendment procedure invites.

blocks.h: 7. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The instrument is MSC.1/Circ.1598, "Guidelines on fatigue", dated 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100 and superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. Two things about its status should be said at once: it is recommendatory, not mandatory, and it is guidance that sits on top of the mandatory rest-hour rules rather than replacing them.
It is arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party - which is itself the point, because fatigue cannot be managed by the seafarer alone:

ol: Module 1 - Fatigue. What it is, what causes it, and what it does. Causes are grouped as crew-specific factors (sleep and rest, body clock, health, stress), management factors ashore and on board, ship-specific factors (design, motion, noise, vibration, accommodation) and environmental factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods - which is the key idea, because it explains why a single good night does not repair a bad fortnight.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company. Manning levels, scheduling, workload, port turnaround, realistic planning, and a reporting culture in which a seafarer can say he is too tired.
Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer. Personal responsibility - sleep hygiene, use of off-watch time, diet, alcohol, caffeine, and recognising one's own symptoms.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training. Fatigue must be taught, because its symptoms are not obvious to the fatigued.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design. Accommodation location, noise and vibration, motion, lighting and habitability designed in from the start.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities. Safe manning determination, inspection of rest records, and the enforcement side.

blocks.h: 8. How the guidance and the mandatory rules fit together

blocks.p: This is where the two limbs of the question join, and it is the best place to finish.

ul: The mandatory layer is a prescriptive formula. STCW regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, expressly for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require watch systems arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The numbers: a minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period; daily rest divisible into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours; and no more than 14 hours between consecutive periods of rest. Where authorised exceptions apply, weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours, exceptions may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
MLC Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7 - hours of work and rest, entitlement to leave, and manning levels - run in parallel and to the same effect.

The central insight of the guidance is that compliance with the formula is not the same as being rested. Rest broken into two short periods against the body clock, in a noisy cabin, in heavy weather, at the end of a long tour, does not restore a seafarer the way an equal number of unbroken night hours would.

The practical consequence, and the sentence worth ending on: a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant and never breaches should be treated as a warning rather than a reassurance. Real operations are untidy; a perfect record usually means the record is being written to the rule rather than to the day.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints no marks against either limb, so you must judge the split. Limb a) asks for a broad overview of two regimes across labour and welfare; limb B) asks about one circular. A straight half-and-half would over-reward limb B, so give limb a) roughly two-thirds and limb B) one-third - but never omit limb B, because it is a named, finite instrument and is the easiest part of the question to score fully. Within limb a) the winning move is to state the IMO/ILO division of labour in the first three lines and then hang everything on it; a list of conventions without that frame reads as recall rather than overview. Finish by joining the limbs - the mandatory rest formula against the guidance - because the examiner has effectively set one question in two parts.

blocks.h: The division of labour - the sentence that frames limb a)

blocks.p: IMO regulates the seafarer as the operator of a ship; the ILO regulates him as a worker; and hours of rest is where the two meet. Rest appears in STCW because a tired watchkeeper is dangerous, and in the MLC because excessive hours are an abuse of labour. Note the examiner's own steer - "such as maritime labour and welfare" - which tells you the MLC side is expected to carry real weight, not just a mention.

blocks.h: The MLC at THIS sitting - the temporal discriminator

ul: The Convention is in force as amended through the 2018 amendments.

The 2022 amendments are ADOPTED but NOT IN FORCE. They cover, among other things, social connectivity as part of the recreational facilities required on board, appropriately-sized personal protective equipment, and facilitating repatriation of the body or ashes of a seafarer who dies during a voyage.

So mention them as coming, and never as current obligations. "Adopted but not yet in force" is a phrase that earns marks in itself, because it shows you know that the ILO, like IMO, amends by a procedure with a delay built into it.
This is the same adopted / accepted / in force distinction that Q1 on this paper turns on, in a different organisation. Two questions on one paper testing the same idea is not a coincidence.

blocks.h: The MLC architecture in four lines

ul: Articles, Regulations, Code - and the Code splits into Part A Standards (mandatory) and Part B Guidelines (due consideration). That is Article VI, and it is the single most quotable provision in the Convention.

Article VI.3 - substantial equivalence. A Member may implement a Standard differently if the provision is substantially equivalent. This is what makes one convention workable across very different legal systems.
Five Titles: 1 minimum requirements, 2 conditions of employment, 3 accommodation and food, 4 health and welfare, 5 compliance and enforcement.
Article V.7 - no more favourable treatment. Non-ratifying flags get no advantage in a ratifying State's ports. It is why the MLC bites almost universally.

blocks.h: The numbers you must have exactly right

ul: STCW A-VIII/1 and MLC Standard A2.3.5: 10 hours of rest in any 24 hours; 77 hours in any 7 days; no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours; no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods.
The MLC alternative formulation: maximum 14 hours of work in any 24 and 72 hours in any 7 days. Most flags adopt the rest-hours version.
Exceptions: weekly rest not below 70 hours; exceptions not for more than two consecutive weeks; daily rest then in no more than three periods.
Maritime Labour Certificate - not more than five years, with an intermediate inspection.
MSC.1/Circ.1598, dated 24 January 2019, six modules, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001.

blocks.h: The idea that earns the best marks in limb B

blocks.p: Compliance with the rest formula is not the same as being rested. The formula counts hours; fatigue is about the quality and timing of sleep. Ten hours split into two blocks, against the body clock, in a noisy cabin in heavy weather, at the end of a long tour, does not restore a person the way an unbroken night would - and sleep debt accumulates across consecutive days, which is precisely why the circular defines it. That is why the guidance is written in six modules addressed to six different parties: manning and scheduling are the Company's, ship design is the builder's and the owner's, and inspection is the Administration's. Fatigue is not something the watchkeeper can fix on his own.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Omitting limb B entirely, or giving it two lines. It is a named instrument and the easiest full marks in the question.
Treating limb a) as "list the conventions". Give the division of labour first.
Ignoring the words "such as maritime labour and welfare" and answering only on STCW.
Stating the 2022 MLC amendments as being in force. They are adopted and not yet in force at this sitting.
Saying Part B is mandatory. Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B Guidelines require due consideration.
Getting the rest numbers wrong, or quoting the work-hours formula and the rest-hours formula as though both applied at once - they are alternatives.
Saying MSC.1/Circ.1598 is mandatory. It is recommendatory; the mandatory layer is STCW chapter VIII and the MLC.
Forgetting Article V.7, no more favourable treatment, which is what makes the MLC effective against non-parties.
Omitting safe manning - fatigue that comes from too few people cannot be fixed by a rest table.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"Your rest records show full compliance every week for six months. Are you satisfied?" No - I would be suspicious. Real operations are untidy, and a record that never breaches usually means it is being written to the rule rather than to the day. I would look at port turnarounds, drills, surveys and unplanned work, and at whether the recorded rest was actually taken.

"Is the ILO fatigue circular binding?" There is no ILO fatigue circular - the guidance is IMO's, MSC.1/Circ.1598, and it is recommendatory. The binding layer is STCW chapter VIII and MLC Title 2.

"Must you provide internet access to the crew?" At this sitting, no - it is a Guideline, to be given due consideration, and the amendment strengthening the social-connectivity requirement is adopted but not yet in force.

"A seafarer complains and the master does nothing. What is his remedy?" The on-board complaint procedure, and then the onshore complaint-handling procedure under Regulation 5.2.2, through a port State control officer in any ratifying State's port.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: How do IMO and ILO divide the human element? IMO regulates the seafarer as operator, the ILO as worker; they meet on hours of rest.
Which IMO resolution frames the human element? A.947(23), adopted 27 November 2003.
What are the four pillars? SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and the MLC 2006.
What does Article VI provide? Part A Standards are mandatory, Part B Guidelines require due consideration.
What is substantial equivalence? Article VI.3 - implementing a Standard differently where the provision is substantially equivalent.
Name the five Titles. Minimum requirements; conditions of employment; accommodation and food; health, welfare and social security; compliance and enforcement.
What are the two parts of the DMLC? Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner.
What is no more favourable treatment? Article V.7 - non-ratifying flags get no advantage in a ratifying State's port.
Which circular gives the IMO fatigue guidance, and is it mandatory? MSC.1/Circ.1598 of 24 January 2019; recommendatory.
Define sleep debt. Insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
State the rest hours. Ten in any 24 and 77 in any 7 days, in no more than two periods one of at least six hours, with no more than 14 hours between.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Two limbs, two spines. Limb a) - OPERATOR versus WORKER (1), then IMO: competence, fitness, manning, management (2), then ILO: architecture (3), five Titles (4), enforcement (5), and joint work plus what is not yet in force (6). Limb B) - ONE CIRCULAR, SIX MODULES: F-C-S-T-D-A - Fatigue itself, the Company, the Seafarer, Training, ship Design, the Administration (7). Then join them: the formula counts hours; fatigue is about sleep (8).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: One evidence issue dominates this question and it was handled by exclusion rather than by avoidance. The corpus copy of the MLC is LATER than this sitting: it is the ILO consolidated text which says on its own title page that it includes the amendments of 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022. It was read for the architecture and for the Titles, which the 2022 layer does not disturb, and the 2022 additions were then identified provision by provision and excluded - social connectivity in the recreational facilities of Standard A3.1, appropriately-sized personal protective equipment in Standard A4.3, repatriation of the body or ashes under Standard A4.1, and the internet-access Guidelines. Each is recorded in this answer as adopted and not yet in force, which is what it was at this examination. MSC.1/Circ.1598 is not held by the corpus at all; its module structure, its definition of sleep debt and its supersession of MSC/Circ.1014 are carried through MIW internal records of two answers that trace it to a recorded full-text reading, and are labelled as such. Three smaller restraints are deliberate: no figure is given for the number of ILO instruments the MLC consolidated, because commonly quoted figures vary between sources; no party or ratification count is given for either the MLC or STCW, both being status facts that date; and no Indian implementing instrument is cited, since none is held and the printed question sets no Indian limb.

They entered into force on 23 DECEMBER 2024 - twenty months after this examination. The route donor QP2509-Q8 states in terms that they are in force and 'are simply the law at this sitting', which is correct for September 2025 and wrong here. quick_revision.recall_15s: THE FRAME (say this first). Most casualties originate in human performance, not equipment. IMO frames it through resolution A.947(23), adopted 27 November 2003. IMO regulates the seafarer as the OPERATOR of a ship; the ILO regulates him as a WORKER; and hours of rest is where the two meet - in STCW because a tired watchkeeper is dangerous, in the MLC because excessive hours are an abuse of labour. The stem's words 'such as maritime labour and welfare' point the answer at the MLC side. a) THE IMO REGIME. STCW 1978 as amended, Manila amendments in force 1 January 2012. Part A mandatory, Part B guidance; Part A tables give competence, KUP, methods of demonstrating and criteria for evaluating - certification on demonstrated competence, not time served. Manila added leadership and teamworking, bridge and engine-room resource management, and alcohol limits. Fitness: reg I/9 medical standards, reg VIII/1 rest periods for the purpose of preventing fatigue, reg VIII/2 watchkeeping. Quality and responsibility: I/6 training and assessment, I/8 quality standards independently evaluated, I/11 revalidation, I/14 company responsibility. Safe manning - SOLAS V/14 with resolution A.1047(27) (30 November 2011). ISM Code (as amended through MSC.353(92)) elements 6 resources, 7 shipboard operations, 8 emergency preparedness, 9 reports and analysis. a) THE ILO REGIME - MLC 2006, the FOURTH PILLAR beside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW, adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session. Three parts: Articles, Regulations, Code. ARTICLE VI - Regulations and Part A Standards are MANDATORY; Part B Guidelines given DUE CONSIDERATION. Article VI.3 substantial equivalence. Article IV rights. FIVE TITLES: 1 minimum requirements (minimum age, medical certificate, training, recruitment with NO fee to the seafarer); 2 conditions of employment (SEA, wages, hours of work or rest, leave, repatriation, manning, abandonment financial security); 3 accommodation, recreation, food and catering free of charge; 4 medical care comparable to that ashore, shipowner liability, health and safety, welfare, social security; 5 compliance and enforcement. Standard A2.3.5 ELECTION: either max 14 hours work in 24 and 72 in 7 days, or min 10 hours rest in 24 and 77 in 7 days - most flags take the rest version. Abandonment support defined: adequate food, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board and necessary medical care, plus outstanding wages and repatriation. TITLE 5 - the enforcement machinery: Maritime Labour Certificate, not more than 5 years, with an intermediate inspection; DMLC Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner; Appendix A5-I lists the matters; Reg 5.2.1 port State control, certificate and DMLC as prima facie evidence; Reg 5.2.2 onshore complaint handling; ARTICLE V.7 NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT; Reg 5.3 labour-supplying States (bears directly on India). JOINT WORK: ILO/IMO fair treatment of seafarers guidelines; the joint abandonment database; ILO Convention No. 185 identity documents. STATE OF THE MLC AT THIS SITTING - the temporal mark: in force as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2022 amendments are ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE - social connectivity in recreational facilities, appropriately-sized PPE, and facilitating repatriation of the body or ashes of a seafarer who dies on a voyage. Describe them as coming, never as current. B) THE IMO FATIGUE GUIDANCE. MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. RECOMMENDATORY, not mandatory. SIX MODULES: 1 Fatigue - causes grouped as crew-specific, management, ship-specific and environmental, and SLEEP DEBT defined as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods; 2 the Company - manning, scheduling, workload, port turnaround, reporting culture; 3 the Seafarer - sleep hygiene, diet, alcohol, caffeine, self-recognition; 4 Awareness and Training; 5 Ship Design - accommodation location, noise, vibration, motion, lighting; 6 the Administration and Port State Authorities. HOW IT JOINS THE MANDATORY LAYER: STCW reg VIII/1 requires rest periods expressly for the purpose of preventing fatigue, per section A-VIII/1: 10 hours in any 24, 77 hours in any 7 days, no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, no more than 14 hours between. Exceptions: not below 70 hours weekly, not more than two consecutive weeks, then up to three periods. MLC Regs 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7 run in parallel. THE KEY IDEA: compliance with the formula is not the same as being rested - broken rest against the body clock, in noise and motion, does not restore a person, and sleep debt accumulates. So treat an always-exactly-compliant rest record as a WARNING, not a reassurance.

questions.understand_first: Two different organisations look after the people on ships, and they look at the same person for different reasons. One is interested in whether he can do the job safely - is he trained, is he fit, are there enough of him, is the ship run properly. The other is interested in whether he is being treated decently - paid, fed, housed, given time off, looked after when he is ill, and brought home at the end. For most purposes those are separate concerns, but there is one place where they become the same question, and that is how much sleep he gets. Too little sleep is both a working condition and a safety hazard, which is why the same limits appear in two entirely different rulebooks. The second half of the question is about the deeper problem behind those limits: they are written as arithmetic, so many hours in so many hours, and arithmetic cannot capture what actually restores a person. Sleep taken in two broken pieces at the wrong time of day, in a noisy cabin, in a ship that is moving, after weeks of the same, leaves someone tired even though the paperwork says he has had his entitlement. So the guidance is addressed not only to the tired person but to everyone whose decisions made him tired - the office that set the schedule, the designer who put the cabin over the engine room, and the inspector who reads the record.
questions.memory_cue: Two limbs, two spines. Limb a): OPERATOR versus WORKER (1), then IMO competence, fitness, manning and management (2), then the MLC architecture (3), the five Titles (4), the enforcement machinery (5), and joint work plus what is not yet in force (6). Limb B): one circular, SIX MODULES - F-C-S-T-D-A - Fatigue itself, the Company, the Seafarer, Training, ship Design, the Administration (7). Then join them: the formula counts hours, fatigue is about sleep (8).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the human element and fatigue question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The human element and how IMO and ILO divide the work. 2 The IMO regime - competence, fitness and manning. 3 The ILO regime - MLC architecture. 4 What the Titles require. 5 Title 5 enforcement. 6 Joint work and the state of the regime at this sitting. 7 The IMO fatigue guidance. 8 How the guidance and the mandatory rest rules fit together.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb a) needs six sections because it covers two regimes; limb B) needs two, one for the circular and one to join it to the mandatory layer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do IMO and ILO divide the human element between them?
retrieval_cards.answer: IMO regulates the seafarer as the operator of a ship - competence, fitness for duty, safe manning and safe management. The ILO regulates him as a worker - wages, hours, accommodation, food, medical care and repatriation. The two interlock wherever working conditions become safety conditions, and hours of rest is the clearest example, appearing in STCW because a tired watchkeeper is dangerous and in the MLC because excessive hours are an abuse of labour.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the frame that turns a list of conventions into the overview the question asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does MLC Article VI provide, and what is substantial equivalence?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Regulations and the provisions of Part A of the Code are mandatory; the provisions of Part B are to be given due consideration. Article VI.3 permits substantial equivalence - a Member may implement a Part A Standard through a different provision, provided that provision is substantially equivalent, which is what allows one Convention to operate across very different national systems.
retrieval_cards.why: The most quotable provision in the Convention, and saying Part B is mandatory is a straightforward error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the MLC 2022 amendments in force at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They are adopted but not yet in force. They cover, among other things, the inclusion of social connectivity in the recreational facilities required on board, appropriately-sized personal protective equipment, and the facilitation of repatriation of the body or ashes of a seafarer who dies during a voyage. They should be described as coming, not as current obligations.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the discriminating temporal fact of the question, and the same adopted-not-in-force distinction that Q1 on this paper turns on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the hours of rest, and the alternative formulation.
retrieval_cards.answer: Minimum ten hours of rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any seven-day period; daily rest divisible into no more than two periods, one of which must be at least six hours; and no more than 14 hours between consecutive periods of rest. MLC Standard A2.3.5 allows a Member to elect instead a maximum of 14 hours of work in any 24 and 72 hours in any seven days.
retrieval_cards.why: The two formulations are alternatives, not cumulative, and most flags adopt the rest-hours version because it aligns with STCW.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes the MLC enforceable, under Title 5?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Maritime Labour Certificate valid for not more than five years with an intermediate inspection; a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance with Part I drawn up by the competent authority and Part II by the shipowner; Appendix A5-I listing the matters to be inspected; port State control under Regulation 5.2.1 where the certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence; onshore complaint handling under Regulation 5.2.2; and Article V.7, no more favourable treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: Title 5 is what distinguishes the MLC from earlier ILO conventions, which conferred rights without machinery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which circular gives the IMO fatigue guidance, and what is its status?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', dated 24 January 2019 and approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - it sits on top of the mandatory rest-hour rules in STCW chapter VIII and MLC Title 2 rather than replacing them.
retrieval_cards.why: Both halves are marks - the identity of the instrument, and the fact that it is guidance rather than requirement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the six modules of the fatigue guidelines.
retrieval_cards.answer: Module 1 Fatigue; Module 2 Fatigue and the Company; Module 3 Fatigue and the Seafarer; Module 4 Fatigue Awareness and Training; Module 5 Fatigue and Ship Design; Module 6 Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Six modules addressed to six different parties is itself the argument - fatigue cannot be managed by the watchkeeper alone.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is sleep debt, and why does the definition matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods. It matters because it explains why a single good night does not repair a bad fortnight, and therefore why a rest record that satisfies the daily formula every day can still leave a seafarer seriously impaired.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the concept that connects the guidance to the criticism of the prescriptive formula.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The rest records show full compliance every week for six months. Are you satisfied?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - that should be treated as a warning rather than a reassurance. Real operations are untidy, with port turnarounds, drills, surveys and unplanned work, so a record that never breaches usually means it is being written to the rule rather than to the day. Check whether the recorded rest was actually taken, and look at manning and scheduling rather than at the record alone.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the practical judgement the whole of limb B is building towards, and it is a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is 'no more favourable treatment' and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article V.7 of the MLC provides that ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified the Convention are not to be treated more favourably in the ports of a State that has. It gives the Convention practical universality, because a non-ratifying flag confers no commercial advantage once the ship calls at a ratifying State's port.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the mechanism by which a labour convention achieves the reach of a safety convention, and it is easily forgotten.

blocks.h: 1. What a classification society is, and its two distinct roles

blocks.p: Open by separating the two hats, because almost every confusion in this subject comes from merging them.

ul: The classification role is private and contractual. The society publishes its own rules, and it assigns and maintains class to a ship built and kept in accordance with them. Its contract is with the owner. Nothing in that role is delegated by anybody.

The statutory role is delegated. Acting as a recognized organization under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code, the society surveys and certifies on behalf of a flag Administration - the load line, the safety construction and equipment certificates, and so on.

The distinction that earns the mark: the Administration transfers the work, not the responsibility. It remains answerable for the ship's compliance, and the RO Code exists to govern how it authorises, oversees and monitors the organisation acting for it.

blocks.h: 2. How class rules are made

blocks.p: The stem asks specifically about rule formation, which most answers skip. Class rules are not written from theory alone; they are an empirical body of knowledge fed by the fleet the society surveys.

ul: Service experience and defect returns. The society surveys thousands of ships and records what cracks, wastes, buckles and fails. That feedback is the largest single input, and it is why a society with a large surveyed fleet has better rules.
Casualty investigation. Structural losses drive rule change directly - which is how bulk carrier hold and hatch requirements, and side-shell and fore-end strengthening, came about.
Research and direct calculation. Finite element analysis, fatigue assessment, model testing and full-scale measurement, increasingly replacing empirical formulae with direct strength assessment.
Technical committees of members, owners, builders, underwriters and Administrations, which subject a draft rule to the people who will have to build and live with it.

Harmonisation between societies - the unified requirements, unified interpretations and procedural requirements of the international association of classification societies, and the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers, which removed the incentive to compete by lowering scantlings.

blocks.h: 3. What the rules actually cover

blocks.p: Take the three headings the examiner printed, in his order:

rows: Scantlings, hull girder strength, local strength, buckling and fatigue, corrosion additions and allowable diminution, close-up survey and thickness measurement requirements, and the loading manual and loading instrument
Main and auxiliary machinery, shafting and propellers, boilers and pressure vessels, piping systems, steering gear, refrigeration, and the type approval of components and materials
Generation and distribution, short-circuit and discrimination studies, essential and emergency services, cabling and protection, high-voltage installations, and hazardous-area equipment

blocks.h: 4. Implementation through the ship's life

blocks.p: The stem names three phases, so answer them as three phases.

ul: Design. Plan approval against the rules, direct strength and fatigue calculation where required, and type approval of equipment before it is ever ordered.

Construction. Material and component certification, welder and welding procedure qualification, non-destructive examination, survey during fabrication and erection, and tank, pressure and sea trials. The class certificate is issued on completion.

Maintenance - the whole of the ship's service life. The periodical survey cycle: annual, intermediate, renewal or special survey on a five-year cycle, together with docking or bottom surveys, tailshaft and boiler surveys. For bulk carriers and oil tankers the enhanced survey programme under the ESP Code adds close-up survey and thickness measurement.

The mechanisms that keep it honest. Continuous survey and approved planned maintenance schemes spread the work; a condition of class or recommendation records a defect that must be rectified by a date; and class may be suspended or withdrawn. That last point leads directly into limb a)'s closing question.

blocks.h: 5. Why compliance is NOW mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1

blocks.p: The word to explain is "now". For most of its history SOLAS contained no scantling rules at all. It required subdivision, stability, fire protection and life-saving appliances, but it never told a builder how thick a plate should be. That work was done by class rules, which meant class was technically indispensable but legally optional - a ship could in principle comply with SOLAS while her classification had lapsed.
Regulation II-1/3-1 closed that gap. Its words are worth reproducing, because the whole answer to this half of the limb is in them:

In addition to the requirements contained elsewhere in the present regulations, ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society which is recognized by the Administration in accordance with the provisions of regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety.
Five things follow from that sentence, and each of them is a mark:

ul: It makes class rules a SOLAS obligation. Compliance with a private rulebook becomes compliance with the Convention - so loss or suspension of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance, inspectable and detainable by port State control. That, in one sentence, is why the reference is there.
Note the three verbs - designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED. The obligation is continuing. It is not discharged at delivery, which is exactly the point an examiner is looking for.

Note the alternative - applicable national standards providing an equivalent level of safety. The regulation does not compel classification as such; it compels compliance with a recognized society's rules or with an equivalent national standard, which preserves the Administration's ultimate authority.
Note the link to XI-1/1, which is what makes "recognized" mean something, and behind it the RO Code and the Administration's duty of oversight.

And note where the logic ended up. Regulation II-1/3-10, goal-based ship construction standards, goes one step further for bulk carriers and oil tankers: the society's own rules are themselves verified against IMO goals and functional requirements. SOLAS first made the rules mandatory, then began auditing the rules.

blocks.h: 6. The harmonized system, and where these surveys sit

ul: The harmonized system of survey and certification was introduced by the 1988 SOLAS Protocol and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol, and extended to the MARPOL Annexes. Its object is simple: before it, each certificate ran on its own cycle with its own dates, so a ship was surveyed almost continuously and never conveniently.

What harmonisation actually did: a common five-year certificate cycle; a common anniversary date for all certificates; a three-month window before or after each anniversary in which a survey may be held without moving the anniversary; the ability to combine surveys in one attendance; and a common set of survey types.

The IMO Survey Guidelines under the HSSC give the detailed items for each survey. They are recommendatory, revised by the Assembly roughly every two years, and the edition in circulation at this sitting is the 32nd Assembly edition. The survey types themselves, however, are created by SOLAS chapter I - not by the guidelines - which is why the answer below is taken from the Convention.

blocks.h: 7. Annual versus periodical - the difference

blocks.p: This is where marks are won or lost, because the two words are widely used loosely and SOLAS uses them precisely. Both are intermediate checkpoints between renewal surveys, but they attach to different certificates and run on different intervals.

rows: Cargo Ship Safety Construction and Safety Equipment certificates (and the MARPOL and Load Line certificates in the harmonized scheme)
Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Safety Radio certificates only
Within 3 months before or after EACH anniversary date
Equipment: within 3 months before or after the SECOND or THIRD anniversary date. Radio: within 3 months before or after EACH anniversary date
For equipment it takes the place of one of the annual surveys. For radio there is no annual survey at all - the periodical occupies that position
A general inspection, to confirm the ship has been maintained in accordance with regulation 11(a) and remains fit for her service
A fuller inspection of the equipment, to confirm it complies with the requirements, is in satisfactory condition and is fit for service

ul: Two further points complete the picture. On the construction certificate the mid-cycle deepening is called an intermediate survey, not a periodical one - within three months before or after the second or third anniversary, again taking the place of one of the annual surveys. And the same regulation requires a minimum of two inspections of the outside of the ship's bottom in any five-year period, with no more than 36 months between them.

Endorsement. The intermediate, annual and bottom inspections are endorsed on the certificate, and the radio periodical surveys are endorsed on the Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate. That endorsement is what a port State control officer actually looks at.
One tidy way to remember the whole scheme: ANNUAL is the yearly baseline; PERIODICAL is the deeper mid-term check that displaces an annual - except on radio, where it IS the yearly check.

blocks.h: 8. Annual versus periodical - the relevance

blocks.p: The stem asks for relevance as well as difference, so give the reasoning rather than only the schedule.

ul: A five-year certificate needs mid-cycle checkpoints to remain credible. Without them the certificate would assert a condition established up to five years earlier. The graded ladder - annual, then periodical or intermediate, then renewal - keeps a live statement of condition behind the paper.

Survey depth is matched to the rate at which things deteriorate. Structure wastes slowly and predictably, so it can be checked generally each year and thoroughly at the mid-point and at renewal. Equipment is consumed rather than worn - liferafts, extinguishers, immersion suits, pyrotechnics all have service lives and expiry dates - so it needs a fuller look sooner.

Radio is treated most strictly of all, and for a good reason. It gets a periodical survey at every anniversary rather than a general annual look, because distress communication can degrade invisibly - a battery, an EPIRB or an antenna may look perfect and be useless, and the failure is only discovered at the one moment it cannot be tolerated.

Harmonisation is what makes the ladder practical. Common anniversary dates and a common three-month window let the annual, the periodical and the intermediate be taken in a single attendance, so the ship is surveyed thoroughly without being taken out of service repeatedly. That is the direct answer to the words "toward harmonized survey and certification system".

And the whole scheme rests on regulation 11. The condition of the ship is to be maintained between surveys, no change is to be made after survey without the Administration's sanction, and defects are to be reported at the earliest opportunity. The surveys verify maintenance; they are not a substitute for it - which is the same continuing obligation that II-1/3-1 imposes in limb a), and the neatest way to tie the two limbs of this question together.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints no marks against either limb, so treat them as of comparable weight - and note that later sittings of this same question print 10 and 6, while the December sitting prints 8 and 8. Neither split is printed here, so do not import one. Limb a) contains two separate demands - the role of class in rule formation and implementation, and then why compliance is now mentioned in SOLAS - and candidates routinely answer the first and forget the second, which is the more interesting half. Limb b) is a definitional comparison, and the safest way to score it is a table: the two words are used loosely in the industry and precisely in SOLAS, and the marks are in the precision.

blocks.h: The two hats - state them first

ul: Classification - private, contractual, the society's own rules, its own certificate, contracted with the owner.
Statutory work as a recognized organization - delegated by a flag Administration under SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code.
The Administration delegates the work, not the responsibility. That one sentence separates a strong answer from an average one.

blocks.h: The word to explain in limb a) is 'NOW'

blocks.p: SOLAS historically contained no scantling rules - it dealt with subdivision, stability, fire and life-saving, but never told a builder how thick a plate should be. Class rules filled that space, which left class technically indispensable but legally optional. Regulation II-1/3-1 made compliance with a recognized society's structural, mechanical and electrical rules - or an equivalent national standard - a SOLAS requirement. The consequence is the mark: loss or suspension of class became a SOLAS non-compliance, inspectable and detainable by port State control. And the three verbs matter - designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED - so the obligation is continuing and is not discharged at delivery.

blocks.h: Where the logic went next - worth one sentence

blocks.p: Regulation II-1/3-10, goal-based ship construction standards for bulk carriers and oil tankers, went a step further: the society's own rules are verified against IMO goals and functional requirements. SOLAS first made class rules mandatory, and then began auditing the rules themselves. One sentence on this shows you understand the direction of travel; a paragraph on it is answering a different question.

blocks.h: Annual versus periodical - the precision that earns the limb

ul: ANNUAL - within 3 months before or after EACH anniversary, on the construction and equipment certificates. A general inspection confirming the ship has been maintained.

PERIODICAL - only on equipment and radio. On equipment, within 3 months before or after the SECOND or THIRD anniversary, and it takes the place of one of the annual surveys. On radio, within 3 months before or after EVERY anniversary - and there is no annual radio survey at all.
INTERMEDIATE - the equivalent mid-term deepening on the construction certificate, at the second or third anniversary, also taking the place of an annual.
Plus two bottom inspections in any five years, no more than 36 months apart.
The one-line summary: annual is the yearly baseline; periodical is the deeper mid-term check that displaces an annual - except on radio, where it IS the yearly check.

blocks.h: Why radio is treated most strictly - the best single point in limb b)

blocks.p: Radio gets a periodical survey at every anniversary rather than a general annual look because distress communication degrades invisibly. A battery, an EPIRB, an antenna or a power supply can look entirely serviceable and be useless, and the failure is discovered at the one moment when it cannot be tolerated. Structure, by contrast, wastes slowly and visibly, and equipment is consumed - liferafts, extinguishers, immersion suits and pyrotechnics have service lives and expiry dates. Survey depth is matched to the rate and the visibility of deterioration, and saying that explicitly is what turns a schedule into an explanation.

blocks.h: What harmonisation actually changed

ul: Introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to the MARPOL Annexes.
Common five-year cycle, common anniversary date across certificates, a three-month window either side of the anniversary, and combinable surveys.
Before it, each certificate ran on its own dates, so a ship was surveyed almost continuously and never conveniently.

The IMO Survey Guidelines under the HSSC give the item lists. They are recommendatory and are revised by the Assembly roughly every two years - but the survey types themselves come from SOLAS chapter I, not from the guidelines, so quote the Convention if you want to be safe.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering only the first half of limb a) and never explaining why SOLAS mentions class rules.
Saying the Administration delegates its responsibility to the society. It delegates the work.
Merging the class and statutory roles into one.
Using annual and periodical interchangeably, or applying periodical to the construction certificate - there the mid-term survey is intermediate.
Forgetting that the radio certificate has no annual survey.
Forgetting that a periodical or intermediate survey takes the place of one of the annual surveys rather than being additional to it.
Omitting the three-month window, or saying it moves the anniversary date. It does not.
Reciting the schedule without giving the relevance, which is half of limb b).
Quoting a survey-guidelines resolution number when the Convention is the safer and more accurate authority.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

blocks.p:
"Is a ship that has lost class still SOLAS-compliant?" No. Regulation II-1/3-1 requires her to be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with a recognized society's rules, or an equivalent national standard - so loss of class is a SOLAS non-compliance and is inspectable and detainable by port State control.

"When is the periodical survey of the safety equipment certificate due?" Within three months before or after the second or third anniversary date, and it takes the place of one of the annual surveys.

"And of the radio certificate?" Within three months before or after each anniversary - there is no separate annual radio survey.

"Your annual survey window is closing and the ship is at sea. What happens?" The survey must be completed within the three-month window either side of the anniversary; missing it invalidates the endorsement. The window does not extend and the anniversary does not move.

"If class rules are private, how can SOLAS require them?" Because II-1/3-1 requires compliance with the rules of a society recognized by the Administration under XI-1/1, or with equivalent national standards - so the Administration retains authority over whose rules count.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What are the two roles of a classification society? Private classification under its own rules, and delegated statutory work as a recognized organization.
Which SOLAS regulation governs recognition? XI-1/1, with the RO Code.

What does II-1/3-1 require? That ships be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a recognized society, or equivalent national standards.
What is the effect of losing class? It becomes a SOLAS non-compliance.
What feeds class rule development? Service experience and defect returns, casualty investigation, research and direct calculation, technical committees, and harmonisation between societies.
Which certificates carry a periodical survey? Safety equipment and safety radio only.
When is the equipment periodical due? At the second or third anniversary, replacing one annual survey.
When is the radio periodical due? At every anniversary; there is no annual radio survey.
What is the survey window? Three months before or after the anniversary date.
How many bottom inspections in five years? A minimum of two, no more than 36 months apart.
What introduced the harmonized system? The 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols.

blocks.p: Limb a) - TWO HATS, THREE INPUTS, THREE PHASES, ONE REGULATION: the two hats (1), how rules are made (2), what they cover under the printed headings (3), design-construction-maintenance (4), and II-1/3-1 with its three verbs (5). Limb b) - HARMONISE, DIFFER, EXPLAIN: what harmonisation did (6), the difference in a table (7), and the relevance - credibility, deterioration rate, radio, one attendance (8).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This answer is unusually well evidenced, and the reason is worth stating. Every provision it relies on was read verbatim in the MIW corpus: regulation II-1/3-1 in full, and chapter I regulations 8, 9, 10 and 11 in full - which means the survey types, intervals and anniversary windows in limb b) come from the Convention itself rather than from a guidelines resolution. That is deliberate. The operative HSSC survey guidelines are NOT held - the corpus holds only their later successor - so the guidelines are named without any content being asserted from them, and the answer is anchored on SOLAS, which is both held and, being a Convention rather than a recommendation, the stronger authority in any event. One direction-of-travel check is recorded: the corpus SOLAS base is the Consolidated Edition 2024, fifteen months later than this sitting, so each provision consumed was checked against the amendment register and against the filed post-2024 amendment resolutions, and none of them touches II-1/3-1 or chapter I. Three restraints are deliberate: no classification society is named and no society's rules are cited, because that adds nothing to the marks and invites error; no scantling, diminution percentage or acceptance criterion is quoted, since those are society- and edition-specific and none is held; and the passenger-ship survey regime is not set out, because the printed question concerns annual and periodical surveys, which are cargo-ship terms.

quick_revision.recall_15s: a) TWO HATS FIRST. A classification society has two entirely separate roles: CLASSIFICATION - private and contractual, its own rules, its own certificate, contracted with the owner; and STATUTORY WORK - delegated by a flag Administration, acting as a RECOGNIZED ORGANIZATION under SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code (mandatory from 1 January 2015). The Administration transfers the WORK, not the RESPONSIBILITY. HOW RULES ARE MADE (the part most answers skip): service experience and defect returns from the surveyed fleet - the largest single input; casualty investigation; research and direct calculation - finite element analysis, fatigue assessment, model and full-scale testing; technical committees of members, owners, builders, underwriters and Administrations; and harmonisation between societies - unified requirements, unified interpretations, procedural requirements, and the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers. WHAT THEY COVER, in the examiner's three headings: STRUCTURAL - scantlings, hull girder and local strength, buckling, fatigue, corrosion additions and allowable diminution, loading manual and instrument; MECHANICAL - main and auxiliary machinery, shafting and propellers, boilers and pressure vessels, piping, steering gear, type approval; ELECTRICAL - generation and distribution, discrimination, essential and emergency services, high voltage, hazardous areas. IMPLEMENTATION IN THREE PHASES: DESIGN - plan approval, direct calculation, type approval; CONSTRUCTION - material and component certification, welder and welding procedure qualification, NDE, tank, pressure and sea trials; MAINTENANCE - the five-year cycle of annual, intermediate, renewal, plus docking, tailshaft and boiler surveys, with the ESP Code (A.1049(27)) adding close-up survey and thickness measurement for bulk carriers and tankers. Kept honest by continuous survey, planned maintenance schemes, conditions of class, and suspension or withdrawal. WHY 'NOW' IN SOLAS ch.II-1 - the key half of limb a). SOLAS never contained scantling rules; it covered subdivision, stability, fire and life-saving but never told a builder how thick a plate should be. So class was technically indispensable but LEGALLY OPTIONAL. Regulation II-1/3-1 closed the gap: ships shall be DESIGNED, CONSTRUCTED AND MAINTAINED in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society RECOGNIZED by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an EQUIVALENT LEVEL OF SAFETY. Consequences: loss or suspension of class becomes a SOLAS NON-COMPLIANCE, inspectable and detainable by port State control; the three verbs make the duty continuing, not discharged at delivery; and the alternative preserves the Administration's authority. Then note where it went: II-1/3-10 goal-based standards verify the society's own rules against IMO goals - SOLAS first made the rules mandatory, then began auditing them. b) HARMONISATION. Introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to the MARPOL Annexes: common five-year cycle, common anniversary dates, a THREE-MONTH WINDOW either side of the anniversary (which does not move the anniversary), and combinable surveys in one attendance. The IMO Survey Guidelines under the HSSC give the item lists and are RECOMMENDATORY; the survey TYPES come from SOLAS chapter I. ANNUAL v PERIODICAL - the precision: ANNUAL - on the Construction and Equipment certificates, within 3 months before or after EACH anniversary; a GENERAL INSPECTION confirming the ship has been maintained under regulation 11(a). PERIODICAL - on Equipment and Radio ONLY. Equipment: within 3 months before or after the SECOND or THIRD anniversary, and it TAKES THE PLACE OF ONE OF THE ANNUAL SURVEYS. Radio: within 3 months before or after EVERY anniversary - and there is NO ANNUAL RADIO SURVEY AT ALL. On the Construction certificate the mid-term deepening is called INTERMEDIATE (second or third anniversary, also replacing an annual), and the same regulation requires a minimum of TWO BOTTOM INSPECTIONS in any five-year period, no more than 36 MONTHS apart. All are ENDORSED ON the certificate. One-line summary: annual is the yearly baseline; periodical is the deeper mid-term check that displaces an annual - EXCEPT on radio, where it IS the yearly check. RELEVANCE: a five-year certificate needs mid-cycle checkpoints to stay credible; survey depth is matched to the rate and visibility of deterioration - structure wastes slowly and visibly, equipment is CONSUMED (liferafts, extinguishers, immersion suits, pyrotechnics have service lives and expiry dates); radio is checked hardest because distress communication degrades INVISIBLY and is discovered useless at the one moment it cannot be tolerated; harmonisation lets annual, periodical and intermediate be taken in ONE attendance, which is the direct answer to 'toward harmonized survey and certification system'; and regulation 11 ties both limbs together - the surveys VERIFY maintenance, they do not substitute for it.

The stem asks for the role of class in rule formation and implementation AND for why compliance is now mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1 - and the second demand is the more interesting one. The answer is that SOLAS never contained scantling rules, so class was indispensable but legally optional until regulation II-1/3-1 made compliance with a recognized society's rules (or equivalent national standards) a Convention requirement, with the consequence that loss of class became a SOLAS non-compliance.
