questions.understand_first: For most of its life the international safety convention did not say how strong a ship had to be. It said a great deal about lifeboats, fire doors and watertight compartments, but nothing about the thickness of a deck plate or the sizing of a shaft. That work had always been done by private organisations which grew out of the insurance market: they wrote their own rulebooks, inspected ships against them, and told underwriters whether a vessel was fit to insure. The odd result was that the most important technical requirements a ship had to meet were, strictly speaking, voluntary - a matter of contract between an owner and a private body. What changed is that the convention began to point at those private rulebooks and say, in effect, comply with these. That single move turned a commercial arrangement into a legal obligation, so a ship that quietly lost her standing with her society was no longer merely uninsurable but non-compliant, and could be stopped in port. The second half of the question is about the rhythm of checking. A certificate lasting five years is only as good as what happens in between, so there is a ladder of inspections of increasing depth - and the interesting detail is that the ladder is not uniform, because different things go wrong at different speeds and with different visibility.
questions.memory_cue: Limb a): TWO HATS (1), how rules are made (2), what they cover (3), three phases (4), one regulation with three verbs (5). Limb b): what harmonisation did (6), the difference in a table (7), the relevance - credibility, deterioration rate, radio, one attendance (8).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the classification societies and surveys question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The two roles of a classification society. 2 How class rules are made. 3 What the rules cover. 4 Implementation through design, construction and maintenance. 5 Why compliance is now mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1. 6 The harmonized system. 7 Annual versus periodical - the difference. 8 Annual versus periodical - the relevance.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb a) has two demands and limb b) has two - difference and relevance - so eight sections keep all four in view.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two roles of a classification society?
retrieval_cards.answer: Classification is private and contractual - the society publishes its own rules and assigns and maintains class under a contract with the owner. Statutory work is delegated - acting as a recognized organization under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code, the society surveys and certifies on behalf of a flag Administration. The Administration transfers the work, not the responsibility.
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two roles is the root of most confusion in this subject, and the work-not-responsibility line is a reliable mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are class rules developed?
retrieval_cards.answer: From service experience and defect returns across the society's surveyed fleet, which is the largest single input; from casualty investigation, which drives rule change directly; from research and direct calculation including finite element analysis and fatigue assessment; through technical committees of members, owners, builders, underwriters and Administrations; and by harmonisation between societies through unified requirements and interpretations and the Common Structural Rules.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks about rule formation specifically, and it is the part of limb a) most answers skip entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 require, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognized by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety. It matters because it turns compliance with a private rulebook into a Convention obligation, so loss or suspension of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance inspectable and detainable by port State control.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the whole answer to the second demand of limb a), and the three verbs make the obligation continuing rather than discharged at delivery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the word 'now' in the question significant?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOLAS historically contained no scantling rules at all - it dealt with subdivision, stability, fire protection and life-saving but never with how thick a plate should be. Class rules filled that space, which left class technically indispensable but legally optional. Regulation II-1/3-1 is what changed that, and the examiner's 'now' is pointing at the change.
retrieval_cards.why: Explaining the word 'now' is what turns a description of class into an answer to the question actually asked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish annual from periodical surveys.
retrieval_cards.answer: The annual survey applies to the safety construction and safety equipment certificates and falls within three months before or after each anniversary date; it is a general inspection confirming that the ship has been maintained. The periodical survey exists only on the safety equipment and safety radio certificates. On equipment it falls at the second or third anniversary and takes the place of one of the annual surveys; on radio it falls at every anniversary and there is no annual radio survey at all.
retrieval_cards.why: The two words are used loosely in practice and precisely in SOLAS, and the marks are entirely in the precision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is there a periodical survey on the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. On the construction certificate the mid-term deepening is called an intermediate survey, falling within three months before or after the second or third anniversary date and taking the place of one of the annual surveys. The same regulation also requires a minimum of two inspections of the outside of the ship's bottom in any five-year period, with no more than 36 months between them.
retrieval_cards.why: Applying 'periodical' to the construction certificate is the single commonest error in this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the radio installation surveyed at every anniversary?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because distress communication degrades invisibly. A battery, an EPIRB, an antenna or a power supply can appear entirely serviceable and be useless, and the failure would be discovered only at the one moment when it cannot be tolerated. Structure wastes slowly and visibly, and equipment is consumed with service lives and expiry dates, so survey depth is matched to the rate and visibility of deterioration.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts the schedule into a reason, which is what the 'relevance' half of limb b) is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the harmonized system of survey and certification actually change?
retrieval_cards.answer: Introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to the MARPOL Annexes, it gave all certificates a common five-year cycle and a common anniversary date, allowed surveys to be held within a three-month window either side of the anniversary without moving it, and allowed surveys to be combined in a single attendance. Before it, each certificate ran on its own dates and the ship was surveyed almost continuously.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem's phrase 'toward harmonized survey and certification system' is asking exactly this, and the one-attendance point is the practical answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the survey window, and does it move the anniversary?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three months before or after the anniversary date. It does not move the anniversary - the window is an allowance for holding the survey, not a re-dating of the certificate, so missing it invalidates the endorsement rather than shifting the cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely assume a late survey resets the dates, which would defeat the whole point of a harmonized cycle.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does regulation 11 add, and how does it link the two limbs?
retrieval_cards.answer: It requires that the condition of the ship and its equipment be maintained to conform with the regulations between surveys, that no change be made after a survey without the Administration's sanction, and that accidents or defects affecting safety be reported at the earliest opportunity. It links the limbs because it makes the same point as II-1/3-1's word 'maintained' - the surveys verify maintenance, they do not substitute for it.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sentence that turns two separate limbs into one coherent answer, which is worth a mark on its own.

reverify_before_publication.claim: SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 and chapter I regulations 8, 9, 10 and 11, including every survey type, interval and anniversary window stated in limb b)
reverify_before_publication.why: All read VERBATIM in the corpus at 319524c. The corpus SOLAS base is the Consolidated Edition 2024, fifteen months later than this sitting, so each provision was checked against the corpus amendment register and against the filed post-2024 amendment resolutions - MSC.520(106), MSC.532(107), MSC.550(108), MSC.557(108) - and none touches any of them. II-1/3-1 has been unamended since 1 July 2002. The 2024 text therefore states the April 2023 position.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the operative HSSC Survey Guidelines at this sitting are the 32nd Assembly edition, A.1156(32), and that A.1186(33) does not appear
reverify_before_publication.why: A.1186(33) was adopted on 6 December 2023, eight months after this examination, and revoked its predecessor from that date. known_traps.md Entry 22 records the current edition as A.1207(34), which is two Assembly cycles in this paper's future - the register is inverted here by 32 months. The operative edition is NAMED but NO CONTENT IS ASSERTED FROM IT, because it is not held; limb b) is anchored on SOLAS chapter I instead. A reviewer should treat any appearance of A.1186(33) or A.1207(34) as a forward-contamination defect.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The rule-formation and class-practice material in limb a) - the development inputs, the unified requirements and the Common Structural Rules
reverify_before_publication.why: Declared established class and industry practice, carried through the MIW record of the same-year donor QP2312-Q8. No society's rules are held by the corpus and none is cited. No classification society is named anywhere, and no scantling, diminution percentage or acceptance criterion is quoted.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The absence of any imported mark split between the two limbs
reverify_before_publication.why: This source copy prints NO marks, where the December 2023 sitting prints 8 and 8 and three later sittings print 10 and 6. Neither split is imported; the limbs are treated as of comparable weight and the question is recorded at 16 with marks null on both. Treat the appearance of either split as a transcription regression.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two printed limbs, each containing two demands - which is why candidates lose marks by answering half of each. Limb a) asks for the ROLE of classification societies in rule formation and implementation across design, construction and maintenance, AND for an explanation of why compliance with those rules is NOW mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1; the second demand is the analytical one and turns on the word 'now'. Limb b) asks for the DIFFERENCE between annual and periodical surveys AND for their RELEVANCE to the harmonized system; the difference is definitional and the relevance is reasoning.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, and this source copy prints NO allocation against either limb - unlike every other sitting of the question MIW holds, which print either 8/8 or 10/6. Neither is imported. The two limbs are treated as of comparable weight, with limb a) given five sections because it carries two substantial demands and limb b) three.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb a): the class and statutory roles separated, with the Administration delegating work and not responsibility; a real account of how rules are made rather than only what they contain; coverage under the three printed headings; implementation across the three named phases including the survey cycle and conditions of class; and, decisively, regulation II-1/3-1 quoted or closely paraphrased with the consequence that loss of class is a SOLAS non-compliance. For limb b): the precise distinction between annual and periodical with the certificates each attaches to and the anniversary intervals, the fact that a periodical replaces an annual and that radio has no annual at all, and then the reasoning - certificate credibility, deterioration rate, invisible degradation of radio, and the single attendance harmonisation permits.
primary_source_plan: Read SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 VERBATIM from the corpus - the whole of limb a)'s second demand turns on its exact words
Read SOLAS chapter I regulations 8, 9 and 10 VERBATIM, because the survey types are created there and not in any guidelines resolution
Read regulation 11 as well, because it supplies the sentence that joins the two limbs
Check the direction of travel: the corpus SOLAS is the 2024 consolidated edition, so verify against the amendment register that no provision consumed was amended between the sitting and 1 July 2024
Establish which HSSC survey guidelines edition is operative at April 2023 BEFORE writing limb b), and confirm the corpus holds only the later one
Anchor limb b) on the Convention rather than on the guidelines, which removes the Assembly boundary from the critical path
Sweep the same-year donor for content later than April 2023, with particular attention to Assembly resolutions
Apply known_traps.md Entries 22 and 29 with their direction checked for this sitting
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - concentrated in limb b) and resolved by choosing a better anchor. The HSSC survey guidelines are revised by the Assembly roughly every two years and the register records an edition two cycles in this paper's future, so a present-day reference would supply the wrong resolution. That risk is removed by taking the survey architecture from SOLAS chapter I, which is held, verbatim, and unamended. Limb a) carries almost no risk: II-1/3-1 has been unamended since 2002 and the RO Code and ESP Code both pre-date the sitting by years.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the question is wholly international, no Indian statute is engaged, and the maritime administration is not named, so neither the Merchant Shipping Act boundary nor the DG Shipping naming question arises.
technical_ambiguities: 'Periodical' is used loosely in industry practice for any recurring survey, and precisely in SOLAS for a survey type that exists only on two certificates

The mid-term survey is called INTERMEDIATE on the construction certificate and PERIODICAL on the equipment certificate, although both fall at the second or third anniversary and both replace an annual
The radio certificate has no annual survey at all, which breaks the pattern candidates expect
The three-month window is an allowance for holding the survey and does NOT move the anniversary date
Class rules are private and contractual yet mandatory through SOLAS, which reads as a contradiction and is not
'Recognized organization' and 'classification society' are not synonyms - the first is a role conferred by an Administration
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Open limb a) by separating the two roles in three bullets, then how rules are made, then a table of what they cover under the examiner's three headings, then implementation across the three named phases. Give the 'now' question its own section, quote regulation II-1/3-1, and draw out the three verbs, the equivalent-national-standards alternative, the port State control consequence and the onward move to goal-based standards. Open limb b) with what harmonisation actually changed, then give the annual/periodical distinction as a table with certificates, timing, relationship and depth, adding the intermediate survey and the bottom inspections. Close on relevance - certificate credibility, deterioration rate, why radio is hardest, the single attendance, and regulation 11 tying both limbs together.
